articles.title: Ian Huntley killed by inmate in ‘cold-blooded murder’ planned weeks in advance, court told
articles.summary:
Jurors hear Anthony Russell killed Soham murderer by hitting him repeatedly over head with metal bar

A prisoner killed the Soham murderer Ian Huntley with a heavy metal bar in a…
articles.byline: Mark Brown North of England correspondent

blocks.text: A prisoner killed the Soham murderer Ian Huntley with a heavy metal bar in a “cold-blooded” attack that had been planned weeks in advance, a court heard.
Jurors were told that Anthony Russell, 44, repeatedly hit the 52-year-old over the head in the attack at the high-security HMP Frankland, near Durham.

Matthew Bean KC, prosecuting, told jurors at Newcastle crown court that they may feel no sympathy for the Soham killer, who murdered Holly Wells and Jessica Chapman in 2002, but the case was not about his “appalling actions” but the manner in which he had died.
Russell denies a single count of murder.

Bean said: “At shortly after 9am on 26 February 2026, the prosecution say that the defendant in this trial, Anthony Russell, murdered Ian Huntley, by striking him repeatedly to the head with a heavy metal bar. The prosecution case is that this was a cold-blooded murder that had been planned weeks in advance of its execution.
“It happened in a prison, HMP Frankland, where both Anthony Russell and Ian Huntley were serving prisoners. At the time, both men were serving sentences of life imprisonment for offences of murder.

“The defendant, Anthony Russell, you will hear, had previously been convicted of the murder of three people, these offences having taken place in October 2020. The name of the man he killed, Ian Huntley, will be known to many, if not all of you.

“He had been convicted of the murder of two girls, Holly Wells and Jessica Chapman, that took place in the village of Soham in Cambridgeshire in August 2002. These were offences that, for entirely understandable reasons, aroused feelings of disgust and anger.
“Due to the nature of his offences, you may feel little or no sympathy for what happened to him. More than that, the prosecution do not ask for sympathy.

“Ultimately, this case is not about the appalling actions of Ian Huntley during his life, but the manner of his death. The prosecution well understands the emotions that may be stirred during this trial.

“It is essential, however, to be true to your oath or affirmation, to put emotion to one side, to try this case on the evidence and the evidence alone, and to come to verdicts based on that evidence.”
Bean told jurors the two murderers were held on A wing at the high security prison and there had been “tension” between them in the months leading up to the killing.
About a year earlier, in March 2025, prison staff witnessed an argument between them in which they threatened one another and had to be separated.
They later agreed with staff that nothing further would happen, the court heard.
About 10 months later, Russell was seen with a black eye, and told staff he had fallen.
Bean said: “Some members of staff believed, however, that someone had assaulted him and you will hear some evidence during the trial that indicates that it may have been caused by Ian Huntley.”
Those incidents were the only two issues between the men in the prison records, the court heard.
The trial continues.

articles.title: Germany taking seriously reports Russia may be planning to launch nuclear weapons in to space
articles.summary:
Move would be breach of Outer Space treaty and Partial Nuclear Test Ban treaty, which prohibit placing of nuclear weapons in orbit

The German government has said it is taking very seriously…

blocks.text: The German government has said it is taking very seriously reports that Russia may be planning to launch a satellite armed with a ⁠nuclear weapon ⁠into ​space later this year.

The move – if confirmed – would be a breach of 1967 Outer Space treaty of which Moscow is a signatory as well the 1963 Partial Nuclear Test Ban treaty – which prohibit the placing of nuclear weapons in Earth’s orbit and test detonations in space.

The reports by a group of German media outlets reported, based on what they said were assessments by western intelligence agencies, come amid a recent rise in concern over the increasing militarisation of space which had the US Air Force secretary, Troy Meink, admit for the first time in September that Washington had deployed “on-orbit space control weapons”.

Germany’s Bundesnachrichtendienst (BND) intelligence service and armed forces have exchanged ⁠intelligence showing that a Russian satellite, named Sputnik-S, ​was assembled several ‌years ago ‌and is stationed in the Moscow region, ‌a report by broadcasters NDR and WDR, and newspaper Sueddeutsche Zeitung said.
According to the reports, warnings in early November said the satellite could be launched within 60 days and would be operational shortly afterwards.

“No, we haven’t seen ‌the report. But there are so many ‘alleged’ ​and ‘possible’ claims in it, attributed to who knows whom, that ⁠it’s certainly hardly worth ​taking ​them seriously,” Kremlin spokesperson ​Dmitry Peskov told ​reporters.

The Russian Embassy in Berlin said it was not aware of any such plans describing the reports as “unfounded allegations regarding the space activities of the Russian Federation” and calling them “part of a propaganda campaign”.
Moscow’s space measures, the embassy added, proceed “in accordance with international obligations” and serve “exclusively peaceful purposes”.

In 2024, Russia denied assertions by ​US officials that Moscow was developing a weapon that could destroy enemy satellites by setting off a nuclear explosion in ⁠space and triggering an electromagnetic pulse (EMP) to disable the electronic systems of nearby satellites.

US officials have alleged that Russia ​has ​for years been developing ​a nuclear weapon capable of ​destroying ‌entire satellite networks, ​such ​as SpaceX’s vast Starlink internet system that Ukrainian troops have been using.
Concern has been mounting in recent years in Europe and the US that Russia has been seeking to develop an anti-satellite weapon system which experts believe would probably employ an EMP wave.

Two years ago, Russian president Vladimir Putin denied the claim after then US president Joe Biden’s national security spokesperson John Kirby confirmed that the Russian Federation had been developing a “troubling” anti-satellite weapon.
“We’re not talking about a weapon that can be used to attack human beings or cause physical destruction here on Earth,” Kirby said.
Biden told reporters in 2024 that he believed Russia was developing the “capacity to launch a system into space that could theoretically do something that was damaging … my hope is it will not”.

While EMPs can occur naturally, it has long been understood that nuclear detonation has the ability to harm electronic systems, including energy networks, with both the US and Russia conducting high altitude tests in the early 1960s.

There has been increasing discussion over fears that Russia may be planning to place a nuclear weapon in space. Germany’s top military space commander earlier this year said he cannot rule out that Russia is working on technology to place a nuclear warhead in space, warning that such a move could cripple satellite services and make parts of the orbit unusable for decades.

“At the very top end of escalation, there is the suspicion that Russia may be working on technology to place a nuclear explosive device in orbit,” Maj Gen Michael Traut, commander of the German Space Command, said in an interview with Politico.

Asked whether he considered that realistic, Traut said: “I cannot rule it out.” He added that a nuclear detonation in space could impact up to a third of satellites in low Earth orbit with massive global consequences.

Suspicions over Russia’s ambitions to place weapons in space were given fresh scrutiny in 2022 with the launch of the Kosmos 2553 test satellite, which US and intelligence sources suggested could be a dummy run for the deployment of a nuclear weapon in space.

articles.title: Nvidia reinstates former CEO Jensen Huang despite China espionage scandal
articles.summary: Nvidia's board voted unanimously to bring back the disgraced CEO, who resigned this month amid news of his affairs. He's suspected of having had a relationship with a Chinese intelligence asset.

image.caption: Jensen Huang stepped down earlier this month sending shares in the chip giant into sharp declineImage: Soeren Stache/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: US tech company Nvidia said on Monday that it had resinstated Jensen Huang as its CNvidiaEO "effective immediately."
This follows just a matter of days after his resignation after admitting to extramarital affairs, reportedly including a dalliance with a woman who was a Chinese intelligence asset.
The board unanimously decided that his return was in the "best interests of the company," Nvidia said, adding that it was satisfied that Huang had demonstrated his "candor and ability to lead."
The decision was announced as trading started for the new week in New York.

The stock price of what investors deem the world's most valuable company has nosedived amid the scandal, with Nvidia's stock price falling from almost $220 (roughly €200) per share in late October to around $125 per share at the end of last week.

articles.title: Jensen Huang reinstated as Nvidia CEO
articles.summary: Chipmaker reverses decision it made to remove chief executive after reports of affairs including with alleged Chinese spy

blocks.text: Nvidia has said it is reinstating Jensen Huang as chief executive, effective immediately, just weeks after his dramatic resignation after reports of extramarital affairs including with an alleged Chinese spy.
Nvidia shares surged on the news, jumping more than 25% in premarket trading.
The tech company’s move to bring Huang back marks a sharp reversal from its board’s decision just days earlier to rule out his return.
Huang built Nvidia from a video-game chip designer into the dominant supplier of AI processors, steering its roadmap, customer deals and Washington ties along the way.
He resigned on 12 November after revelations of extramarital affairs, including one with a businesswoman US authorities suspect of spying for China, an allegation Beijing denies.
The board said it was satisfied with Huang’s candour and leadership ability and, after receiving input from senior US government officials, saw no national security risk in his return.

Donald Trump called for Huang’s reinstatement overnight, posting on Truth Social: “I hope the Board of Nvidia rehires Jensen Huang. It would be the best thing for the Company, and also, for the U.S.A. President DONALD J. TRUMP.”

articles.title: U.S. futures climb as technology recovers from brutal sell-off last week
articles.summary: U.S. stock market futures are gaining this morning, following last week's steep sell-off driven by heavy losses for artificial intelligence and technology stocks.

image.caption: AI-related stocks including Nvidia, Broadcom and Advanced Micro Devices bore the brunt of the selling on Friday. (Evan Mitsui)

blocks.text: Business·New
U.S. stock market futures are gaining this morning, following last week's steep sell-off driven by heavy losses for artificial intelligence and technology stocks.
AI-related stocks like Nvidia, Broadcom and Advanced Micro Devices bore the brunt of the selling on Friday
U.S. futures are rising as the technology sector looks to rebound following a brutal sell-off of artificial intelligence stocks last week.
Futures for the S&P 500 gained 2.9 per cent on Monday, while those for the Dow Jones Industrial Average added 2.1 per cent. Nasdaq futures climbed 3.6 per cent.

AI-related stocks including Nvidia, Broadcom and Advanced Micro Devices bore the brunt of the selling on Friday, but all three rose sharply before the market opened Monday. Nvidia's stock surged 8.2 per cent in premarket trading, while shares of Advanced Micro Devices rose 4.3 per cent. Broadcom's stock climbed 5.5 per cent.
Anthropic, maker of the Claude AI tool, coming off a successful IPO Thursday, gained 4.2 per cent before the market open.
Shares of AI companies have been under pressure in recent weeks with some believing that the massive company valuations and heavy spending are unjustified.

CrowdStrike announced that it is buying Zscaler in a $44 billion US, all-stock deal in a major consolidation of the cybersecurity sector on Monday. Shares of CrowdStrike declined 7.4 per cent on Monday, while Zscaler's shares jumped 18.6 per cent.

"We view this as the clearest signal yet that cybersecurity is consolidating into a handful of platforms, with the AI era forcing the hand of vendors who had been content to partner," said Dan Ives, a financial analyst at Yorkville Ives & Co.
What's behind Wall Street's huge tech stock sell-off
The U.S. stock market will be closed on Thursday for Thanksgiving, with a shortened trading day on Friday.
Yet there will be a number of economic indicators this week that will capture a lot of attention.
The U.S. Conference Board will release its consumer confidence index on Tuesday.

On Wednesday, the U.S. Commerce Department reports on consumer spending and inflation for October. In September, the Federal Reserve's preferred measurement for inflation, the personal consumption expenditures price index, came in at 3.1 per cent.

The department also issues its second estimate for U.S. economic growth during the third quarter Wednesday. The first estimate found growth of 3.4 per cent from July through September, driven by strong consumer spending and investment in artificial intelligence.
That outpaced second-quarter growth of 2.2 per cent.
Oil prices drip lower

Oil prices fell on Monday, as a recovery in supply continued to help offset concerns even as the U.S. and Iran have yet to reach a permanent deal over the war. Analysts are expecting oil and fuel prices to fall further as global supply stabilizes, which could help ease some inflationary pressures.

Brent crude oil, the international standard, dropped 1.9 per cent to $90.83 US per barrel, but that's still well above the roughly $72 US a barrel in late February before the start of the war. Benchmark U.S. crude slid 1.7 per cent to $82 US per barrel.

In Europe, Britain's FTSE 100 was up 0.6 per cent to 10,411.63. France's CAC 40 rose 0.7 per cent to 7,981.21, while Germany's DAX advanced 0.8 per cent to 25,017.10. Markets in Tokyo were closed for a holiday while other Asian markets were lower.
The U.S. dollar rose to 159.08 Japanese yen from 158.62 yen. The euro slipped to $1.0963 US from $1.10973 US.

articles.title: Cayetano wants to let ‘generous’ Filipinos cover gov’t debt. Any takers?
articles.summary: 'If I want to be a good citizen and pay my share, P170,000, where do I go?' Cayetano asks, apparently keen to 'go beyond' paying his taxes to help settle the national debt

blocks.text: ALAN CAYETANO. Senator Alan Peter Cayetano gestures during a press conference concerning Senator Ronald 'Bato' dela Rosa, who is wanted by the International Criminal Court and who has reportedly fled, a day after gunfire rang out at the Senate, on May 14, 2026.
Noel Celis/Reuters
'If I want to be a good citizen and pay my share, P170,000, where do I go?' Cayetano asks, apparently keen to 'go beyond' paying his taxes to help settle the national debt

items: Senator Alan Peter Cayetano proposes a mechanism for individual taxpayers to contribute their share of the national debt, calculated at over P170,000 per Filipino.

During Senate discussions, Cayetano expressed his desire to pay this amount directly, highlighting a historical example from South Korea's 1997 financial crisis where citizens contributed gold to help their country.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
Senator Alan Peter Cayetano is concerned about the national debt.
So concerned, in fact, that he wants the government to set up a mechanism so that even you — yes, you, individual taxpayer — can directly pay your share of more than P170,000.

That’s P170,598.03, to be exact, which Cayetano calculated as each Filipino’s share of the country’s enormous debt. It’s not money you owe or any citizen personally owes the government, of course, but if you’re feeling particularly generous, the senator thinks you should have a way to chip in. Are you game?
During Senate deliberations on the proposed 2027 budget, Cayetano asked economic officials where exactly he could hand over his contribution.
“If I want to be a good citizen and I want to pay my share, P170,000, where do I go?” he asked.

blocks.caption: Cayetano wants to let ‘generous’ Filipinos cover gov’t debt. Any takers?

blocks.text: For a moment, Senator JV Ejercito, who chairs the Senate finance committee, seemed perplexed. He grinned, turned to the economic team for help, and suggested that perhaps the best contribution Filipinos could make was simply to pay the right taxes.
“That’s not true because I’m already paying the right taxes. I want to go beyond that,” Cayetano responded. “I want to pay my P170,000 — and you won’t accept it?”
The senator went on to paint a vision of how wealthy businessmen might wish to pay for themselves and their families.
“What if they’re feeling generous, and they have one or two kasambahay and they want to pay for it?” he added.
Even overseas Filipino workers might contribute smaller amounts over time — a few hundred dollars here and there, he imagined.
And if you’re wondering where this sudden wave of generosity might come from, Cayetano made an appeal to divine intervention.

“If we pray but we do not act, the Bible says faith without action is dead. So we cannot keep praying for a miracle without doing anything to open the door for that miracle,” he said, hoping the government would pave the way for a little divine intervention and a flood of donations.

blocks.caption: Escudero calls out fire effect in Sara Duterte trial livestream

blocks.text: As unusual as the proposal sounds, Cayetano does reference a historical example.

During the 1997 Asian financial crisis, millions of South Koreans famously gathered their gold jewelry to help their country overcome a severe foreign currency shortage. Around 3.51 million citizens contributed some 227 metric tons of gold, either donated or sold, to raise much-needed dollars.
Of course, South Korea’s campaign was about easing a foreign currency crisis, rather than paying off government debt, and it was only one part of the country’s economic recovery.
“Why can’t it happen to us?” Cayetano asked.
“If our debt were low and our debt payments were small, I wouldn’t be proposing that we bayanihan our way out,” he added in Filipino.

Of course, the good senator’s proposal, however well-intentioned, takes a few liberties with how national debt actually works. But let’s indulge the thought experiment. Can Filipinos really bayanihan their way out of debt?

Philippine government debt had reached P19.66 trillion as of end-September and is projected to reach P21.48 trillion by end-2027. Even if one million generous Filipinos each contributed P170,000, that would raise P170 billion, less than 1% of the projected debt.
Interest payments alone are programmed to reach P1.114 trillion next year, eating up more than 15% of the proposed P7.2-trillion national budget.
Economists previously told Rappler that the country’s debt remains manageable for now, although its rising size and cost are becoming concerning, especially as economic growth slows.

And besides, even Cayetano himself acknowledged what is perhaps the bigger problem with his proposal. Why would Filipinos voluntarily give the government more money when so many already distrust how it spends what they pay in taxes?
“The sentiment now is that everyone in government is a thief, that you’re all thieves, that we’re all thieves, and that no one wants to donate,” he said in a mix of English and Filipino.

And with a sitting vice president on trial for unexplained wealth, a proposed national budget riddled with red flags — roads whose coordinates lead straight into the sea and an overabundance of multi-purpose buildings — who exactly would be lining up to fork over another P170,000? – Rappler.com

articles.title: Plant-based lunches could cut Australia’s emissions by 15m tonnes, new research shows
articles.summary:
Nationwide change in lunch habits could cut more climate pollution than grounding every domestic flight

  • Get our

blocks.text: Australians could collectively cut climate pollution by more than 15m tonnes – more than grounding every domestic flight – simply by changing what they eat for lunch.

A nationwide shift to plant-based lunches could reduce food-related emissions by 29% – 15.4m tonnes per year – while saving the average household about $611 annually, according to a report by Bryant Research and not-for-profit ProVeg.

Nadia Schilling, the executive director of ProVeg Australia, said the findings highlighted the “huge difference” that relatively modest changes, like a meat-free Monday or a plant-based lunch, could make.
That might mean opting for a black bean burrito, a poke bowl with tofu, or a lunchbox with hummus and fresh vegetables – instead of a cheese and ham wrap – she said.
“We realise that Australians aren’t going to change their diets overnight,” Schilling said. “This is a really practical change where everyone wins. Lunch is a huge missed opportunity.”

Australia has the highest per capita food-related emissions in the world, the report found. It modelled the environmental, health and economic impacts for a range of Australia-wide dietary changes, finding the shift to 100% plant-based meals would cut dietary emissions by two-thirds, while just switching lunches would cut nearly one-third.
Emissions from domestic aviation are about 10m tonnes a year, according to government data.

The organisations behind the report, which promote moving from meat to plant-rich foods and alternative protein sources, called for a national campaign to increase vegetable consumption along with policy and funding support for plant proteins.
Almost one-third of global greenhouse gas emissions are connected to the global food system through land clearing, raising animals, growing crops, processing, packaging, transport and waste.

The National Health and Medical Research Council (NHMRC) is reviewing the evidence about sustainability and diet as part of the first update of Australian dietary guidelines in more than 13 years. Draft guidelines are expected to be released for public consultation in December 2026.

An NHMRC spokesperson said the expert committee drafting the new guidelines had prioritised information on health impacts, but “information about the economic, social, and environmental sustainability of diets was then considered as one of the many factors that influence people’s ability to follow a healthy diet”.

Dr Diana Bogueva, who researches food sustainability at Curtin University, said relatively small changes in everyday eating habits – when adopted by a large number of people – could have a major impact on the environmental footprint of food production.
after newsletter promotion
However, Bogueva, who was not involved with the report, said the environmental, health and affordability benefits of eating less meat depended on what foods replaced it.

Whole foods like legumes, grains, vegetables, nuts and seeds provided valuable fibre, vitamins, minerals and plant proteins, she said. “But not every plant-based product is automatically healthy,” Bogueva said. “Simply swapping meat for highly processed products does not necessarily improve the nutritional quality of the meal.”
Sustainable eating didn’t have to be expensive, she added, and some of the most nutritious sources of plant protein – such as beans, lentils and chickpeas – were also among the most affordable.

“We do know there are both health and environmental benefits if you reduce red and processed meat in your diet,” said Alexandra Jones, an associate professor at the George Institute for Global Health, who was not involved with the report.
But rather than focusing on swapping out one protein for another, the emphasis should be on “helping people eat more vegetables, legumes and minimally processed plant foods,” she said.
A good lunch could be as simple as an “old-school salad sandwich” on wholegrain bread, with lettuce, tomato, sprouts and beetroot.

articles.title: Domestic violence perpetrators are misusing smart car features to abuse, researchers warn
articles.summary:
Exclusive: Alarming report reveals how tracking and monitoring functions and digital key access have been used to facilitate abuse

  • Get our

blocks.text: Earlier this year a man in Australia was found guilty of using a connected car app to harass his former partner, including restricting the speed at which she could drive, sometimes to 40km an hour.

In 2022 in the US, a woman found her former husband had used a car app associated with her car to track her; the carmaker then allegedly refused to terminate the former partner’s digital access to the vehicle.
In another case in the US in 2020, a woman found a baseball bat her former partner had used to threaten her in the back seat of her car.

These three cases form part of an alarming report by University of New South Wales researchers, released on Tuesday, which warned this was an emerging problem that could get worse. It found smart car functions that could be misused by perpetrators of domestic violence to facilitate abuse were prevalent across major car brands.

“There is an urgent need for carmakers to adopt safety by design principles from the early stages of designing both the apps and the cars,” said the report co-author Katharine Kemp, a data privacy and consumer protection expert at UNSW.

The researchers found that problems emerged as many of the cars’ functions – which include tracking and monitoring functions, remote control functions and digital key access – could be controlled remotely via an app.

The researchers said that there were three main scenarios that could open the functions to misuse: the abuser being the owner of the car and having created the account themselves; they were granted access as a secondary user of the car; or the victim survivor is impersonated and the perpetrator creates an account on their behalf.
The report said that the problematic functions are mainly marketed by the car manufacturers as being for the purpose of enabling the car owner to “keep an eye on” and protect their car.
It highlighted an advertisement on the carmaker Kia’s Australian website for “Kia Connect”. Kia was contacted for comment.

“Kia Connect is also bundled with geofence and time fencing alerts which let the owner know when another user strays outside preset limits of geographical areas or time limitations. It’s a perfect feature for anyone dealing with a family member who is borrowing the car,” the advertisement said.
The report mapped how prevalent potentially problematic functions were, and whether these functions were advertised by 15 of the top car brands.

One of the functions raised was geolocation, which allows the geographical location of the car in real-time or when it is parked, and was advertised by 100% of the 15 car brands, with some marketing it as “Vehicle Tracking”, “Vehicle Locator” or “Find My Car”. The researchers said this tool could be misused to track people.

The researchers found that 60% of the top 15 brands also advertised a “zone exit alert” which allows users to set an alarm if a car leaves a designated area. They warned this functions could be used to: “Set a zone of 3km from the family home to receive alert if the victim-survivor attempts to leave or fails to follow abuser’s rules limiting travel by the victim-survivor.”
Meanwhile, 20% advertise speed or acceleration restrictions. The explanation of this function by carmakers includes that it is to set speed limits for young drivers or valet parkers.
But the report warned this could be misused to set a speed limit of 40km/h so that a victim survivor cannot safely use highways or escape at speed.

The researchers also raised concerns about digital key access, which allows drivers to use their mobile phone to unlock the car or start the engine and was advertised by 67% of car brands in the Australian market. The report warns: “This function may also allow an abuser to remotely terminate or severely restrict the victim survivor’s ability to use the vehicle.

“An abuser can achieve this, for example, by remotely deactivating the victim-survivor’s digital key access or setting speed restrictions on the vehicle. This could effectively strand the victim-survivor in an unsafe location and/or limit the victim survivor’s ability to escape the abuser’s violence,” the report said.
after newsletter promotion
‘Almost no accountability’ for manufacturers
Emma Buxton-Namisnyk, a co-author of the report, warned this was an emerging problem that could get worse.

“There’s really not a widespread understanding about how these technologies can be misused,” she said, adding that there was “almost no accountability” for car manufacturers to limit potential misuses.

The report recommended carmakers adopt principles which consider at the design phase how a function could be misused to facilitate abuse, and help determine if a function should not be offered because the risks outweigh the benefits.

Last year the eSafety commissioner, Julie Inman Grant, raised the alarm on the issue after receiving reports from frontline workers that cars were being used to monitor and track victim-survivors of domestic violence.
She called for improved industry safeguards, noting that it was estimated that more than 90% of new cars sold in Australia by 2031 would have embedded connectivity.
“We need urgent action to make them safer,” Inman Grant said.

The minister for social services, Tanya Plibersek, said in a statement to Guardian Australia that the government was considering what more it could do to crack down on the risk posed by smart devices, after developing a support service on technology-facilitated abuse that helps frontline workers navigate the issue.
“We’re seeing new frontiers of family and domestic violence emerge every day – we’ve seen smart fridges, cat feeders and electric vehicles all being weaponised to stalk, control and harm,” she said.
“We’ll consider what more we can do as we finalise our Second Action Plan to End Violence Against Women and Children.”

articles.title: Over 100 writers from PEN America to form splinter group over Gaza tensions
articles.summary:
Members of the free-expression literary and human rights group are forming a new chapter called PEN Writes US

More than 100 well-known writers and members of the literary world are to form…

blocks.text: More than 100 well-known writers and members of the literary world are to form a splinter chapter of PEN America, the free-expression literary and human rights group, over tensions within the organization over Israel’s war in Gaza and other issues.

Writers including Ta-Nehisi Coates, M Gessen and Jacqueline Woodson are among those who on Monday announced they are forming a new group called PEN Writes US that will be “guided by the PEN Charter’s vision of ‘one humanity, living in peace and equality in one world’”.

The group describes itself as an “aspiring PEN chapter founded by writers, translators, artists, editors, agents, and booksellers” from all over the US. The group says it is supported by PEN International while it aims “to build a new home for writers committed to free expression, and their range of backgrounds, languages, and perspectives is our greatest strength”.

“We seek to join more than 140 PEN Centers worldwide (and the many that have coexisted in the United States) in mobilizing writers at every stage of their career to defend free expression, support writers and artists at risk, and champion reading, translation, and literature,” it added.
PEN America told the Associated Press that it remains focused on “defending free expression as a universal right that must be protected regardless of viewpoint”.

Novelist Maaza Mengiste told the outlet that the new group does not seek to be a rival of PEN America and will probably share common ground about fighting censorship and oppression and encouraging discussions among writers.

Mengiste said that PEN Writes will differ in its structure and in some of its priorities, ideally becoming “a center where sustained and equal advocacy for all writers guides principles, rather than institutional caution”.

The formation of PEN Writes comes as PEN America has faced criticism from numerous writers and activists who say they are unhappy with the latter group’s response to Israel’s war in Gaza. Critics argue that PEN America has been reluctant to criticize Israel or to defend the rights of Palestinian writers with the same force it has advocated for writers elsewhere.

“I think there’s been a feeling for quite a while that PEN’s response to the war in Gaza has been inadequate,” says PEN Writes member Francine Prose, a former president of PEN America, according to the AP.
Fallout from the war in Gaza led PEN America to call off its annual awards show and World Voices festival in 2024 because so many participants dropped out.

Those events resumed. But in June, Dinaw Mengestu resigned as PEN America president after PEN published a report about obstacles and harassment faced by Israeli and Jewish writers since Israel began waging war in Gaza in 2023 in the wake of the 7 October attacks by Hamas that year.

Mengestu, a prize-winning novelist who is now a member of PEN Writes, at the time cited the report’s criticism of cultural boycotts. He expressed support for the Palestinian-led boycott, divestment and sanctions movement, or BDS.

Organizers advocated for economic and cultural pressure on Israel to end the country’s occupation of territories captured in the 1967 Middle East war, grant full equality to Arab citizens of Israel and promote the rights of Palestinian refugees to return.

PEN America says it “emphatically opposes any efforts to inhibit the free international exchange of literature, art, information, or knowledge, including academic and cultural boycotts”. The group says it also defends the rights of individuals to “be protected from retaliatory efforts” for participating in boycotts.
Mengiste told the AP that PEN Writes takes a broader view, supporting boycotts themselves.

In July, in the aftermath of Mengestu’s departure, PEN America issued a statement citing such initiatives as its direction of $500,000 in emergency aid to Palestinians in Gaza, its legal support for a pro-Palestinian activist threatened with deportation by Donald Trump’s administration, and a 2025 PEN report entitled All That Is Lost: The Cultural Destruction of Gaza.

The new group is aiming for recognition at the PEN International Congress in Montenegro in September 2027. The process includes forming a steering committee, establishing communication with the PEN International secretariat and “seeking interest from the full diversity of writers” in a given country, according to PEN International’s guidelines.

Other prominent members of PEN Writes include Pulitzer prize winner Percival Everett, literary agent Nicole Aragi and novelist Hannah Lillith Assadi, who on Wednesday won the National Book Award for fiction.
Mengiste said PEN Writes aims to be effective as a more stripped-down, egalitarian organization run entirely by writers on behalf of writers.

“I think writers know first-hand what self-censorship or lost contracts or de-platforming looks like,” she told the AP. “We know that what comes for one writer will very likely come for others. We are guardians of each other as much as we are stewards of literature. We do not work with a writers organization, we ARE writers, organized and mobilized to defend all writers.”
The Associated Press contributed reporting

articles.title: ‘Pervert glasses’ named word of the year by Macquarie dictionary, ahead of ‘nudify’ and ‘AI;DR’
articles.summary:
Australian dictionary’s committee of word experts says winning term is ‘a succinct reflection of the state of the world in 2026’

  • Get our

blocks.text: The backlash to “pervert glasses” has been swift and severe.

Smartglasses such as Meta’s Ray-Bans, which have built-in cameras, microphones, and AI assistants have been banned at some Australian swimming pools and playgrounds, and condemned as a possible invasion of privacy.
There are widespread fears about the glasses being used to film people, especially women, without their consent, and the resulting footage being posted on social media.
Now “pervert glasses” have gained a new layer of infamy: being crowned Macquarie dictionary’s word of the year.
The term “pervert glasses”, which also won the people’s choice word of the year for 2026, was described by the committee of word experts as a triumph of linguistics.
“The coinage pervert glasses is a succinct reflection of the state of the world in 2026 in so many ways,” they said.

“On the one hand, we’ve seen a massive acceleration in the capabilities of AI and products that integrate it. At the same time, the undeniably critical nickname mirrors the widespread calls to hit the brakes on this seemingly unchecked development.

“The name represents the year we’ve all endured, with AI, the manosphere, increasing surveillance in supermarkets, and more. Sure these new gadgets might be marketed as smart glasses or camera glasses, but it seems to us that pervert glasses paints a more apt reflection of the year.”

Honourable mentions from the committee went to “PMOS”, or polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome, which has received greater recognition alongside spreading awareness of medical misogyny; “agentic”, which refers to the ability, especially of artificial intelligence, to make decisions independently; and “Marrickville pause”, a colloquial term referring to a temporary halt in conversation by people under Sydney’s flight path.
“Digital dementia”, which refers to short-term memory loss from a reliance on technology and artificial intelligence, received an honourable people’s choice mention.
The committee said digital dementia was “not a real medical diagnosis but that hasn’t stopped the fear of an increasing reliance on digital devices from resonating deeply”.
“People are finding that they’re struggling to navigate without Google Maps and to make and remember plans without iCal,” they said.
“It will be interesting to see if all of this outsourcing does in fact lead to impaired cognition in the long term.”
In a sign of the times, other words on the shortlist included “nudify”, referring to AI-generated pornography, and “AI;DR”, short for “AI; didn’t read”.

Last year, AI slop was dubbed the term that was the epitome of 2025 linguistics, with the committee saying it embodied the word of the year’s general theme of reflecting “a major aspect of society or societal change throughout the year”.

The committee’s choice and people’s choice winning words are chosen from the list of new entries included in the annual update of the Macquarie dictionary online. The people’s choice winner was selected from public votes cast on its website.

articles.title: Lawyers push for Momay's recognition as 58th Maguindanao Massacre victim
articles.summary: Lawyers representing families of the victims of the 2009 Maguindanao massacre on Monday urged the Court of Appeals (CA) to recognize photojournalist Reynaldo “Bebot” Momay as the 58th victim of the…

blocks.text: Published November 23, 2026 9:52pm

Lawyers representing families of the victims of the 2009 Maguindanao massacre on Monday urged the Court of Appeals (CA) to recognize photojournalist Reynaldo “Bebot” Momay as the 58th victim of the killings, 17 years after the gruesome incident.

Center for International Law (CenterLaw) Philippines executive director Gilbert Andres filed a second motion for resolution before the appellate court on behalf of 19 families, seeking action on pending appeals involving the massacre, including the legal recognition of Momay and the release of civil damages.

Momay, a photojournalist for the Tacurong-based Midland Review, was among those who joined the convoy of journalists and supporters of then gubernatorial candidate Esmael Mangudadatu on Nov. 23, 2009. His remains, however, were never recovered.
"Ang aming hinhiling na talagang i-recognize na kasama si Momay sa mga pinaslang sa Sitio Masalay, Ampatuan, Maguindanao. Ang mga biktima ay may right to truth and right to justice," Andres said.

"Sa totoo lang, noong panahon na yun, my youngest son is only nine. Ngayon, may apo na ako sa kanya. Pero hanggang ngayon, nag-aantay pa rin kami ng hustisya; kahit man lang ina-acknowledge ang tatay ko, di pa magawa," said Reynafe, Momay's daughter.
Chief Justice Rodil Zalameda also urged the CA to resolve the pending appeals with dispatch, stressing that the victims' families have waited long enough for justice.
Andres welcomed the chief justice's call, saying it reinforced the families' appeal for the court to act on the long-pending cases.

Chief Justice Rodil Zalameda on Monday urged the Court of Appeals (CA) to promptly resolve the pending appeals in the Maguindanao massacre case, as the country marked the 17th anniversary of the tragedy.

Speaking at his first flag-raising ceremony as Chief Justice, Zalameda said the victims and their families had waited long enough for justice, stressing that the proceedings should no longer be delayed.

“As we speak of protecting those who stand for justice, we must also remember the victims of the Ampatuan Massacre, whose 17th anniversary we commemorate today. The victims and their families have waited long enough,” Zalameda said.

“I therefore urge the Court of Appeals to resolve the pending appeals with dispatch, consistent with due process and rights of all parties. Let us ensure that justice is not delayed any further,” he added.

The Maguindanao massacre, also known as the Ampatuan massacre, took place on Nov. 23, 2009, when a convoy carrying relatives and supporters of then Buluan Vice Mayor Esmael Mangudadatu, along with journalists and other civilians, was ambushed in Ampatuan town, Maguindanao.

The victims were accompanying Mangudadatu’s wife, Genalyn, and other family members as they were on their way to file his certificate of candidacy for the 2010 gubernatorial elections. Fifty-seven people were killed in the attack, including 32 journalists and media workers, making it the deadliest single attack on journalists in history. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Bell says cybersecurity incident affected customers at Virgin Plus, Lucky Mobile
articles.summary: A spokesperson for Bell says customers across its network of subsidiaries, including Virgin Plus and Lucky Mobile, were affected by a Nov. 17 breach but no "highly sensitive" information such as…

image.caption: A Bell sign is seen in Montreal in 2025. A company spokesperson said an 'agentic threat actor' accessed some of its internal systems on Nov. 17. (Christopher Katsarov/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Canada·New

A spokesperson for Bell says customers across its network of subsidiaries, including Virgin Plus and Lucky Mobile, were affected by a Nov. 17 breach but no "highly sensitive" information such as credit card numbers or banking information was impacted.
Company says no 'highly sensitive' data such as credit card numbers affected in Nov. 17 breach
Bell says customers across its network of subsidiaries, including Virgin Plus and Lucky Mobile, were affected by a cybersecurity incident last week.

In an email to CBC News on Monday, a Bell spokesperson said customers with Bell, Bell Aliant, Bell MTS, Virgin Plus and Lucky Mobile were affected after an "agentic threat actor" accessed some of its internal systems on Nov. 17.
But the company did not say how many customers were impacted.
"We can confirm that no highly sensitive personal information such as credit card numbers or banking information was accessed in the incident," the spokesperson said.
Separately, Virgin Plus sent an email to customers late on Sunday saying "an unknown party" gained access to its internal system on Nov. 17.
Virgin Plus said the incident may have affected some of its customers' personal information — including names, mailing addresses, phone numbers, email addresses and account details.
Virgin Plus also said it continues to monitor all systems closely. "We take our obligation to safeguard your information very seriously and we have engaged the RCMP's cybercrime unit to investigate."
Virgin Plus did not immediately respond to CBC's request for comment Monday morning on how many of its customers were affected.

articles.title: North Macedonia remains stalled on its EU path after 21 years as a candidate while Montenegro and Albania move closer to membership
articles.summary: EU enlargement has regained momentum, with Montenegro and Albania moving closer to membership. But North Macedonia, a candidate since 2005, remains stalled by a politically difficult dispute…

image.caption: North Macedonia has been an EU candidate country for 21 years. Pictured here: Prime Minister of North Macedonia Hristijan Mickoski (right) with EU Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos in 2025Image: Petr Stojanovski/DW

blocks.text: The European Union's enlargement drive has regained momentum: Montenegro could become the bloc's 28th member in 2028, while Albania is rapidly advancing through accession talks and could complete accession negotiations by the end of 2027 if it maintains its current pace of reforms.
But North Macedonia, an EU candidate since 2005, remains stalled on the road to accession.
That contrast will be particularly evident at Wednesday's EU-Western Balkans summit in Brussels.

"The Western Balkans' future is in the European Union. Their accession is our priority, our shared ambition and a crucial geopolitical investment in these turbulent times," European Council President Antonio Costa said ahead of the meeting.
Prepared, but the handbrake is still on

North Macedonia formally opened accession talks with the EU in July 2022 but has yet to open the first of the EU's six negotiating clusters, the groups of policy areas through which candidates align their laws and institutions with EU standards.
But the lack of movement does not mean the country is unprepared for membership.

blocks.caption: 'The Western Balkans' future is in the European Union,' European Council President Antonio Costa said recently. Pictured here: European leaders gathered for the EU-Western Balkans Summit in JuneImage: Kay Nietfeld/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: EU Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos said in November that North Macedonia was "among the countries with the highest level of preparedness" in aligning with EU law and had recently accelerated reforms under the EU Growth Plan.
However, she added, "the handbrake on its accession negotiations is still on."
Kos said that to release this handbrake and open the first cluster, North Macedonia must adopt the constitutional amendment agreed with the EU in 2022.
What's blocking N. Macedonia's EU progress?
The stalemate has deep roots.
For years, a dispute with Greece over the country's name blocked North Macedonia's progress along the EU accession path.
Although the 2018 Prespa Agreement resolved the dispute, and the country changed its constitutional name, clearing the way for NATO membership, a breakthrough on EU accession did not follow.

Bulgaria later blocked the process amid disputes over history, language and identity. A compromise brokered during the French EU presidency in 2022 lifted the veto but made further progress conditional on North Macedonia amending its constitution to explicitly include Bulgarians among the country's recognized communities.

blocks.caption: Gert Jan Koopman of the European Commission has said that North Macedonia is not blocked by an EU member state but 'is blocked because it doesn't want to date to do what it knows needs to be done'Image: Ognen Teofilovski/REUTERS

blocks.text: The amendment requires a two-thirds majority in parliament, which has so far proved unattainable.
'Not blocked by a member state'
From the EU's perspective, this is no longer a Bulgarian veto, but a condition North Macedonia accepted as part of its negotiating framework.

"It [North Macedonia] is not blocked by a member state. It is blocked because it doesn't want to date to do what it knows needs to be done," Gert Jan Koopman, the European Commission's director-general for Neighbourhood and Enlargement Negotiations, recently told an Atlantic Council podcast.
North Macedonia's government sees the problem differently.
EU membership remains its declared strategic goal, but Skopje wants guarantees that amending its constitution will not simply pave the way for further demands from Sofia.

Those concerns are rooted partly in long-running disputes over identity and history: Bulgarian governments have challenged North Macedonia's interpretation of a centuries-old distinct Macedonian identity, while some Bulgarian politicians have gone further, describing Macedonian as a regional variant of Bulgarian, and Macedonians and Bulgarians as one people.

President Gordana Siljanovska-Davkova says North Macedonia is ready for talks with Bulgaria and the EU but wants certainty that one constitutional change will not simply be followed by demands for another.
"We only want certainty. We only want this not to be yet another amendment for the sake of an amendment, followed by another one," she said.
Strong support for membership, little appetite for compromise
After more than two decades of waiting, the deadlock has also become a domestic political problem in North Macedonia.

blocks.caption: North Macedonia's President Gordana Siljanovska-Davkova says Skopje wants guarantees that constitutional changes will not be followed by new demandsImage: Macedonian Information Agency

blocks.text: A nationally representative survey by the Institute for Democracy "Societas Civilis" illustrates the contradiction: 71% of respondents support EU membership, but only 24% back the constitutional amendments needed to advance the process. Among ethnic Macedonians, support for the amendments falls to just 11%.

Skopje-based political analyst Petar Arsovski describes the public mood as "passive-aggressive:" Strong support for joining the EU coexists with weak support for making the concession currently required to move forward.
That, he says, helps preserve the status quo.
High domestic political stakes
The dispute is now deeply embedded in domestic politics in both North Macedonia and Bulgaria, where retreat from established positions could easily be portrayed as a national defeat.
The political cost is particularly high in Skopje, where the current government came to power in part on a platform of opposition to constitutional changes under the existing conditions.
For North Macedonia's government, accepting the amendments without further guarantees carries considerable domestic political risks.
The EU, meanwhile, is not offering to reopen the negotiating framework.

The uncertainty is compounded by debate over how future EU enlargement should work. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and French President Emmanuel Macron have proposed allowing candidates to gradually gain some benefits of membership before formally joining, while stressing that full membership remains the ultimate goal.
According to Arsovski, uncertainty over the future course of enlargement gives ammunition to Eurosceptic narratives and reduces the political incentive for a difficult compromise.

"If these overall conditions remain unchanged, the most likely scenario is that EU summits come and go, while political actors remain dug in, with no real convergence of positions and no genuine commitment to a substantive compromise," Arsovski told DW.

articles.title: Geo Ong rides helicopter from Ilocos Sur to QC after LTO suspends license
articles.summary: With his driver's license suspended for 90 days after he posted a motorcycle ride that showed him without a helmet, social media personality Geo Ong on Monday rode a helicopter from Ilocos Sur to…

blocks.text: Published November 23, 2026 9:41pm

With his driver's license suspended for 90 days after he posted a motorcycle ride that showed him without a helmet, social media personality Geo Ong on Monday rode a helicopter from Ilocos Sur to Quezon City en route to the Land Transportation Office.
According to Oscar Oida's report on "24 Oras," Ong was driven in a luxury car to the LTO, where he was met by fans.
He had posted about his helicopter ride and plan to be at the LTO on Monday. He deleted his posts, but still followers came to the agency in droves.
The visit also coincided with a protest staged by transport group MANIBELA.

LTO chief Assistant Secretary Markus Lacanilao expressed displeasure over Ong’s announcement and manner of going to the agency’s Quezon City office, saying the visit appeared to have been turned into a fan meet and an opportunity to create social media content.
Lacanilao said Ong had initially requested a meeting with him, even though it was not part of the influencer’s scheduled appearance before the agency.
The LTO chief also stressed that influencers should be mindful of the example they set for their followers, particularly children who may imitate their actions.
He added that popular personalities, especially those who can afford to travel comfortably, should set a good example instead of flaunting their wealth when visiting government offices.
Ong, for his part, admitted that riding a motorcycle without a helmet was wrong.
“We are only human, and sometimes we make mistakes. Not everything we do should be imitated. Sometimes, we learn from our mistakes, and that is why we can tell you what you should do,” he said.
However, Ong saw nothing wrong with taking a helicopter to Quezon City, explaining that it was their available means of transportation.
Ong surrendered his driver’s license on Monday in compliance with the 90-day preventive suspension imposed by the LTO. –NB, GMA News

articles.title: After Japan's APEC snub, what's ahead for China ties?
articles.summary: Japan has long-running concerns over Chinese military expansionism, and Beijing has bristled over Sanae Takaichi's comments on Taiwan. The frosty ties were on full display at last week's APEC summit.

image.caption: China-Japan ties were not prioritized on the 2026 APEC agenda Image: Go Nakamura/REUTERS

blocks.text: Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi received a cold shoulder from China during the recent Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in the tech hub of Shenzhen.

After Takaichi arrived in Shenzhen on November 18 for the two-day summit, there was an immediate issue when the mobile stairs to the door of her aircraft were some way short of the threshold, requiring her to hold on to the door frame to step down around 40 centimeters (about 15 inches) to the top step.

It may have been completely inadvertent, but upon safely reaching the airport tarmac, her official welcome was decidedly low-key. There were no musical performances, no cheering crowds or traditional dances, which were laid on for many other APEC leaders as they arrived.

blocks.caption: Sanae Takaichi was received by a mid-level foreign ministry official and a small honor guard in ShenzhenImage: Bai Xueqi/Xinhua/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Japan's Yomiuri newspaper reported on November 20 that when Takaichi met Chinese leader Xi Jinping at the dinner reception, "his reaction was cold." And while many other regional leaders managed at least a brief one-on-one with Xi on the sidelines of the main event, the Japanese delegation was not granted such access.
Frosty China-Japan ties on full display
"The level of frostiness from the Chinese side was on full display from the moment Takaichi's plane landed," said William Yang, a Taiwan-based analyst for the International Crisis Group.
"I cannot think that the issue with the plane steps was anything other than deliberate and there was a huge contrast between the welcome she received and virtually everyone else," he told DW.
Yang added the ice didn't break when Takaichi tried to speak to Xi at the dinner reception and the entire occasion "just reflects the state of bilateral relations."
China and Japan share a troubled history, marked by the Japanese invasion of China in the 1930s and the often brutal occupation of cities that were captured and subjugated.
Chinese schoolchildren learn about the horrors of the Nanjing Massacre and the use of chemical and biological weapons by Japanese forces.
Japan maintains that its repeated post-war apologies and massive economic aid that helped China to become the economic powerhouse it is today are overlooked amid the criticism.

Diplomatic relations were normalized in 1972 and Tokyo pursued a policy of engagement over the following decades, although that came to a halt in the mid-2000s, points out David Adebahr, a professor of international relations and Asia-Pacific security policy at Kobe University.
Pacifist Japan is rearming — this is why
Japan's Taiwan comments open new rift with Beijing

"China's rising military spending, the breakdown of talks over the East China Sea in 2006, and a resurgence of nationalism raised concerns even among Japan's more China-friendly diplomats, while defence analysts noted an increase in Chinese submarine activity near Japanese waters," he told DW.

The nationalism on display during the 2008 Beijing Olympics, coupled with China's more assertive stance over the Senkaku Islands, which Japan has sovereignty over but which Beijing claims, accelerated this shift.

Ties took a sudden nosedive in November 2025 when Takaichi responded to a question in Japan's parliament, the Diet, by saying that any "contingency” involving Taiwan would also inevitably threaten the national security of Japan.
According to Adebahr, the Japanese leader was merely saying out loud what "had long been the internal logic of Japanese security planning." Nevertheless, Beijing has reacted with fury.

China has demanded that Takaichi retract the statement and raised pressure on Japan by restricting exports of rare earth minerals critical to Japanese industry, banning imports of Japanese seafood and telling tourists to take Japan off their destination list.
And while ruffled national feelings have been smoothed in the past with shows of reciprocal goodwill, China is standing firm on its demands this time.
"From Tokyo's perspective, it is clear that Beijing believes it holds more cards than in the past," said Adebahr.

"Today, Beijing has considerable leverage: Japan's dependence on Chinese rare earths; an increasingly visible military presence around Japan, sometimes in conjunction with Russia; and a US administration that has urged Tokyo to de-escalate rather than firmly backing it."

"This gives China little incentive to offer Takaichi a face-saving compromise," he said. "However, this approach comes at a cost to Beijing too: the more it relies on coercion, the more it pushes Japan towards increased defence spending and closer ties with other partners."

blocks.caption: Unlike in 2026, Takaichi did meet with Xi at the 2025 APEC summit in South Korea Image: Japan Pool/Jiji Press/AFP

blocks.text: Japan's leadership faces the China test
Still, the Japanese leader finds herself in a difficult position, said analyst Yang.

As a committed conservative who has talked tough on Beijing's rapid military buildup, its seizure of islands and atolls in the South China Sea and the inexorable pressure on Taiwan to capitulate and become one with mainland China, Takaichi cannot give in to Xi's demands for fear of losing face with her hardline base.

"This is a major test of her abilities and wisdom as the nation's leader," Yang said. "She is walking a political tightrope between reducing tensions with China but, at the same time, preparing the nation and its allies for a potential contingency over Taiwan."

"I foresee China maintaining its current approach, continuing to step up the pressure by limiting targeted exports and amplifying the assertion with Russia and North Korea that Japan is embracing remilitarization," he said.

"I expect Japan to try to find areas where it can signal goodwill and seek to improve relations in return for small-scale compromises, but a reset in the dynamics will be determined by how the Trump administration shapes its foreign policy for the remaining years of his term," Yang added.
Analyst Adebahr said that while he expects diplomatic relations to remain frosty, there are too many interdependencies for a full decoupling between China and Japan.

"I would not be too pessimistic about the relationship, because in the medium term, trade, technology and critical minerals are now seen as security issues," he added. "Therefore, complex interdependence will prevent a return to the old pattern of keeping politics and economics separate."
"While economic interdependence alone will not be enough to stabilize the relationship, full decoupling is highly unlikely, as transaction costs would be far too high for both sides."
A new power bloc is emerging. Should the West worry?

articles.title: Mexican soldiers attacked in wake of drug lord's arrest
articles.summary: Eight suspects are arrested after firing on soldiers trying to re-establish order following the arrest of 'El Chapo Isidro'.

blocks.text: Mexican soldiers have detained eight alleged members of a drug cartel whose leader was arrested on Friday, sparking a wave of violence in northern Sinaloa state.

The Mexican defence ministry said the soldiers were shot by the suspects on Sunday while on patrol in the town of Sinaloa de Leyva, trying to re-establish order in the wake of the arrest of Fausto Isidro Meza Flores.
Meza Flores, also known as "Chapo Isidro", was on the FBI's 10 most wanted list and had managed to evade capture for years.
The ministry said the eight had also been involved in the retaliatory violence unleashed by Meza Flores's cartel in the hours after his arrest on Friday.
In a statement published on social media, external, the ministry of defence said that one of the detainees was under age.
It added that its special forces had seized six vehicles as part of their operation, two of which had been fitted with bullet-proof armour and gun turrets.
The US Department of Justice described Friday's arrest of Meza Flores as "a spectacular military operation" and congratulated Mexico's military and special forces on his capture.
It said that the US Homeland Security Task Force had supported the Mexican military and praised the "bilateral effort".
Mexico's defence ministry said its special forces had used stealth and surprise to reach the home of the wanted man.
They also established a security perimeter to prevent Meza Flores from escaping and cartel reinforcements from arriving.
Nevertheless, a bloody firefight ensued.
Along with Meza Flores, his second-in-command, known as "Serafín", and his financial operator, were also arrested and quickly transferred by air to Mexico City.
As news of their arrest spread, members of their cartel erected barricades on major roads and set cars and some shops alight.
There were also reports of shoot-outs between the security forces and cartel members.
The prosecutor's office in Sinaloa says 17 people, four of them members of the Mexican security forces, were killed as a result of the violence on Friday and early Saturday.
US Assistant Attorney General A Tysen Duva has described Meza Flores as "the most dangerous man in Mexico".
"For decades Meza Flores has promoted the terrorist objectives of the Sinaloa cartel," Duva said, accusing him of "flooding the United States with deadly substances".
The 44-year-old is believed to have started his criminal career with the Juárez cartel decades ago.
He later moved on to become the right-hand man of the leader of the Beltrán Leyva Organisation, a drug gang once allied to the Sinaloa cartel before the two groups split and became bitter enemies.
As early as 2013, the US Treasury identified Meza Flores as the leader of his own drug-trafficking organisation, named after him.

The US Treasury said at the time, that the Meza Flores drug trafficking organisation was responsible for "the distribution of large quantities of methamphetamine, heroin, marijuana, and cocaine to the United States".
It added that the turf war between the Meza Flores cartel and the Sinaloa cartel had "resulted in the quadrupling of drug-war killings" in between 2009 and 2013.
According to think tank Insight Crime, external, Meza Flores himself kept a low profile over the last decade while continuing to run his cartel out of Guasave, in Sinaloa state.

The head of the US Drug Enforcement Administration said that his capture was a "significant blow to a ruthless criminal organisation that has used extreme violence to traffic deadly drugs, including fentanyl, a designated weapon of mass destruction, into American communities".
His arrest, and the co-operation between US and Mexican officials which led to it, will be seen as a win for the government of Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum.
Sheinbaum has stressed that she is keen to work with the US authorities to capture high-profile target as long as Mexican's sovereignty is respected.

articles.title: Uganda minister at COP31: 'We need a just transition'
articles.summary: Funding from wealthy countries to help deal with the impacts of climate change hasn't materialized, says Uganda's environment minister. The East African country is hoping oil and carbon credits will…

image.caption: 'We are here begging for funds that are not forthcoming,' Beatrice Atim Anywar, Uganda's environment minister, told DWImage: DW

blocks.text: Ugandan Environment Minister Beatrice Atim Anywar has come to the UN climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, seeking to secure more funding for her country as it grapples with climate change.

"This is a thing we are living with," she told DW on the sidelines of the COP31 summit, where she's leading the Ugandan delegation. "People are displaced, people are dying of harm, hunger. It has implications on food security and livelihoods."

In recent years, the East African nation has been hit by a series of climate-related disasters, from deadly landslides and floods washing away villages, to droughts damaging harvests and hydroelectricity production.
"When we come to COP and we talk of what the reality is on the ground, we Ugandans have suffered it," Anywar said, referring to the effects of climate change.
"It has an implication for the health of our people, on national budgets," she added.

blocks.caption: In October 2025, landslides triggered by heavy rainfall in Uganda's Kaptang village destroyed people's homesImage: Abubaker Lubowa/REUTERS

blocks.text: Climate financing for developing countries to deal with the impacts of a warming planet has become a major sticking point at this year's climate talks. The gathering of some 200 states is seeking to close gaps on how to scale up financing from developed states and whether support should be provided through grants or loans.
Africa contributes less than 4% of the global greenhouse emissions that drive rising temperatures globally, but the continent is among the most vulnerable to climate impacts.
Ramping up electricity production
As it deals with the affects of climate change, including extreme weather, Uganda is also rapidly expanding investment in electricity production from renewables such as hydropower and solar.

In the country of some 53 million people, more than 90% of Ugandan households still rely on wood and charcoal as the most affordable fuel for things like cooking. Biomass accounts for 90% of the country's final energy consumption.

While using wood and charcoal leads to deforestation, Ugandans have little choice. Only around 2% of the country's energy comes from electricity — which is largely derived from hydropower — and less than half of the population has access to electricity.

"Now we are deliberately going into scaling up the production of electricity — hydropower electricity — and making it cheaper for cooking," Anywar said. "We have other alternative energy sources... to mitigate this charcoal use. But the use needs to be phased out in a systematic manner by giving them alternatives."
As pipeline nears finish, resistance in Uganda holds firm
Drilling for oil

At the same time, the country is seeking to boost economic development by becoming an oil producer. Due to open in 2027, a controversial 1,443-kilometer (897-mile) pipeline is nearly complete. It connects two oil sites in eastern Uganda with a port on the Tanzanian coast.

Environmentalists have criticized the East African Crude Oil Pipeline project, which can transport up to 246,000 barrels per day. Environmentalists say it runs counter to the goal of limiting global temperature rise and could damage fragile ecosystems.
The Climate Accountability Institute said it would release 379 million tons of climate-heating pollution over its 20-year lifetime.
Oil wells for the project, operated by French energy giant TotalEnergies, are also located in Uganda's largest and oldest national park, Murchison Falls.

"That has been also a sticky issue. And actually, that is one of the challenges we are facing at COPs," Anywar said. She stressed that measures have been taken to limit emissions, and that the project was progressing in a "very deliberate way."

blocks.caption: Climate activists in New York protesting JP Morgan Chase bank's support of the Total Energies East African Crude Oil Pipeline (EACOP), which is displacing farmers in Uganda and TanzaniaImage: picture alliance / ZUMAPRESS.com

blocks.text: The minister also urged developed countries to cut less wealthy nations some slack for using the resources they have to drive much-needed development, saying oil revenues could help fund the transition to cleaner energy.

"You cannot tell us to cut off the umbilical cord that feeds us, as much as it has to be cut off," Anywar said, criticizing the lack of financing from developed countries to deal with climate change. "We are here begging for funds that are not forthcoming."
Anywar added that developing countries "need a just transition," referring to an equitable shift away from fossil fuels that focuses on protecting workers and communities.
Carbon trading 'breakthrough?'
Another way Uganda is looking to finance climate change adaptation is through carbon credits, Anywar said, describing them as a potential "breakthrough."

Carbon credits are tradeable permits representing one ton of carbon dioxide that has been reduced or removed from the atmosphere through initiatives such as forest protection, renewable energy projects or tree planting schemes. Companies or governments can buy them to offset emissions they have not cut themselves.
"Our country is rich with biodiversity. And that is what we are looking forward to — attracting investors into our natural setup so that we earn some finances," Anywar said.

blocks.caption: Uganda is rich in biodiversity, including lush tropical forests with plenty of wildlifeImage: C. Kaiser/blickwinkel/picture alliance

blocks.text: Carbon credits have been promoted as an important source of income for developing countries. But they have also faced criticism, for a lack of transparency and allowing polluting activities to continue.

"We need to have a bankable approach to all interventions. Otherwise… it's not going to work for us," Anywar said, adding that her country also wants to attract investment and build partnerships in smart agriculture and the energy transition.
"If we rely on begging for funds which are not forthcoming, we shall go back empty handed."
This interview also appeared as a video.
