articles.title: Environment Agency and Natural England face axe in Labour quango cull
articles.summary:
Louise Haigh says the two environmental regulators are being reviewed as part of shake-up of arm’s length bodies

Ministers are considering abolishing two of England’s biggest environmental…

blocks.text: Ministers are considering abolishing two of England’s biggest environmental regulators in an attempt to give politicians greater control over what gets built and where.
Louise Haigh, the de facto deputy prime minister, said on Monday that the Environment Agency and Natural England were being reviewed as part of a wider shake-up of arm’s length bodies.

Successive governments have argued that reforming or scrapping large environmental watchdogs would help free companies to build more houses and infrastructure. Environmentalists, however, warn such a move would endanger wildlife and would do little to boost growth.

Haigh told the CBI conference on Monday: “Over decades, politicians were content to duck accountability by giving responsibility away from ministers to a sprawling web of regulators and arm’s length bodies, more than 20 statutory consultees, all with veto power, notionally bound by statutory deadlines. But obfuscation has become normal.”

blocks.caption: Louise Haigh speaking at the CBI conference on Monday. Photograph: Neil Hall/EPA

blocks.text: She added: “As part of rewiring the state, we will reform arm’s length bodies to increase public control. We will look at each of their functions and pose the challenge: what should be devolved, what can be dissolved and what can be delivered by departments?
“We’ve already begun that process with the Environment Agency, Natural England, Ofwat and the Drinking Water Inspectorate.”

Ministers in successive governments have taken aim at both the Environment Agency and Natural England for blocking housebuilding in particular. The former prime minister Rishi Sunak wrote this weekend in the Sunday Times: “Natural England was able, without explicit parliamentary consent, to issue planning advice which held back the construction of 100,000 homes.”

Many of those frustrations were shared by the former chancellor Rachel Reeves, who blamed environmental regulators for choking economic growth by demanding developers build expensive wildlife protections such as the £100m “bat tunnel” over the HS2 high-speed rail line.

She told Sky News on Monday morning: “We’ve had successive governments complain about this, but unfortunately, successive governments have created more of these and pushed more decision-making out of their own departments, so that then when they make decisions they don’t agree with, they turn around and look in horror.”

Many of the proposals are likely to follow the recommendations made in a report by Jon Cunliffe last year, who proposed replacing Ofwat with a new super-regulator that would take in powers from Natural England and the Environment Agency.
Last month, the Conservatives announced that if they won power they would abolish both agencies, saying this would help create more new homes.
after newsletter promotion

blocks.caption: The HS2 ‘bat tunnel’ in Buckinghamshire. Photograph: Jill Mead/The Guardian

blocks.text: The proposals have angered many in the environmental world. Tony Juniper, the chair of Natural England, said his organisation had helped speed up building by reviewing rules such as those that protect bats and newts.

Supporters say Natural England and the Environment Agency enforce legal duties that would still have to be enforced even if they did not exist. “A healthy natural environment is vital for economic development and at Natural England we are very proud of all the work we have done during recent years to unite our national ambitions for growth while achieving nature’s recovery,” Juniper said.
“It’s never been the case that healthy nature is in opposition to economic development, but actually enables it. It’s possible to do both.”

Craig Bennett, the chief executive of the Wildlife Trusts charity, said: “For over 16 years, politicians have been claiming that the regulations and regulators who protect English wildlife are some sort of obstacle on a path to prosperity. They are not. For over 16 years, protections have been chipped away and the woods, meadows, skylarks and hares they protect are suffering a death by a thousand cuts.”
Haigh said the review of quangos would be announced as part of next month’s 10-year plan, alongside further detail of how the government intends to bring utilities into public control.

She told her business-dominated audience it should not fear public control of companies currently in the private sector, saying it would help bring long-term certainty for investors. “We’ve built a hulking, complex behemoth of a regulatory state. It satisfies no one – not consumers, not investors. That is why public control should not alarm anyone in this room. It’s not ideological. It’s pragmatic, and it’s essential for people, for places, and for business.”

articles.title: Students from Gaza win visa battle to study in Ireland
articles.summary:
Decision to deny visas to more than 60 students overturned after high court orders justice department to reconsider

Twenty students from…

blocks.text: Twenty students from Gaza are to travel to Ireland to take up scholarships after winning a battle for visas that undercut the Irish government’s reputation as a champion of Palestinians.

The group is due to leave the territory on Monday under strict Israeli controls and travel via Jordan to Dublin to take up places at Irish universities. Another group is expected to follow next month.
The evacuation comes after a four-month campaign to overturn a decision by the Irish Department of Justice to deny visas to more than 60 students in Gaza who had been offered scholarships in Ireland.
The decision dismayed opposition politicians and other critics who accused the department of betraying Ireland’s record of solidarity with Palestinians.

The government backed down last week after a Dublin high court ordered the department to reconsider the decision. The minister for justice, Jim O’Callaghan, approved 48 visas. The first group is expected to arrive on Tuesday, with the remainder coming in late December.

“It’s a mix of feelings I still can’t fully describe,” Amir Alareer, 26, who is to study cybersecurity and artificial intelligence at University College Dublin, said via email on the eve of his departure from Gaza.

“There is hope and relief after months of waiting and fighting for this moment. But it is hard to feel complete joy when I am leaving my family behind in Gaza, and when 28 of my fellow students, who hold the same visas and share the same dreams, are still here waiting.”

The students originally expected to come in summer, and had supporting paperwork from Irish universities, but in July the Department of Justice rejected the visa applications. “The refusals hit us hard,” said Alareer.

The department demanded bank statements, proof of intention to return and other documents and said any appeal would have to be made by post, saying screening and verification were integral to the immigration system.

The students said such documents had not previously been requested and that Gaza’s banking and postal service had been destroyed. Ivana Bacik, a legislator and leader of the Labour party, accused the department of using “spurious reasons” amid a hardening of immigration policy.

Alareer helped to lead a campaign from Gaza that was backed in Ireland by demonstrators, a petition and an open letter signed by actors, writers and artists including Hozier, Nicola Coughlan and the rap group Kneecap. “Running a campaign from Gaza, through blackouts and displacement, was not easy, but I knew that if we stayed silent, our case would be forgotten,” said Alareer.

In October, the high court ruled that there were “significant and demonstrable errors” in the refusal of a visa to Shaymaa Abudalu, a 20-year-old who had been offered an engineering scholarship at University College Cork, and who was the lead case in a batch of similar lawsuits. A high court judge welcomed the decision last week to grant 48 visas and said “huge progress” had been made.
Among the students are five members of a dance troupe who have been offered places at the Irish World Academy of Music and Dance at the University of Limerick.

Alareer, who studied engineering at Al-Azhar University – Gaza, said Israel’s attacks on Gaza had destroyed his home and displaced the family several times. “The hardest experience of all was the famine, when we couldn’t find even a single kilo of flour.” Floods have impeded recent relief efforts.

His family was proud of his scholarship, he said, but saying goodbye would be hard. “They are happy that I finally have this opportunity, but leaving them behind after everything we have been through together is incredibly difficult.”

After studying software and innovation in Dublin, Alareer plans to return to Al-Azhar University and establish a cybersecurity department. “I want to build a generation of Palestinian engineers and researchers who can protect our digital future. Gaza will be rebuilt, and its systems must be rebuilt securely, by its own people.”

articles.title: A reset for climate diplomacy?
articles.summary: COP31 has been branded a failure after countries couldn't reach a deal. But was the decision to walk away from what would have been a step back actually a show of strength? What the result means for…

image.caption: Climate summit talks collapsed as nations failed to come to an agreement over fossil fuelsImage: Yasin Akgul/AFP

blocks.text: The longest-running climate talks in history came to a disappointing conclusion on Sunday as negotiators failed to come to an agreement on a shared political direction on climate change.
After two days of extended talks, representatives from country after country, tiredness etched into each face, voiced their opposition to the so-called "Antalya Pact."
"I understand that there is no agreement on this text. For that reason, these decisions have not been adopted," said Murat Kurum, Turkish president of the COP31 climate summit.
'Fossil fuels' as one of main sticking points

One of the main sticking points: the words "fossil fuels." While some nations, including petrostates like Saudi Arabia and Russia, wanted them omitted from the text, others saw it as a "step backwards" not to include them.

Around 130 parties — including the vulnerable island nations, and other developing countries, richer states like the EU — called for the reintroduction of the two words into the text to no avail. And so many refused to support the adoption of the final COP agreement.

blocks.caption: This year's COP31 climate talks were hosted in Antalya, TurkeyImage: Yasin Akgul/AFP

blocks.text: While it signals a failure for the UN process, that so many countries were willing to walk away from what they saw as a weak text was, arguably, a show of strength and one that had been long coming.

Three years after appearing in the closing decision of COP28 in Dubai with the promise of "transitioning away from fossil fuels in energy systems, in just, orderly and equitable manner", the words "fossil fuels" have been omitted from every decision since.
More extreme weather as climate change accelerates

But this year is different. This climate summit was the first to acknowledge that the world will breach the critical 1.5-degree Celsius (2.7-degree Fahrenheit) threshold that scientists said would avoid the worst impacts of planetary heating.
And so, the pressure was on for progress; to turn pledges from previous years into concrete action. But that progress didn't come.

"We don't celebrate the deep divisions exposed or the lack of a political signal from COP31 capable of driving climate action in line with science, equity, and the law," said Nikki Reisch, director of the climate and energy program at the Center for International Environmental Law, reiterating the value of multilateral space.
"But the rejected text would have done more harm than good," she added.
The lack of agreement was not just purely about "fossil fuels" but also about money.
Financing climate action in the Global South

Developing nations have long argued that they need additional financing, both as a means for them to move away from coal, oil and gas, but also to help them cope with the consequences of rising temperatures.

Countries all over the world are being battered by extreme weather events and catastrophes like flooding, drought, and wildfires fueled and worsened by rising global temperatures. Some of the worst hit are poorer countries that have contributed the least greenhouse gas emissions causing the problem.
UN warns climate change could force millions to move

And yet, richer states behind much of the historical emissions are increasingly unwilling to foot the bill. Dissatisfaction at home due to higher food and fuel prices has left many governments loathe to pay more to finance climate action abroad.

With the United States — the world's biggest historical emitter — now absent from negotiations and on the verge of leaving the United Nation's Framework Convention on Climate Change, the European Union was portrayed as this year's villain with some observers highlighting the EU's "hypocrisy."
"You can't demand action and then block the finance that makes this possible," Fanny Petitbon, policy analyst at 350.org, said in a statement.
As the world's largest provider of climate finance, the EU reportedly refused to negotiate on providing additional finance and has repeatedly called for other nations to step up.
Moving forward on climate action beyond climate summits

The failure to find an agreement is a particularly bitter turn of events for countries that face ever worsening impacts of climate change, like the island states that are being confronted by a reality that could see their countries wiped off the map as sea levels rise.
But things are not all bad.

Although the Turkey-led electrification agenda calling for an increase in global electricity consumption to 35% by 2035 was not formally adopted as it made up part of the rejected final agreement, more than 90 countries pledged to move forward regardless.

It's not a silver bullet. There was no agreement on ensuring the increase was forged only through clean, renewable energy. But it would still signal forward momentum — momentum that is also being driven by economic forces and a need for home-grown energy security.
Maldives environment minister: 'We are not going to live in the dark'

And there are other hopes. The second conference on the Just Transition Away from Fossil Fuels will take place in Tuvalu in July 2027. Initiated at the COP30 conference last year in Belem, Brazil, it has seen increasing support from countries putting together concrete roadmaps for abandoning coal, oil and gas.
Who's responsible?

There has been much talk of blame and who is responsible for the breakdown and collapse of talks. What is clear is that the UN climate summits need reform. Progress, when it does happen, is slow. While currently based on consensus, with all countries having to agree on every measure, there have been many calls for majority-rule decision making. That could force the inclusion of language like "fossil fuels" into the text.

But ultimately, this is not the time to focus on fault. As the climate crisis accelerates, governments need to reflect — and quickly — on what can be done outside of these UN processes, within their nations, to speed up climate action.
"The take-home message from COP31 is clear: the world must do much more to confront the climate crisis — and it must do it now," said UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres in a statement.

articles.title: Nine people shot at central California concert with one in critical condition
articles.summary:
Authorities say they believe the Saturday night shooting at a concert in Strathmore ‘may be gang-related’

Nine people were shot at a concert in central

blocks.text: Nine people were shot at a concert in central California, leaving one person critically injured with a chest injury, the local sheriff said Sunday.

The shooting broke out at about 7.30pm Saturday at a concert attended by about 150 people in Strathmore, a small town in Tulare county, a mountainous region in the center of the state, the local sheriff’s department said in a statement. An unspecified number of suspects opened fire on the crowd. No arrests were announced.

One 26-year-old man was shot in the chest and required surgery. He remained in critical condition, the sheriff’s department said. Two other victims ages 19 and 22 also required surgery, while six people sustained minor injuries.

Authorities said that they believe the shooting “may be gang-related” but didn’t elaborate. The show in the town of roughly 3,000 people featured performers from neighboring states, the department said.
The department didn’t immediately respond to emailed questions seeking further details but said there was no longer any immediate threat to the public.

As of Monday, there had been more than 420 mass shootings in the US so far for the year, according to the Gun Violence Archive. The archive, a nonpartisan resources, defines mass shootings as cases in which four or more victims are either wounded or killed.
High numbers of mass shootings reported annually in the US have prompted many to call for more substantial federal gun control. But Congress over the years has not passed such restrictions.
Guardian staff contributed reporting

articles.title: Asylum seekers removed from UK subjected to ‘unnecessary and intimidating’ force
articles.summary:
Incidents include suicidal man being carried on to plane in waist, leg and ankle restraints, freedom of information data shows

“Unnecessary and intimidating” behaviour was used against…

blocks.text: “Unnecessary and intimidating” behaviour was used against asylum seekers being deported under the UK’s controversial “one in, one out” scheme, including a vulnerable person being carried on to a flight in restraints, according to a report.

Many of those deported to France under the scheme – which involved one asylum seeker who arrived in the UK in a small boat being forcibly returned to France in exchange for another in northern France brought legally to the UK to claim asylum – have fled conflict zones and are survivors of torture or trafficking.

According to freedom of information data shared with the Guardian about Home Office deportation charter flights between June and September 2026, 26 use-of-force incidents were recorded on 26 deportation charters – 21 to France and the others to Albania, Lithuania and Romania. Not every deportation flight involved a use-of-force incident.

After reviewing body-worn footage of four previous deportation flights to France the HM inspectorate of prisons team identified nine incidents of use of force, at least one that was not formally recorded by escorts. Monday’s HMIP report looked specifically at the deportation charter flight to France on 4 September.

In the case of the three documented use-of-force incidents on the flight, one man described by inspectors as “fragile”, who was not eating consistently, posed no threat and had no history of active resistance or violence, was taken from his cell by staff in full protective gear including helmets and riot shields and was placed in a waist restraint belt and leg restraints, even though he had not resisted. Techniques to carry him out were found to be “poorly applied” and “disproportionate”. During the flight he “remained slumped and non-communicative”.

In a second case a man who was on constant suicide watch was carried out to the plane in a waist restraint belt, along with leg and ankle restraints. In a third case a man was placed in a waist restraint belt because he said he was not going to comply with his removal.

The Guardian has previously highlighted concerns about the state in which one in, one out asylum seekers were being returned to France. A report from Samusocial de Paris, which was commissioned by one of France’s regional health agencies to provide healthcare to returned asylum seekers, found: “Consultations are revealing signs consistent with recent physical and psychological violence as well as the consequences of prolonged detention in conditions described as particularly degrading.”
It states that the physical and psychological conditions documented are “explicitly linked to the implementation of the France-British agreement”.

The HMIP report said inspectors “mostly observed caring and respectful interactions” but also found that leadership of collection teams was “not always active enough to address some unnecessary and intimidating behaviour”.

A bodyworn video camera that doubled as an interpreting tool was found not to work effectively and many asylum seekers were unable to access either adequate interpretation or lawyers to represent them.
Inspectors also found that the asylum seekers were referred to by numbers rather than by their names and that those taken to the plane by van were given bags to urinate into.
The Guardian reported in November that despite the scheme ending in October, there were still incidences of people being removed.

Emma Ginn, director of the charity Medical Justice, said: “This report’s findings come as no surprise. Medical Justice has long evidenced the severe and avoidable harm of the government’s dehumanising mistreatment of vulnerable people during immigration enforcement – it cannot be described it as accidental.

“Our independent clinicians assessed that most of our clients detained under the ‘one-in one-out scheme’ had clinical evidence of torture. It should be a source of shame that torture survivors have been mistreated and retraumatised in UK immigration removal centres and while being deported back to France having suffered additional severe harm here.”
The Home Office has been approached from comment.

articles.title: EXCLUSIVE: Marcos confronted Romualdez over insertions that would have laid off 7,000 DPWH staff --Bonoan
articles.summary: Pres. Marcos Jr. confronted then-House Speaker Romualdez over the near-layoff of some 7,000 daily wage employees of the DPWH due to congressional insertions in 2024, Manuel Bonoan said.

blocks.text: Published November 23, 2026 8:01pm

President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr. confronted then-House Speaker Martin Romualdez over the near-layoff of some 7,000 daily wage employees of the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) due to congressional insertions in 2024, former DPWH secretary Manuel Bonoan stated in a judicial affidavit exclusively obtained by GMA News.

Bonoan said the DPWH was cash-strapped after legislators took the budget allotted for its Maintenance and Other Operating Expenses (MOOE) to allocate it to more than 9,000 congressional insertions worth P 380.48 billion.
Legislators also took the more than P70.701 billion allocated for infrastructure projects or foreign-assisted projects like the Metro Manila Subway Project or the North South Rail Commuter Project.
“… the legislators took everything leaving nothing for the IFP/FAP,” Bonoan said.
Bonoan said the President immediately called Romualdez after he had informed him about this.

“The President was so concerned about laying off 7,000 DPWH daily wage employees, so he immediately called [then-] Speaker Ferdinand Martin Romualdez in my presence. To my recollection, the President told Speaker Martin, ‘Ano ba naman kayo, magtatanggal si Secretary Manny ng 7,000 employees dahil kinuha n’yo pati MOOE n’ya. Hindi pwede ito,” he said.
Bonoan said Romualdez reprimanded him for reporting to the President..
“Sometime after that Speaker Martin Romualdez called me up and told me ‘Pambihira ka naman Sec., pwede ka namang dumeretso sa akin, nagsumbong ka pa kay Presidente,” Bonoan recounted.
Bonoan told Romualdez that the President was his boss.
But despite the President’s warning, it continued even in the 2025 budget.

“Notwithstanding the phone call of the President, the House Of Representatives and the Senate of the Philippines still slashed the Department’s proposed budget for the Fiscal Year 2025 to fund their ‘congressional initiatives’ or ‘insertions,” Bonoan said.
In 2025, there was some P436 billion in congressional insertions according to Bonoan which irked the President that he wanted to veto the whole 2025 budget.
“The President was furious that he wanted to veto the entire 2025 GAB but his economic managers advised the President not to,” Bonoan said.

The President then instructed Bonoan to identify which projects he could veto and Bonoan identified some P26 billion pesos of infrastructure projects which he called “guni-guni” projects that included highways in mountains that run to legislators’ resorts.

“These projects I recommended to be vetoed are ambiguous or ‘guni-guni’ projects that I reported to the President. These projects were construction of highways to the mountains leading to resorts of legislators, construction of new buildings, hostels and swimming pools, etc. These projects are not aligned with the core programs of the government,” Bonoan said.

Of the P400 billion in insertions, P192 billion came from the House of Representatives while some P17 billion were “jointly tagged under the names of both senators and members of the House of Representatives.”
Bonoan furnished the court with a listing of Romualdez alleged insertions including that of former House Committee on Appropriations Chair Zaldy Co.
A GMA News source said Romualdez’ amount of insertions is around P27 billion.
GMA News sought the Romualdez and Co’s comments but their counsels refused comment. — BM, GMA News

articles.title: Sold! Why live cattle auctions still matter to Alberta ranchers in an era of online bidding
articles.summary: Ranchers say you can still tell when it’s auction day in farming towns: trucks are lined up on the streets, the coffee shops are busy and local commerce surges.

image.caption: Over 2,000 cattle a day can move through the auction mart in Stettler, Alta. (Bob Grieve/CBC)

blocks.text: Edmonton
Ranchers say you can still tell when it’s auction day in farming towns: trucks are lined up on the streets, the coffee shops are busy and local commerce surges.
Physical auction rings vital for smaller operations and rural communities, producers say

Amidst rapid-fire auction chants and high-stakes bids, cattle lumber through the gates of the auction ring in Stettler, Alta. Trotting in and out in twos and threes, they’re mostly cooperative, though a few stubborn ones keep the handlers hustling.
More than 2,000 head are on the block this crisp day. It’s the thick of the fall run, the annual October-November window when many ranchers bring their spring-born calves to market.

“We'll sell $12-million worth of cattle here today,” says Dave Mailer, owner of the Stettler Auction Mart, a fixture in the central Alberta community since 1953. Standing on a boardwalk above the pens, he raises his voice to be heard over the bawling cattle below.
A calf bawls in a pen at the Stettler Auction Mart, Alta. (Bob Grieve/CBC)

Live auction marts like this one anchor life in rural Alberta, even as online bidding grows in popularity. Ranchers say you can still tell when it’s sale day in farming towns: trucks are lined up on the streets, the coffee shops are busy and local commerce surges.
Mailer says it’s difficult to replace the live floor. “For the customer to be able to see their cattle sell and the customer to buy… [it’s] the best thing.”
Inside the ring, an auctioneer’s rapid-fire chant rolls by in a rhythmic blur: “Two-seventy-five, two-seventy-five,” he prompts, pushing the crowd to beat bids locked at $2.65 and $2.70 a pound.
Stettler Auction Mart owner Dave Mailer, top, auctions off a pair of cattle in the ring as a rancher, bottom left, bids from the stands. (Bob Grieve/CBC)
Decades ago, producers had to ship cattle to stockyards in major cities like Edmonton or Calgary. Over time, independent country markets helped decentralize beef trade in western Canada.
Today, ranchers can browse online catalogues and video clips to buy cattle remotely, or log in to bid live on sale days like this one.

“That's your whole year's paycheque, your whole year's income happening in roughly a few seconds,” says Lance Neilson of a typical auction. He pulled an empty trailer the 30 kilometres from his ranch, hoping to fill it with calves, then return in a few days with a load of heifers to sell.
Physical rings are vital for smaller operators, Neilson says.
“They end up being able to bring 20 calves or 10 calves, or maybe only bring one or two cows. And that gives you options to keep smaller producers in.”
Beef producers Jack and Shirley Neilsen at the Stettler Auction Mart. (Bob Grieve/CBC)

Jack and Shirley Neilsen have raised purebred Simmental cattle for decades, though they recently downsized their herd by about three-quarters. Up in the bleachers, the couple sit side by side, waiting intently for their calves to enter the ring.

“I guess we're people of old habits,” Jack says. “The staff here is very good to us. They know our name, they know us, whereas [at] some of the larger auctions, they don't. We're not just a number, we're a name here.”
For the Neilsens, sale day is woven into the rhythm of rural life.
“Jack, especially, coming in here — [he’ll] have coffee with a lot of the old guys and reminisce and talk about the past and hopefully the future,” Shirley says.
'Tough to beat that live atmosphere'

About 130 kilometres west, in the shadow of the Rocky Mountains near Rimbey, Dan Skeels walks his fourth-generation ranch, checking cattle for signs of pneumonia — a risk at this time of year with warmer days and chilly nights.
Skeels, who is also a world-champion auctioneer, says auction days don't just support ranchers, they fuel entire towns.
Dan Skeels stands on his fourth-generation ranch near Rimbey, Alta. Skeels is a cattle rancher and former world-champion auctioneer. (Nadeer Hashmi/CBC)

“I'm going to use our small town of Rimbey as a prime example. When it's sale day, the community's hustling, it's bustling. There's that much more commerce taking place in the town... It really helps the local economy.”
Skeels says he knows livelihoods are riding on every call he makes as auctioneer.

“I think it's pretty tough to beat that live atmosphere," he says, noting the main advantage is what the industry calls true price discovery — competitive bidding that determines what cattle are actually worth on a given day.
“You may have a producer that we sell their entire calf crop in 10 minutes… So, it's a big job.”
Cattle stand in the ring surrounded by handlers and auctioneers at the auction mart in Stettler, Alta. (Bob Grieve/CBC)
Second year of record prices

Rick Wright, CEO of the Livestock Markets Association of Canada, says online bidding now accounts for about 12 per cent of sales at commercial auction marts, which remain the benchmark for producers to see their livestock's true market value.
“I can sit and watch sales in Alberta, I can watch sales in Kansas, I can watch sales in Ontario, and get a real feel of the real market,” he says.
Ranchers can now preview video livestock listings in an online auction catalogue, then bid remotely during live sales. (Bob Grieve/CBC)
Wright says after a long drought, a second year of record cattle prices is giving much-needed breathing room to cow-calf producers, which make up the largest share of beef farms in Canada.
“They're certainly in a better financial position over the last two years than they have been in the previous five to seven,” he says.
“But their expenses have also gone up — interest has gone up, diesel fuel has gone up. The cost of raising the cattle has gone up by quite a bit.”
A handler moves a small group of cattle through the back pens toward the auction ring in Stettler. (Bob Grieve/CBC)
Back in the Stettler ring, Mailer and his crew are on hour 12 of a marathon sale day, with the bids and the auctioneer’s chant showing no sign of slowing down.
“It's the adrenaline of today,” Mailer says of the rush that keeps them going.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Nadeer Hashmi is a reporter for CBC News in Red Deer, Alta. He was formerly a reporter in Yellowknife.

articles.title: Arctic air brings colder temperatures to Europe this week
articles.summary:
After a warmer-than-average November so far globally, a cold snap is on the horizon in parts of Europe

While average global temperatures continue to set records through one of the strongest…

blocks.text: While average global temperatures continue to set records through one of the strongest El Niños on record, temperatures across a large swathe of Europe could plunge this week, as Arctic air sweeps in.
On Friday, the global average temperature was 2.12C higher than the preindustrial average, the biggest ever anomaly and equivalent to 1.22C above the 1991-2020 climate average.

But in parts of Europe, high pressure building over Scandinavia and low pressure shifting south-east into western Russia will open a corridor of cold air from the north. Temperatures in the Baltics and in countries such as Germany, Poland and Ukraine are likely to fall widely below zero from Monday, with ice days – in which temperatures stay below 0C all day – expected from midweek. By the weekend, temperatures could be 5-15C below average, reaching double-digit negatives on higher ground.

The low pressure over eastern Europe and western Russia will bring extensive snowfall. Southern Poland, Belarus, eastern Ukraine and south-eastern parts of the Baltics will be the first to see widespread snow, which could reach up to 10cm in southern Poland.

blocks.caption: Temperatures are expected to fall below zero in  Germany, Austria and Czechia. Photograph: Peeradon Warithkorasuth/Getty Images

blocks.text: Later in the week, as a smaller area of low pressure pushes into western and central Europe, significant snow is expected to spread across southern Germany, Austria and Czechia, where depths of 10-20cm could build. The Alps could get a significant dumping of snow, a welcome boost for the region’s ski resorts which will open in the coming weeks.

Into the weekend and the start of December, high pressure is set to remain dominant across northern Europe, maintaining below-average temperatures in central and eastern Europe and possibly extending into the Balkans. There are also hints that the sudden stratospheric warming earlier this month could finally begin influencing the lower atmosphere, with high pressure extending farther west and perhaps bringing cold easterly winds into western Europe and the UK, although confidence on this is low.

The cold in Europe is in stark contrast to the global picture. This October was the warmest on record, with an average global temperature of 15.35C, 0.9C above the 1991-2020 average and 1.75C above the estimated preindustrial level. It was the third month in a row above 1.5C, following August and September, and while parts of Europe, including the UK, have seen below-average temperatures so far this November, global temperatures this month have continued to run above average.

articles.title: Israeli attacks have turned Gaza into 'toxic wasteland', Oxfam says
articles.summary: The report says there are signs of possible contamination across almost all of Gaza as a result of Israel's actions.

blocks.text: Image source, NurPhoto via Getty Images
The UN estimates that Israeli forces dropped more than 200,000 tonnes of explosives on Gaza in almost two years (file photo)
ByYolande Knell
Middle East correspondentReporting fromJerusalem

Gaza has been turned into "a toxic wasteland", with more than 99% of the Palestinian territory showing indicators of environmental contamination from Israeli military attacks, a new report from the non-profit organisation Oxfam says, external.

Heavy metals, explosive residues, and asbestos from destroyed buildings, dioxins and biological contaminants in the air, soil and water supply are threats to Palestinians now and potentially for decades to come, it says.
Oxfam International's executive director, Amitabh Behar, accuses Israel of "environmental war crimes" as part of an "ongoing genocide in Gaza."
"The destruction and contamination of Gaza will have fundamentally degraded the environmental conditions necessary for human safety and survival," he says.
Israel's government has been asked for its response to the report.

It has rejected genocide accusations in an ongoing case at the International Court of Justice as baseless and distorted. Israel maintains that its military campaign in Gaza is an act of self-defence against Hamas in response to the group's deadly attack on Israel on 7 October 2023, and that it takes steps to mitigate civilian harm.

blocks.caption: Image caption, The report says 99% of Gaza shows indicators of potential environmental contamination

blocks.text: Image source, Anadolu via Getty Images
The report says 99% of Gaza shows indicators of potential environmental contamination

Oxfam and the UK-based Conflict and Environment Observatory (CEOBS) used satellite imagery, remote sensing, spatial analysis and other open-source data to draw their conclusions in the most comprehensive report to date on the severe environmental impacts caused by three years of intense war in Gaza.

The report details how munitions used in Israel's intense bombardment, as well as the debris from destroyed buildings and infrastructure, all have an impact on the environment. In February, a UN special rapporteur stated that more than 200,000 tonnes of explosives were dropped on Gaza in almost two years - "the equivalent of the total energy of approximately 13 Hiroshima-type nuclear bombs".

Last year, the UN Environment Programme (UNEP) estimated that Israel's military operations destroying homes and infrastructure had generated more than 61 million tonnes of debris across the territory, with about 15% potentially carrying a high risk of contamination from hazardous materials.
"There are going to be chronic health impacts that are long term because a lot of these contaminants are persistent in the environment," Oxfam report author Lama Abdul Samad told the BBC.
She says that now and in future Gazans are likely to suffer from increased respiratory diseases, cancers, organ damage and a rise in birth defects and stillbirths.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Only a small fraction of the more than 60 million tonnes of debris in Gaza has been cleared

blocks.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images
Only a small fraction of the more than 60 million tonnes of debris in Gaza has been cleared

With all six wastewater treatment plants out of operation in Gaza, untreated sewage currently makes its way into groundwater and the Mediterranean Sea. The health impact has recently been exacerbated by heavy winter storms causing rainwater to mix with wastewater and flow through streets and tent sites housing displaced people.

Testing types and levels of contamination is often not possible because Gazan laboratories have been destroyed and there are Israeli restrictions on the entry of specialist testing equipment and scientists. The BBC has approached the Israeli military for comment.
UNEP said security concerns also prevented its expert staff from previously travelling to Gaza.

The Oxfam report calls for a full, independent environmental assessment to be carried out in Gaza to identify contamination risks ahead of a clean-up. It says special attention must be given to the protection of workers involved.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Recent winter storms caused rainwater to mix with wastewater and flow through streets and tent camps

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
Recent winter storms caused rainwater to mix with wastewater and flow through streets and tent camps

Already, Gazan doctors have been reporting increased acute respiratory infections caused by dust and pollution from destroyed buildings and displaced people burning plastic, rags and cardboard to keep warm and cook food. Gastrointestinal diseases are linked to unsafe water and poor sanitation.

A Palestinian dermatologist, Dr Alaa Abu Hajar, told the BBC he had seen a five-fold increase in chronic skin diseases since the start of the war, putting this down to environmental pollution and overcrowded, unhygienic living conditions in tents and displacement camps.
"There are rodents, rubbish and sewage that's spread through the streets," he says. "Unfortunately, the age group most affected is children."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Dr Alaa Abu Hajar has seen a five-fold increase in chronic skin diseases since the start of the war

blocks.text: Dr Alaa Abu Hajar has seen a five-fold increase in chronic skin diseases since the start of the war
Farmers and those working in fishing say that pollution of the soil and sea mean they are unable to produce food that is safe.

"Sewage and wastewater are discharged into the sea without treatment and this is a great disaster," complains fisherman Abu al-Abed Sultan. "There is also rubble from destroyed houses that's dumped into the sea. When we lower our nets, we catch rubble and garbage. This harms the marine environment; the fish are affected and so are the fishermen."

At least 74,746 Palestinians have been killed since the start of the war in Gaza, according to the Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN. The UN says that humanitarian conditions remain dire.

Israel has conditioned large-scale Gaza reconstruction on the full disarmament of Hamas and other Palestinian armed groups. In July, Hamas accepted a plan put forward by the US-led Board of Peace to give up its weapons in exchange for an Israeli troop withdrawal. articles.title: Ukraine confirms it used naval drones to strike two Russian ships off Libya
articles.summary:
Ukraine’s security service says seven drones were launched from mothership in operation that sank Merkury warship

Ukraine has confirmed it deployed naval drones in

blocks.text: Ukraine has confirmed it deployed naval drones in strikes on two Russian vessels off Libya on Sunday, including one that sank the corvette Merkury, one of Russia’s newest vessels.
Ukraine’s security service, the SBU, said seven domestically made naval drones were launched from a mothership in the operation, which Volodymyr Zelenskyy described as “exemplary”.
“We continue our operations in designated waters. We are responding to Russia’s aggression. We are developing Ukrainian weapons,” the Ukrainian president added.

Zelenskyy released video footage, filmed by an approaching drone, showing the drones as they smashed into the side of the warship at its berth in the Benghazi naval base, triggering huge explosions that lit up the night sky.

In its own statement, the SBU said: “The defence forces of Ukraine have once again demonstrated that the Russian military fleet and its logistics networks have no safe routes, even far beyond the Black Sea.”
Zelenskyy said the other vessel hit on Sunday, the dry cargo ship MV Angara, was being used by Russia to transport weapons.

The operation, conducted 1,500 miles (2,400km) from the frontline in Ukraine, was the latest daring long-range assault by Kyiv’s forces. Last week Ukraine hitthe Kerch bridge - a key supply line to Russian-occupied Crimea – and the Russian Baltic sea port of Kaliningrad.
Residents in Benghazi heard loud explosions and saw flames at the naval base early on Sunday. Civil defence units rushed to the site and extinguished the fire, authorities in eastern Libya said.

The Merkury had docked to refuel and take on supplies as part of a cooperation agreement between Russia and the eastern-based government in Libya, the statement said without providing details about the vessel or its cargo.

Vladimir Putin had taken a personal interest in the ship. In 2019 he toured the St Petersburg yard where it was being built and backed naming it after a tsarist-era brig celebrated for fighting off two Turkish warships in the Black Sea in 1829.

At the 2023 Navy Day parade, the Russian president singled it out among 30 new vessels as evidence that Russia was “consistently building up the power of its fleet”. He hailed its St George flag as “a sign of the inviolability of our naval traditions” and said it was “gratifying” that the brig’s name had been revived.
Russian state media also talked up the ship. The news agency Tass called it the “newest missile corvette”, while the channel TV Tsentr claimed its stealth technology made it “invisible to radar”.

Divided Libya has emerged in recent years as a proxy battlefield. Moscow has long supported the breakaway government in Benghazi of Khalifa Haftar in its efforts use eastern Libya as a staging post for its military presence in north Africa and the Sahel.

More recently there have been reports of increasing Ukrainian operations. In April, the Associated Press reported that Ukrainian drone specialists had been operating at military sites in Misrata, Tripoli and Zawiya in Libya’s west. In September Libyan authorities denied reports by CNN that it allowed Ukraine to use a military base in the to launch drones against vessels from Russia’s “shadow fleet” in the Mediterranean.
The rival UN-recognised government in Tripoli said in a statement it was alarmed by “risks posed by involving civilian ports and facilities in activities linked to external conflicts”.

There was no immediate comment from Russia about the strikes. The UN mission in Libya (UNSMIL), however, expressed “serious concern” over the attacks, calling for “an immediate, independent and transparent investigation”. It said on X: “Libya cannot afford, and must not become a battleground for foreign conflicts.”

Ukraine prides itself on its military industry, particularly its progress in drone technology, which it has extensively developed since Russia invaded more than four and a half years ago. It has repeatedly touted the effectiveness of its domestically produced drones, including naval drones deployed throughout the war to hit Russian ships and infrastructure in the Black Sea.

In 2024, the Ukrainian general staff announced it had destroyed the Russian landing ship Cesar Kunikov with naval drones off the coast of Ukraine’s peninsula of Crimea, which was annexed by Russia in 2014.

Ukraine has also claimed to have attacked Moscow’s so-called shadow fleet – believed to carry Russian oil to circumvent sanctions – including in the Mediterranean last December. In March, a Russian liquefied natural gas carrier sank off the Libyan coast following an attack that Putin blamed on Ukraine.
Additional reporting by Pjotr Sauer

articles.title: Flagship UK gigafactory plan in turmoil after it loses second builder in five months
articles.summary:
Tata-owned Agratas plant to build EV batteries for sister company Jaguar Land Rover seen as crucial for long-term health of British car industry

One of the UK’s flagship electric vehicle…

blocks.text: One of the UK’s flagship electric vehicle battery projects has been thrown into turmoil after its second building contractor in five months walked away, adding to questions over when Jaguar Land Rover cars will use British-made batteries.

The £5.2bn gigafactory in Bridgwater, Somerset, is being built by Agratas, to provide batteries for Britain’s largest automotive employer, its sister company. Agratas and Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) are both part of Indian conglomerate Tata Group.

The UK government has pledged £380m in financial support for the factory because it is seen as crucial to the long-term survival of the British car industry, but the build has suffered several setbacks. The construction specialist contracted by Agratas, TSL, has decided to leave the project after failing to agree terms with Agratas, according to three sources.

Batteries are among the important parts of EVs, but global supply is now dominated by China, South Korea and Japan. Successive Conservative and Labour governments have strongly supported efforts to build a British battery supply chain, and it also fits with Andy Burnham’s hopes to “reindustrialise” the UK. Not all of the subsidy has yet been paid out.

Tata announced the gigafactory in 2023, aiming for a 2026 start of production with as many as 4,200 employees, before pushing it back to 2027. Replacing the lead contractor for the second time in five months is likely to add to doubts over whether Agratas can hit its latest target of January 2028 – although the company has not yet pushed back its planned start date.
A spokesperson for Agratas said: “We are on track to meet our customer requirements.
“The Somerset site is a large and complex industrialisation project, and all of our supplier partners are supporting us well as we prepare for the facility’s launch phase.”
The inability to reach an agreement with TSL, formally known as Tonroe Group, stemmed from disagreements over the timeline and cost of the project, two sources said.

TSL is expected to leave the site within two or three months, leaving no other main build contractor lined up. However, it is thought that NG Bailey, the project’s mechanical, electrical and plumbing contractor, could be one option to take over the entire build.

The issues at the heart of the dispute are similar to those with TSL’s predecessor, Sir Robert McAlpine (SRM). Agratas fired SRM at short notice in June, and one source suggested discussions over the terms of its departure remain ongoing.
Morale within Agratas has also been hit by the company’s decision to relocate some workers from Coventry, in a building shared with other Tata Group companies, to Somerset.

Some of those workers are expected to take redundancy rather than uproot families and move 120 miles away. If they did so it would continue a stream of senior staff leaving the business in recent months, two sources said.

The UK’s only operating gigafactory, AESC’s plant in Sunderland, north-east England, has also faced problems as carmakers have scaled back plans for EVs, with governments delaying bans on petrol and diesel cars. The Guardian revealed in August that AESC had shelved expansion plans after it failed to agree a separate deal to supply JLR.
after newsletter promotion

It is understood that JLR has secured batteries from other suppliers, so its plans to increase sales of new electric Land Rovers and Jaguars will not be affected. However, those initial cars will not have British-made batteries, although the manufacturer could also avoid EU tariffs under “rules of origin” if it uses batteries made in Europe.

Agratas has made some progress at the Somerset factory, as well as another site in Sanand, western India. Some Agratas managers have travelled to India this week to share experiences with their counterparts in India and discuss the UK situation.

The shell of the building site in south west England is mostly complete, and National Grid has started work on the electricity substation that will provide the large amounts of power needed to make batteries.

People close to the project suggest Agratas could still succeed in producing batteries and avoid the fate of an earlier rival project, Britishvolt, which collapsed after failing to secure firm orders. The former Britishvolt site in north-east England is now being turned into a datacentre for artificial intelligence – a potentially attractive prospect for an empty building with a high-capacity connection to the electricity grid.
Agratas was approached for comment. TSL declined to comment. JLR declined to comment. NG Bailey was approached for comment.

articles.title: Flights grounded in Belgium due to strike against austerity measures
articles.summary: A series of strikes have hit Belgium in recent months as the prime minister struggles to agree a budget to cut costs.

blocks.text: Hundreds of flights have been cancelled and train services have been severely disrupted across Belgium as a result of a strike against planned austerity measures.
All air traffic has been halted in Zaventem airport in the capital, Brussels, as well as Charlerois, home to low-cost airlines such as Ryanair.
Trains and underground services have also been halted in Brussels where large numbers of people are expected to join a protest march.

The protest comes as Prime Minister Bart De Wever has so far failed to agree a budget to cut costs with his coalition allies. King Philippe declined his resignation earlier this month, giving De Wever more time to negotiate.

No flights are taking off or landing at Brussels Airport between 07:00 and 21:00 local time (06:00-20:00 GMT) as a result of the strike by air traffic controllers. More than 50,000 travellers' plans were being disrupted - with more expected to be affected overnight and on Tuesday.
A similar situation has affected Charlerois, where all flights were shown as "scheduled", regardless of the time of departure of arrival.
"Without air traffic control, no flights can take off or land," the airport said on Saturday when the strike action was announced, warning of "disastrous consequences".
As thousands descended on Brussels for the protest march, the leader of one of the country's main unions, FGTB, said the government had alternatives to "dismantling the social protection system".
"A genuine wealth tax, fair taxation, and the elimination of tax loopholes," Bert Engelaar, head of FGBT, said.

"Political responsibility is not about keeping a government afloat at all costs. It's about knowing when to stop," Engelaar said, praising the left-wing Vooruit party - the only member of the five-party governing coalition reported to have stalled efforts to agree the budget.
Vooruit wants to raise taxes on the rich, and fewer cuts to pensions and the health sector.
Another union leader, Ann Vermorgen of the CSC, criticised government plans to cut bank holidays when they fall on weekends.
Public transport, schools and other public services are also facing disruptions.

articles.title: Democrats reveal details for 2028 presidential primary following midterm victories – US politics live
articles.summary: Party says there will be 12 debates to select a candidate from what is expected to be a large number of hopefuls

blocks.text: Democrats plan 12 debates for 2028 presidential primary
Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog.
Democrats are planning 12 presidential primary debates for what’s expected to be a crowded field of 2028 candidates, with the first scheduled for June, the Democratic National Committee has said.

The DNC’s announcement on Monday comes before major candidates have launched campaigns to succeed term-limited Republican president Donald Trump and follows the party’s convincing midterm performance, AP reported.

DNC Chairman Ken Martin said in a statement the party is aimed at staying united and helping the eventual nominee win the White House. “The DNC is keeping our foot on the gas as we head into the 2028 cycle,” he said.
Anticipating a large number of presidential hopefuls, the DNC said it will cap participation in each debate to 20 qualifying candidates over two nights, if needed.

The criteria for making the debate stage will be similar to 2020, when there was also a big field and a dozen debates, the DNC said, and will include meeting polling and other criteria such as grassroots fundraising.

More details are set to be announced in January, including specific times and locations for the debates, the DNC said, though the party confirmed that five debates will be in 2027 and seven in 2028. The final primary debate is planned for March 2028.

For the first time, candidates must pledge to reject dark money as a condition of making the debate stage. The new requirement is part of a ​DNC effort to curb the influence of outside groups that can spend unlimited amounts to support or oppose candidates without having to reveal funding sources.

The debate schedule is one of the most closely watched decisions the DNC makes, along with selecting the city for the 2028 convention. Earlier this year, the DNC narrowed the list of cities to Boston, Denver and Philadelphia.

blocks.text: Trump administration deported US citizen to Mexico, DoJ admits in court
Ramon Antonio Vargas
The Trump administration recently admitted in federal court that it deported a US citizen to Mexico after American authorities incorrectly concluded he was an undocumented immigrant.

Attorneys for the US justice department made that admission on Friday while requesting the dismissal of a lawsuit for damages that the deported man – Brian José Morales García of Austin, Texas – has been pursuing against the federal government.

Morales García’s case took that turn as the White House has faced bipartisan criticism for the aggressive mass deportation campaign pursued by Donald Trump throughout his second presidency – widely seen as a factor in the electoral battering his Republican party suffered during the 3 November midterms, costing it control of Congress.

The Denver-born, Mexico-raised Morales García was riding with his boss to his job as an air-conditioning installation technician on 3 April when they were pulled over by state and local officers near Fredericksburg, Texas.

Morales García was his boss’s passenger and did not have his identification on him. The 25-year-old also told the officers that he had his birth certificate and social security card at home, but they didn’t believe him – so they called immigration agents, who detained Morales García.

Court filings recount how Robert Gil Jr, a US Customs and Border Protection agent, consulted records from Mexico that listed a Mexican birthplace for Morales García. Gil Jr also accused Morales García of saying he was born in Mexico and observed that he only spoke in Spanish, according to court records.
Morales García was deported on 7 April, with the Trump administration later accusing him in a media statement of being in the country illegally.

articles.title: SC: Child remains legitimate even if father is unnamed in birth certificate
articles.summary: The Supreme Court (SC) has ruled that a child born during a valid marriage remains legitimate even if the father is not identified in the child"s birth certificate.

blocks.text: Published November 23, 2026 7:06pm
The Supreme Court (SC) has ruled that a child born during a valid marriage remains legitimate even if the father is not identified in the child’s birth certificate.

In a nine-page resolution, the SC Third Division granted a woman’s petition to correct her birth certificate to reflect her proper middle name and surname, as well as the date of her parents’ marriage.

“Under Article 164 of the Family Code, ‘children conceived or born during the marriage are legitimate.’ This means that legitimacy as a status attaches once a person is born within wedlock,” the Court said.

The petitioner’s parents were legally married when she was born. However, her mother registered her birth under her maiden surname, used her own middle name for her daughter and left the father’s identity blank because the couple were not on good terms at the time.
The High Court said Article 167 of the Family Code provides that a child remains legitimate even if the mother declares otherwise, including in the child’s birth certificate.
The petitioner grew up using her father’s surname in her school and employment records, including her Professional Regulation Commission identification card.
She discovered the discrepancies in her birth certificate only in 2017, prompting her to seek its correction.

The SC said substantial corrections to civil registry records may be sought under Rule 108 of the Rules of Court through adversarial proceedings, in which interested parties are notified and given the opportunity to contest the requested changes.
In her concurring opinion, Associate Justice Maria Filomena Singh also cited Rule 108, saying it may be used to correct entries in civil records that affect a person's legitimacy or filiation.

“A petition under Rule 108 is a procedural device to cancel or correct entries in the civil register, including entries relating to birth and filiation, subject to due process requirements,” Singh wrote.

She cited Section 2 of Rule 108, which allows the cancellation or correction of civil registry entries on valid grounds, including births, marriages, deaths, legitimations, adoptions, acknowledgments of natural children, judicial determinations of filiation and changes of name.

The Court ordered the concerned local civil registrar to amend the petitioner's birth certificate by replacing her middle name with her mother's maiden surname, changing her last name to her father's surname and indicating the date of her parents' marriage.
The resolution was penned by Associate Justice Japar Dimaampao and promulgated on April 7, 2026.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: German police respond to multiple school bomb threats
articles.summary: Police in Germany are responding to bomb threats against a series of schools, but say that at present they don't believe them to be credible. Danish authorities are reporting a similar series of…

image.caption: Police responded to bomb threats against multiple schools but were working on the preliminary assumption they were hoaxesImage: Carsten Rehder/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Police in several locations across Germany are reporting large numbers of bomb threats targeting schools.

They say that while they are investigating the claims, they do not currently have reason to treat them as credible threats. Police in Erfurt and Freiburg were among the first to report the phenomenon on Monday.
What did police say about the bomb threats?

Police in Erfurt in Thuringia were among the first to issue a statement on the threats, saying they were responding to threats at "multiple schools" after morning warnings, including in Jena, Erfurt, Mühlhausen, Zella-Mehlis, Nordhausen, Gotha, Rudolstadt and Greiz.

"The same word-for-word threats were received this morning at the various eductional institutes," police wrote in a press release. "Based on preliminary findings other federal states are also affected by the threatening messages."
Police said they had no information yet on the potential author or sender of the emails. They were investigating breach of the peace-based crimes via the threat of criminal activity.

"At present the police is not working on the assumption of the bomb threats being serious and recommends that schools do not implement evacuation measures and continue their normal operations," they said.
Police in Freiburg in the southwest and authorities to the north in Hanover also said they were responding to emailed bomb threats directed against schools.
Similar reports are emerging to the north of Germany in Denmark.
As in Germany, Danish police said they did not believe the threats were credible, "but they understandably create insecurity locally at the schools."
Various disruptive incidents targeting Europe in recent weeks
This follows other recent cases of coordinated bomb threats against multiple schools that turned out to be hoaxes in Europe.

It also comes amid various apparent bids to create disruption within Europe in recent weeks, such as multiple bomb threats targeting commercial airlines, or hacking into supermarket refrigeration systems to spoil produce en masse.
This is a developing story, more to follow...

blocks.text: The Trump administration recently admitted in federal court that it deported a US citizen to Mexico after American authorities incorrectly concluded he was an undocumented immigrant.

Attorneys for the US justice department made that admission on Friday while requesting the dismissal of a lawsuit for damages that the deported man – Brian José Morales García of Austin, Texas – has been pursuing against the federal government.

Morales García’s case took that turn as the White House has faced bipartisan criticism for the aggressive mass deportation campaign pursued by Donald Trump throughout his second presidency – widely seen as a factor in the electoral battering his Republican party suffered during the 3 November midterms, costing it control of Congress.

The Denver-born, Mexico-raised Morales García was riding with his boss to his job as an air-conditioning installation technician on 3 April when they were pulled over by state and local officers near Fredericksburg, Texas.

Morales García was his boss’s passenger and did not have his identification on him. The 25-year-old also told the officers that he had his birth certificate and social security card at home, but they didn’t believe him – so they called immigration agents, who detained Morales García.

Court filings recount how Robert Gil Jr, a US Customs and Border Protection agent, consulted records from Mexico that listed a Mexican birthplace for Morales García. Gil Jr also accused Morales García of saying he was born in Mexico and observed that he only spoke in Spanish, according to court records.
Morales García was deported on 7 April, with the Trump administration later accusing him in a media statement of being in the country illegally.

Morales García’s attorneys sued on 1 May, maintaining that he had falsely said he entered the US illegally and signed papers for a rapid deportation in response to threats of imprisonment by agents. His lawsuit, which seeks an unspecified amount of money, also contended that family and friends tried to deliver documents proving his US citizenship before this deportation.
But those efforts were unduly rebuffed, Morales García’s lawsuit said.

The Trump administration denied Morales García’s assertions, saying on Friday that he went to Mexico voluntarily and therefore lacked any basis to sue the federal government for damages. Nonetheless, in court filings on Friday, the administration conceded that Morales García “was permitted entry” back into the US on 30 August after it reviewed “information concerning plaintiff’s place of birth”.
“Plaintiff is a dual citizen of the United States and Mexico,” Justin Simmons, the US attorney for the western district of Texas, wrote in a court filing first reported by the Texas Tribune.

Americans are not required to carry proof of citizenship when going about their daily business. Lawyers across the US have seen cases such as Morales García’s, which begin after an encounter with local authorities demonstrate how those officials are generally not aware of the nuances of immigration policy.
Texas’s public safety department is among many US state and local agencies that collaborate with federal immigration authorities under their 287(g) program.

The judge presiding over Morales García’s lawsuit, Robert Lee Pitman, did not immediately rule on the Trump administration’s request on Friday to dismiss the case. The lawsuit also named unspecified local and state Texas law enforcement officers as defendants.
An October 2025 report by ProPublica found that immigration agents had detained more than 170 US citizens during the first nine months of Trump’s second presidency.

Meanwhile, the media statement incorrectly saying Morales García was in the US illegally is among several related to immigration enforcement under the Trump administration that has unraveled under scrutiny.

A Guardian analysis published in July reviewed Trump administration press releases on 26 cases of cars allegedly being used to assault immigration enforcement agents – and nearly all were either disproven or dropped.

articles.title: This B.C. man found some historical parkas at a thrift store — now he's trying to get them back to Nunavut
articles.summary: Mike Williams of Kamloops discovered that the parkas were made in Taloyoak, Nunavut, for the 1974 Arctic Winter Games in Alaska. He's determined to get them back to the northern community where they…

image.caption: Mike Williams, left, of Kamloops, B.C., shows CBC reporter Doug Herbert some hand-made parkas he recently found at a thrift store in his city. Williams has since found out they were made in Taloyoak, Nunavut, more than 50 years ago, and he wants to see them go back to the community. (Peter Cameron-I

blocks.text: North

Mike Williams of Kamloops discovered that the parkas were made in Taloyoak, Nunavut, for the 1974 Arctic Winter Games in Alaska. He's determined to get them back to the northern community where they were made.
Mike Williams found 4 hand-made parkas from Taloyoak, Nunavut
Selena ‘Kublu’ Tucktoo of Taloyoak, Nunavut, remembers making parkas with her mom back when Tucktoo was in her early 20s.
“It was kind of complicated at first, but I learned,” she said. “They were fun to do. Lots of sewing.”

Tucktoo said she and other seamstresses in her community were making the parkas for the 1974 Arctic Winter Games happening in Anchorage, Alaska. Once the garments headed to the event, she didn’t expect to see them again.
Until now.
Selena 'Kublu' Tucktoo of Taloyoak was surprised to learn that a parka she created for the 1974 Arctic Winter Games was among those found at the Kamloops thrift store. (Liny Lamberink/CBC)
Some of those parkas were recently found at a thrift store in Kamloops, B.C. — and could soon be heading back to where they came from.

Mike Williams, a retired IT worker in Kamloops, found a parka bearing Tucktoo’s name at a Value Village in his city in mid-October, along with three others of a similar style. They caught his eye, but he didn’t buy them right away.
“I think it was the next day I went in, and they were still there, and I took a closer look at them and I knew they were special. So I bought them,” he recalled.
Williams bought the 4 parkas in mid-October, originally thinking he'd re-sell them. But as he learned more about their history, he decided to do something else. (Submitted by Mike Williams)
At the time, Williams thought he might be able to make money re-selling the parkas. They’d cost him $325 altogether.
But he was curious about them, so he posted about his find on social media and soon was in touch with people who knew more about the garments. That's when he realized he didn't want to sell them.
“I think they were meant to return to the community, and I think I was meant to get them there,” he said.
Hundreds of outfits made by craft collective

Arnaqarvik was a craft collective that started in the early 1970s in Taloyoak, then known as Spence Bay. Judy McGrath, who moved there from Newfoundland, and Arnaoyok Alookee, of Taloyoak, were instrumental in getting it off the ground, according to the Kitikmeot Heritage Society.
The society says the collective was contracted to design and produce nearly 400 outfits for athletes and dignitaries from the Northwest Territories for the 1974 Arctic Winter Games.
Archival photos show the parkas being worn by flag-bearers marching at the event in Alaska.

A photo in the N.W.T. Archives shows flag-bearers marching at the 1974 Arctic Winter Games in Anchorage, Alaska. (NWT Archives/Northwest Territories. Department of Public Works and Services fonds/G-1995-001: 0819)

In an email to CBC News, a collections manager with the Kitikmeot Heritage Society in Nunavut said the four parkas Williams found seem consistent in their materials and manufacturing, and pointed out that some have a “WG,” which stands for "Winter Games," on their labels.

Three of the parkas Williams found still have labels attached bearing the names of the people who made them. The fourth, an amauti-style parka designed to carry a baby in the hood, has the name of its steamstress embroidered in Inuktitut syllabics.

Three of the parkas Williams found have labels attached to them with the name of the seamstress who made them. The seamstress who made the an amauti-style parka designed to carry a baby in the hood, is identifiable by a name embroidered in Inuktitut syllabics. (Mike Williams)
Tucktoo was surprised when she heard about Williams's find at the Kamloops thrift store, and curious about how they ended up there.
“How come the people that wore them didn’t keep them, I wonder?” she said, speaking to CBC News on Tuesday during a visit to Yellowknife. “Maybe it’s not their style? I don’t know.”
Getting them back to Taloyoak
Williams was eventually able to get in contact with people in Taloyoak about the parkas, including some living family members of seamstresses who’ve since died.
He's now trying to figure out the best way to get the garments back home.
A photo of the parka designs that the Arnaqarvik collective created for the Arctic Winter Games in 1974. (Kitikmeot Heritage Society)
Worried that a parcel might get lost somewhere along the 2,500-kilometre journey, Williams started thinking about delivering the parkas himself.

He was initially discouraged when he looked up the cost of flights. A return flight between Edmonton and Taloyoak in early December would cost more than $3,000, so he decided to reach out to airlines and ask for help.
Canadian North responded, and offered Williams and his wife free flights to the community.
The challenge now, however, is finding accommodation when they get to the community of around 1,000 people. But Williams said he’s determined to get the parkas back to Taloyoak, one way or another.
What happens to the parkas after that has not yet been decided. One idea that’s emerged from speaking with community members, Williams said, is to put the parkas on display at Taloyoak’s high school.

items: Repatriation of Indigenous artifacts key for cultural identity: Northern leaders
A Tlingit artist is on a mission to return a traditional artifact to its original home

blocks.text: Pangniq High School principal Rod Drover told CBC News on Thursday he was just learning of the garments — but he was enthusiastic about making them part of a display the school is working on in its foyer. He encouraged Williams to get in touch with him.
"This is exciting stuff," Drover said.
“Our desire is to celebrate the culture, making sure we have artifacts, things of history, relevance, and to showcase it, not only to our students but to the community.”
Williams said he’d bring the garments to the school and let the community decide from there what to do with them.
"They know what's best," he said.
Tucktoo supports having the parkas put on display somewhere in Taloyoak, but she’s also interested in having the one she made returned to her directly.
“I’m sure my daughter would love to use it for patterns.”
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Liny Lamberink is a reporter for CBC North, covering the Northwest Territories, Nunavut, and Yukon. She moved to Yellowknife in March 2021, after working as a reporter and newscaster in Ontario for five years. You can reach her at liny.lamberink@cbc.ca

articles.summary: NVIDIA's former CEO is alleged to have been compromised by a Chinese spy. We explore the state of spycraft in the contemporary age.

blocks.text: Front Burner
NVIDIA's former CEO is alleged to have been compromised by a Chinese spy. We explore the state of spycraft in the contemporary age.
LISTEN | FRONT BURNER:
Front Burner32:28Who's spying on whom and why?
The allegation that NVIDIA's former CEO is alleged to have been compromised by a Chinese spy raises all kinds of questions that sit at the heart of espionage and spycraft.
Since the time of antiquity, societies have sought to surveil and intercept communications both their friends and enemies.

Today, foreign intelligence services are working to cultivate relationships with politicians, penetrate businesses and universities, cultivate assets, steal valuable technology, and monitor dissidents living thousands of kilometres from home.

David Gioe is a former U.S. intelligence officer who now works as a visiting professor of intelligence and international security in the department of War Studies at Kings College London. He's our guest today.
