articles.title: 'I've Lost Her Forever' — Why German voice actors are refusing to sign Netflix's AI contract
articles.summary: For decades, Germans have known Hollywood's biggest stars through the same familiar voices. Now an AI clause in Netflix contracts is splitting the industry over whether it protects performers or…

image.caption: Because she won't sign a new contract with an AI clause, Katrin Fröhlich will no longer be the German voice of Cameron Diaz on NetflixImage: Netflix/ZUMA/picture alliance

blocks.text: When does Cameron Diaz not sound like Cameron Diaz? When you're in a German cinema.
For over 30 years, whenever the Oscar-winning actor has appeared on German screens, she has spoken with the voice of Katrin Fröhlich.

The same goes for all other famous actors. In Germany's €125-million ($138-million) voiceover industry, Hollywood's up-and-comers are "adopted" by a voice actor who provides their German voice — often for decades — ensuring continuity and a certain relationship to the stars for audiences.
But on Netflix, and perhaps elsewhere, many of those voices might be about to change.
Netflix contract sparks AI dispute

Recently, Fröhlich and fellow voice actors Anne Helm (Margot Robbie) and Luise Helm (Scarlett Johansson) published a video on social media, letting their followers know they wouldn't provide their voices anymore.
The reason? They refuse to sign Netflix's contract, seen by DW, which contains a clause that lets the American entertainment giant use their voices for training its AI.
They're not the first voiceover artists to speak out on the topic. But they are the first ones to go viral.

blocks.caption: Katrin Fröhlich, who has dubbed the German voice of Cameron Diaz for over 30 years, is worried about the future of the voiceover industryImage: Nicole Kubelka/Geisler-Fotopress/picture alliance

blocks.text: "It was unexpected, completely," Fröhlich said. "For whatever reason, we managed to reach people, perhaps because … we are three well-known women in the voiceover industry."
"Over the years, we've managed to make good names for ourselves. It seems to have touched people that we made this statement together," she said.
Union says deal offers legal safeguards
The new AI clause has been in Netflix's contracts since January 2026. Voice actors sign one ahead of every production. It was negotiated by BFFS, Germany's union for film and television actors.

Fröhlich, like a significant number of voice actors, is not a member and feels as though the union went over their heads. However, BFFS says the deal gives them protection they wouldn't otherwise have.
Till Völger, an attorney and member of the union's board, says previous contracts and those with other streaming services are silent on AI or contain sweeping AI permissions.

If an AI-generated voice doesn't sound like a particular person, companies are free to use the data they have gathered as they wish. Training can take place in other jurisdictions and may not require the actor's consent at all, he pointed out.
"We have a massive, massive protection gap," Völger told DW.
Is AI killing creative jobs?

Against that backdrop, BFFS argues the deal with Netflix is a step forward. It allows the company to train its own systems with recordings, but voice actors must give separate, explicit consent before their recordings are used to create actual AI-generated voices, even if the voice isn't recognizable as theirs.
"We've created a contractual right that the law doesn't provide," said Völger. "Is the situation perfect? No. Is it better than before? Yes."
He would like to see other streaming services agree to the same conditions that Netflix has. In his view, only legislation could create the necessary protections voice actors are seeking.
Netflix says human performance "is and remains important to us," in statement provided to DW.
"In recent years, we have commissioned thousands of hours of German dubbing, and we intend to continue supporting a similar volume of work and the use of human voices," the statement continued.

blocks.caption: Matti Klemm is the voice of children's character Benjamin BlümchenImage: RTL+/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Voice actor plans legal challenge
Matti Klemm, the voice of Jason Momoa and beloved children's cartoon character Benjamin Blümchen, sees things differently. Like Fröhlich, he is refusing to sign the new contract.

"In short, it says: as soon as I record something for Netflix, I'm automatically training their AI, for free," he told DW. "My job is to create a German original, a dubbed version with my performance, not to train the computer systems of some tech companies."
He is taking Netflix to court, backed by the Society for Civil Rights (GFF), to find out how his voice has been used for training in previous projects.

According to Davy Wang, who is coordinating the case for Klemm and GFF, the lawsuit will seek to stop Netflix using his recordings for training, disclose how previous data was used and establish whether Klemm is entitled to any damages.
The suit will be filed at the end of the year or in early 2027. Supporters donated more than €50,000 to the legal fund in the first week following its announcement.

blocks.caption: Matti Klemm wants to find out exactly how Netflix has used his voice to train its AI and is suing the companyImage: Christoph Soeder/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: For Klemm, what is at stake goes beyond training. "It's not about our voice, it's about our soul, our performance, the way we are," he said. "How far have we come when AI training matters more than my actual work?"
Netflix said it cannot comment on a case that has not yet been filed.
Industry fears growing AI impact

For a multimillion-euro industry, the outcome of the case could reach well beyond Netflix and other companies and creative branches are watching. But no matter what the outcome of the lawsuit or contract agreements, voice actors' fears for their future run deep.
Those who don't sign contracts can't work, and streaming companies can make up a significant part of their income.
"Many say: I've held out for 10 months, but I can't anymore. I have to sign this contract, I have to pay my rent, I have to feed my children," explained Fröhlich.
Beyond that, many fear the future of their industry and the connections they have formed with stars and audiences.
"For a many people I'm connected with Cameron Diaz and I evoke something within them," said Fröhlich.
But if Diaz is involved in more Netflix projects, "then I've basically lost her," she concluded. "I'll never be her voice again."

articles.title: Senate begins plenary deliberations for 2027 national budget
articles.summary: Senators are proposing P204.634 billion in amendments in the 2027 national budget

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines – The Senate on Monday, November 23, began plenary deliberations on the proposed P7.2-trillion national budget for 2027, with lawmakers proposing P204.634 billion in amendments that prioritize “basic needs,” including health care and education, while cutting billions of pesos in infrastructure projects.

Senator JV Ejercito, chairperson of the Senate finance committee, sponsored Committee Report No. 131 on House Bill No. 10858, or the General Appropriations Bill (GAB), formally bringing the proposed budget to the plenary for deliberations.
In his sponsorship speech, Ejercito bat for a “back to basics” approach in the proposed P7.2 trillion national budget, emphasizing the need to prioritize essential services.

“Health care, food security, education, livelihood, employment, and security — these are the things that we want to focus on during our outlining and deliberations of the 2027 national budget. Back to basics,” Ejercito said.
“Before we focus on complicated matters, we should focus what limited resources we have on ensuring that the basic needs of our people are provided,” he said.
The Senate’s P204.634-billion proposed amendments include a P97-billion reduction in the allocation for 3,463 projects of the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH).

These include 36 DPWH buildings, 295 projects deemed noncompliant for lacking proper documentation under the National Expenditure Program, and 3,132 noncompliant projects that appeared only in the House-approved GAB.
Ejercito previously said the reductions in the DPWH budget would be realigned to foreign-assisted infrastructure projects, which saw a P130-billion decrease in the House-approved GAB.

Budget watchdogs People’s Budget Coalition and BetterGovPH had earlier flagged nearly 7,000 projects worth P190 billion that lacked published project attachments in the House-approved 2027 budget. PBC also tracked some 6,200 DPWH projects worth P170 million that were inserted into the budget.
“This, Mr. President, is the direction we want to pursue in the 2027 national budget. Back to basics, but with a clear vision for economic recovery and nation-building,” said Ejercito.
Under the Senate version of the budget, the health sector received a P52-billion increase, with funding partly sourced from realignments within the Department of Health (DOH).

State health insurer Philippine Health Insurance Corporation, or PhilHealth, received an additional P19.8 billion, raising its allocation from P74.4 billion under the House-approved GAB to P94.2 billion in the Senate version.

The DOH Office of the Secretary received an additional P9.6 billion, increasing its budget to P378.6 billion. This includes P5.49 billion for the Health Facilities Enhancement Program, P1.09 billion for health promotion programs, P1.5 billion for immunization programs, and P736 million for the Sulu transition.
The Senate realigned funding for medical assistance to the Zero Balance Billing program, allocating P1 billion for local government-run hospitals.

The education sector, meanwhile, received P915.4 billion in the Senate’s budget bill. Of this amount, P11.8 billion will go to the Department of Education, including P11 billion for the School-Based Feeding Program to support the universal feeding program for kindergarten to Grade 1 students.

State universities and colleges will receive P138.2 billion for the continued construction and improvement of their school buildings, with each SUC receiving P7.5 million for the Smart Campus Project — a program that would provide internet connectivity to over 100 campuses.
The Senate budget bill also provides additional P33.1 billion in funding for foreign-assisted infrastructure projects, primarily to restore funding cuts in the House-approved GAB.
Among these are P4.7 billion to restore the government’s counterpart funding for the Metro Manila Subway Project and P15 billion in loan proceeds for the North-South Commuter Railway project.
A combined P146.5 million will also be allocated for the NCR Busway Project, Active Transport Bike Share System, and Safe Pathways Program.
The Senate also allocated budget to enhance food security and ensure productivity of farmlands amid the threat of Super El Niño, earmarking P251 billion for the Department of Agriculture (DA).

This includes an additional P4 billion for the DA’s Rice Program to help boost rice production; a P250 million fund for programs helping farmers amid the impending drought; and an augmentation of P1 billion for the DA’s Quick Response Fund to “assist our farmers the earliest time the streams and wells show signs of drying up.”

More than P1 billion was allotted for the establishment of the storage facility Benguet AgriPinoy Trading Center, while P50 million and P200 million were allocated for the construction of a cold storage facility in Barlig, Mountain Province and Oriental Mindoro, respectively.
The Department of Human Settlements and Urban Development will also receive P4.04 billion to support the Expanded Pambansang Pabahay para sa Pilipino Program.

Meanwhile, senators provided an additional P1.73 billion to the Department of National Defense, hiking its budget to P326.9 billion. This is on top of the P50 billion earmarked for the continued modernization of the Armed Forces of the Philippines.

Ejercito also underscored the need to strengthen the capabilities of the Philippine Navy to improve maritime patrols and reinforce the country’s presence in the West Philippine Sea. The Philippine Coast Guard, for its part, will receive P45.6 billion, including an additional P146.8-million allocation, to support its operations and maritime security efforts.

Ejercito filed the committee report on November 20. It was signed by 18 senators, including senators Tito Sotto, Migz Zubiri, Bam Aquino, Bong Go, Risa Hontiveros, Kiko Pangilinan, Erwin Tulfo, Joel Villanueva, Ping Lacson, Chiz Escudero, Lito Lapid, Raffy Tulfo, Imee Marcos, Robinhood Padilla, Mark Villar, Pia Cayetano, and Camille Villar.
In a manifestation, Senate Minority Leader Alan Peter Cayetano explained why he did not sign the committee report.

“My signature is not on that committee report not because I did not want to sign but because it is physically impossible to come up with a good judgment, even if I do trust the chairman of the committee on finance, Senator JV,” Cayetano said.
Senators are working on a tight schedule to ratify the budget bill and avoid a reenacted budget in 2027.
Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian said over the weekend that the country could not afford another reenacted budget, arguing that a fresh spending plan would help stimulate the economy.

“If we have a new budget, we will have new spending, because if we analyze it, one of our country’s economic problems is slow spending. So, the 2027 budget will serve as a stimulus program to it,” Gatchalian told DZBB Super Radyo.
The Senate is eyeing holding an open bicameral conference committee on the proposed 2027 budget on December 13, with ratification targeted for December 17.

Apart from the budget, the Commission on Appointments (CA) is also racing against time to process the appointments of at least 35 presidential appointees, including Cabinet secretaries, ambassadors, and military officers, before its December 17 adjournment.
Gatchalian said the CA would hold three hearings before the break, from 8 am to 12 pm, ahead of the Senate’s plenary budget deliberations at 1 pm.
Senators are hoping to conclude the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte before the end of the year. The trial is currently on a brief break and is scheduled to resume on December 1.
“Whatever the ruling is — be it conviction or acquittal — the consensus is we want to finish the trial before end of the year,” Gatchalian added. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Budget cuts threaten Germany's fight against antisemitism and racism
articles.summary: Numerous grassroots initiatives in Germany are facing funding cuts. Affected organizations are sounding the alarm, pointing to growing challenges posed by far-right extremism.

image.caption: Demonstrations against the far-right AfD have drawn thousands of participantsImage: Fabian Sommer/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Initiatives and organizations in Germany are speaking out against planned budget cuts to the work of strengthening democracy and fighting racism and antisemitism. Berlin is planning drastic savings measures in its draft federal budget for 2027, which is to be debated in parliament this Friday.

The "Living democracy" (Demokratie Leben) program from the Ministry for Family Affairs is set to receive a total of €170 million ($187 million). That is about €20 million less than the current year's budget allocation.

The draft was agreed upon by Germany's governing coalition of the conservative Union – of the Christian Democrats (CDU) and its Bavarian sister party, the Christian Social Union (CSU) – and the center-left Social Democrats.

Numerous organizations consider the cuts a dire signal. Tahera Ameer from the Amadeu Antonio Foundation, a Berlin-based NGO which campaigns against right-wing extremism and discrimination, sees many initiatives in Germany under existential threat.

"In view of the antisemitic agitation, the open violence and the ever-increasing legitimization of its normalization, it is concerning that the very structures and grants which do something to oppose them are now standing on the verge of collapse," Ameer explained during a media briefing alongside other like-minded organizations.
Politically-disillusioned youth? Far from it!
Lasting damage to democracy in Germany?
According to the initiatives, the work to strengthen democratic civil society could suffer lasting damage, because long-established structures cannot simply be rebuilt after they have been destroyed.
The thing that outraged many organizations: The cuts come at a time when the extreme right is celebrating numerous election victories in Germany.

The Alternative for Germany (AfD), parts of which are considered far-right extremist, achieved record-high results in several elections in 2026, most notably in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt. "Especially in view of the AfD possibly coming into government in Saxony-Anhalt, we need these structures more urgently than ever," urged Tahera Ameer.

The promotion of democratic civil society in Germany has been controversial for years. While initiatives and associations regularly appeal for more money, some conservative politicians repeatedly criticize an alleged one-sidedness in the allocation of public funds.

During the federal parliamentary debate on the funding program in March 2025, Christian Democrat politician Marvin Schulz supported the planned changes, which were put forward by German Families Minister Karin Prien, also of the CDU: "We need new areas of focus," he said. Projects working against extreme Islamism and antisemitism were underrepresented, he said.

But initiatives to combat antisemitism will also receive less funding in the future. The Central Committee of German Catholics (ZdK) criticized cuts to the Federal Association of Departments for Research and Information on Antisemitism (RIAS), the nationwide OFEK counselling center for people affected by antisemitic violence and discrimination, and the German Alliance against Islamophobia and discrimination against Muslims, CLAIM.

The ZdK called on the German government to continue its advocacy for the protection of Jewish and Muslim life and secure this structurally and financially. They say planned cuts achieve the opposite and are a fatal signal to a diverse and democratic society.
Games with purpose — more than entertainment
AfD: 'Program to secure power by the Left'
The AfD went further in its criticism: The party called for the funding to be stopped entirely, calling the initiatives a "program for the Left to secure power for itself."

If the AfD governs in Saxony-Anhalt, it wants wide-ranging cuts. The party wants to completely abolish the renowned State Center for Civic Education and cut state funding from numerous other organizations.
In December, the AfD, which has been classified as right-wing extremist in Saxony-Anhalt, wants its lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund to be the first AfD state premier to head a state government.

A spokesperson from the federal government's Family Affairs Ministry responded to questions from DW by referring to the need for the government to consolidate its budget. The goal was that funding programs "reliably continue, also in 2027, and make the biggest and widest impact possible with the means available."

However, an alliance of several organizations does not want to give up and is calling for a complete reversal of the decision: Instead of implementing the cuts, the organizations want the government to boost the funding pool by €50 million.
German influencer fights extremism on TikTok
How is democratic civil society prioritized?
"Work to strengthen democracy must be funded," urged Tahera Ameer from the Amadeu Antonio Foundation. "That is a priority that we are currently not seeing. And that is very unsettling."

Many organizations point out that the consequences of the cuts will not remain abstract. They will have very real effects on people who experience discrimination in Germany, Lina Mitschke fears. She leads the Berlin association "Each One Teach One" (EOTO), an education and empowerment organization for people of color.

"The needs haven't gone away. But from January, people coming in have nobody to properly speak with; the phone will no longer be picked up; emails will go unanswered if someone needs support," she said.

For organizations such as EOTO, the planned cuts are a bitter setback. In past years, they had managed to raise awareness of the lived reality of Black people in Germany. "The experiences of more than a million Black people in Germany would be negated with the cuts," Mitschke said.
The associations want to fight until the very end to reverse the decision. They say work to promote and support democracy is what holds society together.
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Chamonix mayor plans tourist limits for Alpine beauty spot
articles.summary:
Rising numbers around Lac Blanc are having big impact on environment and on visitors’ enjoyment, mayor says

In the Alpine town of Chamonix, most tourist paths lead to the national park with…

blocks.text: In the Alpine town of Chamonix, most tourist paths lead to the national park with spectacular views across Mont Blanc and the shrinking blue glaciers. In the summer, up to 4,000 tourists a day hike or take the cable car to the lakes high in the Aiguilles Rouges nature reserve.

Many of them descend disappointed. Once a place of nature and tranquility, the beauty spot’s visitor numbers have more than doubled since 2020, spoiling the experience and leaving trails of litter, threatening the environment and wildlife.
Now Chamonix plans to become the first town in the Alps to introduce visitor quotas, to limit the number of hikers around Lac Blanc and the Lacs des Chéserys.

The town’s mayor, Francois-Xavier Laffin, announced last week that from next June tourists would be required to book in advance to visit the area. After booking, they will receive a QR code granting them access.

blocks.caption: People visit the ice cave of the Mer de Glace glacier in Chamonix. Photograph: Delpixart/Getty Images/iStockphoto

blocks.text: Laffin championed the quotas after visiting Marseille, where a similar scheme was introduced limiting access to the Calanques national park in 2022. He said the aim was “reserve to preserve”, adding that visiting the mountains would still be free but subject to conditions.

Laffin said mass tourism was having a major impact on the environment, wildlife and on visitors’ enjoyment of the reserve. “Lac Blanc is one place we cannot let continue to deteriorate” he said, adding that the council was looking at additional regulations in other areas.
The plan, which needs the final approval of the local prefect, would restrict the number of visitors to the Lac Blanc area to between 600 and 1,000 a day for four months from June to September.

Christian Schwoehrer, the director of the Haute-Savoie Nature Conservation Agency, which manages the reserve, said: “We will see how it works for the next three years and if it does then it will be extended and maybe applied to other areas. This is a nature reserve but when there are thousands of visitors a day there’s no peace for the protected species or local people and we need stronger measures to control this.

“At points of entry [to the reserve] there will be ‘eco guards’ to verify that people have reserved. If they haven’t, they could be fined, though our intention is to avoid fining people by making sure they know in advance and cannot say they weren’t warned.”

blocks.caption: Visitors near Lac Blanc in the Aiguilles Rouge nature reserve above Chamonix. Photograph: Simon Turner/Alamy

blocks.text: The quota plan has met some local opposition from the land’s legal owners. Lac Blanc sits in just under 3 square miles of private estate held by 35 families under a historic entity that has existed for centuries and is now managed by the Montagne de Chéserys company.
One of the landowners, Guillaume Ravanel, a mountain guide, agreed tourist numbers need controlling but suggested visitors should be asked to pay a small entry fee to access the reserve.

Frédéric Charlet-Berguerand, a co-manager of Montagne de Chéserys, told Le Monde: “This quota system is innovative and virtuous.” Contacted by the Guardian, he added: “That said, there will be no quotas on our private property until they are approved by a meeting of the owners,” due to be held in December. “Let’s not put the cart before the horse.”

blocks.caption: The mayor is also looking at tighter controls on the Ultra-Trail du Mont Blanc. Photograph: AscentXmedia/Getty Images

blocks.text: Laffin said the quota plan would cost about €590,000 for the three-year “experimental” period. Financing has yet to be arranged but he said part would be raised by Chamonix and other local authorities and the town would be applying for a grant from the government’s “green fund” to help protect the environment. Private sponsors are also being sought.

The mayor, elected in March, has made managing tourist numbers a priority. He is also looking at tighter controls on the three-week Ultra-Trail du Mont Blanc, an ultramarathon circling the Mont-Blanc massif through France, Italy and Switzerland that begins in Chamonix. The event, started in 2003, now attracts 10,000 runners and up to 50,000 visitors each August.

Schwoehrer said summer crowds meant local people were avoiding the reserve. A recent survey found that 55% of visitors who ascended to Lac Blanc said they were disappointed by the experience, he said.
“We don’t want to stop people going there, just have a few stronger rules. It’s a compromise to ensure that visitors have a good experience and at the same time the natural environment is protected.”

articles.title: Samchan exec's testimony crucial to Romualdez plunder case -- Ombudsman spox
articles.summary: The testimony of Felicito Guevarra, an executive of Samchan Foreign Exchange Corp., could prove crucial to the Ombudsman's P7.4-billion plunder case against former House Speaker Martin Romualdez and…

blocks.text: Published November 23, 2026 6:38pm

The testimony of Felicito Guevarra, an executive of Samchan Foreign Exchange Corp., could prove crucial to the Ombudsman's P7.4-billion plunder case against former House Speaker Martin Romualdez and his co-accused, Assistant Ombudsman Mico Clavano said on Monday.

Clavano made the statement after the Ombudsman asked the Sandiganbayan to discharge Guevarra as a co-accused so he could act as a prosecution witness in Romualdez's bail hearing, replacing former Public Works Secretary Manuel Bonoan
In the same omnibus motion, the Ombudsman also asked the court to allow Guevarra to remain in the custody of the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI).
Guevarra surrendered to the NBI on Nov. 19.

Clavano said Guevarra's testimony could prove crucial to the case because, as a foreign exchange firm executive, he may provide insight into how large-scale corruption proceeds are handled in cash, often leaving little documentary or financial trail in the banking system.

“Pag ganito na kalaki 'yung nangyayaring korapsyon, usually hindi talaga dumadaan sa bangko 'yan," Clavano said during the Ombudsman's weekly radio program, TanodBayan, aired over state-run Radyo Pilipinas.
(When corruption reaches this magnitude, transactions usually do not go through banks.)
"Walang deposit slip, walang pirma, walang AMLC record na may nag-transfer ng funds from account A to account B. Usually diyan, cash na ang transactions nila,” he added.
(There are no deposit slips, signatures or Anti-Money Laundering Council records showing transfers between accounts. These transactions are usually conducted in cash.)
Guevarra could help investigators establish how cash was handled and moved, Clavano said.
He also suggested that the use of cash explained why investigators found little documentary evidence in financial records.
“Alam na ng mga public officials na hindi talaga dapat sila gumamit ng bangko kasi mahuhuli ka agad. That's all recorded. May paper trail 'yan, may pirma pa," Clavano said.
(Public officials already know they should not use banks because transactions are immediately recorded, leaving a paper trail and signatures.)
"So itong pagsuko ng isang foreign exchange [firm official], it will be substantial [to our case],” he added.
(That is why the surrender of a foreign exchange firm official would be substantial to the case.)

Clavano did not identify the transactions or individuals involved. However, the prosecution's AMLC financial investigator, Atty. Jan Mark Busa, had earlier told the Sandiganbayan that remittances worth P560.5 million to accounts linked to Romualdez from 2022 to 2025 were not related to flood control projects.
Clavano stressed that the Ombudsman had never claimed that the alleged proceeds of corruption were transferred directly to Romualdez through bank accounts reflected in AMLC records.

“Wala naman talagang dadaan sa account. Hindi naman talaga 'yan ang theory ng Ombudsman. Ngayon, sumuko na 'yung sa money exchange [firm executive], dito natin malalaman kung ano talaga ang nangyari,” he said.

(Those transactions would not actually pass through bank accounts. That has never been the Ombudsman's theory. Now that the money exchange firm executive has surrendered, this is where we will find out what really happened.)

Meanwhile, Romualdez's lawyer, Judd Roy III, questioned the prosecution's move to replace Bonoan as a witness, saying the defense had prepared its strategy based on the original set of prosecution witnesses and the criminal information filed against his client.

“The lines of defense were prepared, evidentiary positions were taken… even our cross-examination of the other witnesses was all in recognition of that [criminal] information [filed]. And now they're saying that it will not substantially affect the case," Roy said in a separate interview.
"Put yourself in our shoes. Do you honestly believe that is the case?” he added.— MCG, GMA News
Follow GMA News Online on Facebook for real-time news and developments in the Philippines and around the world.

articles.title: From mocked to mainstream: how Spain’s far-right Vox transformed its fortunes
articles.summary:
Party that won just 0.2% of the vote in 2016 is on course for almost 20% this time and could be part of next government

Almost exactly eight years ago, a video clip of a stocky, bearded man…

blocks.text: Almost exactly eight years ago, a video clip of a stocky, bearded man riding a horse through western Andalucía went viral in Spain. The rider was Santiago Abascal, the leader of the far-right Vox party, the soundtrack was a bombastic snatch of the Lord of the Rings score, and the caption was an equally unsubtle callback to the 700-year fight to wrest the Iberian peninsula from Islamic rule. “La Reconquista comenzará en tierras andaluzas,” it read – the reconquest will begin on Andalucían soil.

Celebrated by some, jeered by others – and inventively lampooned by those with sufficient skill and time on their hands – the video didn’t seem quite as amusing three weeks later when Vox broke through into the political mainstream by winning 12 seats in Andalucía’s regional parliament.

Until that moment, the prevailing wisdom had been that Spain’s experiences of the Franco dictatorship had inoculated the country against the far right, and that Vox was a tiny, fringe outfit whose prospects were terminally limited after it had picked up just 0.2% of the vote in the 2016 general election.

Fast-forward to late 2026 and the horseman seems less comical still. Vox, now the third largest party in Spain, is poised to pick up almost 20% of the vote in the snap general election on 29 November and, very possibly, to form a coalition government with the conservative People’s party (PP).

blocks.caption: Abascal addresses supporters during an election campaign rally in Cornellà de Llobregat. Photograph: Josep Lago/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Abascal is going all out as the campaign enters its final days, peppering his patriotic appeals with familiar, baseless conspiracy theories. Last week he suggested that the socialist prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, was conspiring with dark forces to undermine democracy and change the country’s demographic makeup.
“The next elections may be the last that Spaniards get to decide,” he posted on X. “That’s what Sánchez and his accomplices at home and abroad are working toward … Vote so you don’t get replaced.”
Catalan catalyst

How did Vox’s fortunes transform so massively and so quickly? The party was founded in late 2013 by disenchanted PP members who felt the conservatives had grown too indulgent of the demands of Basque and Catalan nationalist parties, but it struggled to make its mark. The highlight of its early years, during which it relied on hefty sum donated by the Iranian exile group the National Council of Resistance of Iran, was unfurling a large Spanish flag on the Rock of Gibraltar.

All that changed in the autumn of 2017 when a Catalan push for independence pitched Spain into crisis and left the PP government looking soft and ill-prepared. The crisis proved a godsend for Vox, simultaneously vindicating its distrust of Catalan and Basque nationalist parties and allowing it to position itself as an uncompromising defender of Spanish unity.

“Vox’s initial growth was driven by a reaction to Catalan nationalism – specifically, the sense around 2017 that Spain might fall apart,” says Miguel González, an El País journalist who covers Vox and the author of a new book, The Extremist Galaxy: Funders, Allies and Strategies of the New Far Right.

blocks.caption: Pro-independence Catalan flags in Barcelona in 2017. Photograph: Lluís Gené/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: It gave Vox the profile it needed to pursue what González considers its most significant move: dragging immigration into mainstream politics and forcing a rattled PP to lurch further to the right.

“It was only an issue in a few specific places with high levels of immigration – such as El Ejido in Almería, or certain areas in Murcia,” González says. “[But] Vox has managed to put this issue on the political agenda, and, what’s more, the PP has gradually come to adopt some of their positions.”

This summer’s mass influx into Spain’s north African territory of Ceuta, when more than 80,000 men, women and children crossed over from Morocco, is a case in point. Abascal called it “an invasion and an act of war promoted by Morocco”, while the PP’s leader, Alberto Núñez Feijóo urged the expulsion of all who had entered, regardless of their age and individual circumstances.

The PP’s efforts to stop its voters slipping into the embrace of its far-right rival have led it into all sorts of contortions. Although Feijóo’s predecessor, Pablo Casado, famously rounded on Vox in 2020, accusing Abascal and co of peddling a politics based on “fear, anger, resentment and revenge”, the PP has repeatedly entered into regional coalition governments with Vox and now runs four of Spain’s autonomous regions with the party.

Vicente Valentim, a professor of political science at Spain’s IE University and the author of The Normalisation of the Radical Right, says that when centre-right parties adopt the language and postures of the far right, they end up legitimising it.

“After the initial normalisation moment when these parties first become successful – entering parliament etc – there’s a second step,” he says. “The centre right moves closer to them, starts speaking the same way that they do, starts going into coalitions.”

This can prove electorally expensive, he says. “The PP has moved closer to Vox, and when you have two parties that have such similar views on an issue as important as immigration, [some] voters simply prefer the original to the copy, and so they’re going to vote for Vox.”
Hate figures

Alongside a fixation on immigration, Vox has also brought its predilection for hate figures into the mainstream of Spanish politics – be they the secessionist former Catalan president Carles Puigdemont, the former leader of the leftwing Podemos Pablo Iglesias, or Sánchez.
“Vox talks about traitors and about criminals,” says González. “What Vox is doing isn’t offering political assessments, it’s making legal judgments.”

Abascal’s loathing of Sánchez is well documented – in 2023, the Vox leader said a day would come when the Spanish people would “want to see [Sánchez] strung up by his feet” – and his party’s manifesto vows to “undertake legal proceedings to have Sánchez and his government prosecuted for treason and crimes against the security of the state, based on their actions during the invasion of Ceuta”.

blocks.caption: Vox has vowed to prosecute Pedro Sánchez and his government for treason. Photograph: SOPA Images/LightRocket/Getty Images

blocks.text: The party’s increasingly strident language has been matched by a more recent refusal to sever ties with some of the more extreme figures in its ranks and in its orbit.

In the run-up to the first of the two general elections in 2019, Vox was forced to drop the historian and commentator Fernando Paz from its list of candidates after Jewish groups complained about his “denialist and revisionist” approach to the Holocaust. Today he sits on the honorary board of the Foundation for the Defence of the Spanish Nation, a Vox-aligned platform of which Abascal is a co-founder and board member.

One pro-Israel lobbying group has expressed concerns in the past about Jordi de la Fuente, a Vox member and former neo-Nazi party leader who heads the Solidarity trade union, which was created by Vox. De la Fuente, who is awaiting trial for his alleged role in a violent attack on a centre housing unaccompanied migrant children in 2019, is standing as Vox’s candidate in Tarragona. Vox has insisted its candidate is innocent of a charge of “inciting hatred, hostility, violence or discrimination on the grounds of national origin”.

Alejandro Baer, a sociologist at the Spanish National Research Council who specialises in memory, genocide studies and contemporary Jewish studies, says: “A few years ago, the party was forced to distance itself from them, but now they don’t seem to represent a liability. Vox appears to be sufficiently consolidated and legitimate to openly incorporate people with backgrounds in these extremist spaces.”
Generation gap

Vox’s trajectory is plain to see in Rioja, a small town in the eastern Andalucían province of Almería. Long a socialist stronghold, Rioja was the only municipality where Vox finished first in May’s regional election – a poll that resulted in another PP-Vox coalition, after the conservatives lost their absolute majority. And yet the quiet town, whose palm trees and bougainvillaeas rustle in the warm November breeze, doesn’t exactly have the feel of a far-right frontier. Its divisions appear more generational than political.

blocks.caption: A Vox supporter at a rally in Madrid. Photograph: Francisco Seco/AP

blocks.text: Few of the younger people walking down the main road that bisects Rioja are surprised by Vox’s strong showing here. Fewer still appear bothered by Sánchez’s warning that a PP-Vox coalition will “roll back progress” and lead to the loss of hard-won social advances.

“My own ideology tends more to the right,” says Patricio López, 29, who works in an agricultural company. “I’ve noticed that people of my age tend to be more rightwing than leftwing, and I think that’s because they feel like they’ve been shortchanged. Housing, for example, is a much bigger issue for young people than it is for older people. And the left hasn’t looked after young people over the past eight years.”
One older resident, however, believes Vox’s surge in Rioja has more to do with protest votes from the young and the proximity of a large military camp than a rejection of its socialist past.

“I think it was just a gesture of distrust and revenge in the way Spanish politics is these days – it’s pure partisan theatre and it’s all very Game of Thrones,” says Rafael Ruiz Martínez, 63, who works for the local council. But he adds: “For those of us who lived through some of the Franco era, the Vox stuff doesn’t sound good.”
Another younger local man, who prefers not to give his name, agrees many people are sick of traditional politics and of a political class that has failed them.
“I reckon whoever gets in – whatever their political stripe – will do what others have done; they’ll dip into the till,” he says. “But politics is politics and people want a change.”

articles.title: Rembrandt's 'The Night Watch' is more alive than you'd expect
articles.summary: A new project and exhibition, "The Night Watch Lives," lifts the veil on the hidden world of microbes covering one of the most famous paintings of the Dutch Golden Age.

image.caption: The exhibition 'The Night Watch Lives' shows which microorganisms were found on the famous Rembrandt paintingImage: Noemi Achthoven/ARTIS

blocks.text: Rembrandt van Rijn's "The Night Watch" is one of the most famous paintings of the Dutch Golden Age. Amsterdam's Rijksmuseum, where the work is on display, hails the artist's 1642 masterpiece as "the turning point in his career and as the superlative example of his creative genius."

In the painting, Rembrandt made dramatic use of light and shadow to guide the viewer's eye to key figures. And unlike static group portraits typical of his era, the artist depicted Amsterdam's civic guards in mid-action, as they prepare to march out.
Beyond the sense of movement featured in "The Night Watch," the painting itself is also alive in a way that's rarely taken into consideration — through the microscopic organisms living on the canvas.
The research project "The Night Watch Lives" explores exactly that question: What kinds of life forms inhabit the surface of the famous painting?
The study is a collaborative scientific and exhibition project between the Rijksmuseum and ARTIS-Micropia — an Amsterdam museum dedicated to the world of microorganisms.

It's part of the broader "Operation Night Watch" restoration and research project described as the "biggest and most wide-ranging ever study and restoration of Rembrandt's most famous painting," started in 2019. Conservators and scientists in this project have been examining every aspect of Rembrandt's masterpiece using cutting-edge technology, seeking new insights into its materials, condition and history — and now, its microbiome.

blocks.caption: 'The Night Watch Lives' study is conducted in collaboration with a major restoration and research project called 'Operation Night Watch'Image: Niels de Vries/Artis/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Putting microbes in the spotlight

The idea behind "The Night Watch Lives" was to "put microbes in a positive spotlight," Eline van Bloois, who led the research, told DW. "Honestly, if you're asking me — I'm a microbiologist, so I'm biased of course — but they really deserve more positive attention."

Over a period of six months, van Bloois will be taking samples once a month directly from the famous painting at the Rijksmuseum, accompanied by the people working on the restoration of "The Night Watch."
Using small sterile discs gently pressed against selected areas of the painting, the samples collect microscopic material from both varnished and unvarnished sections.
These samples are then cultivated in laboratories, allowing previously invisible microbes to grow into visible colonies that can be studied and identified.

At the "The Night Watch Lives" exhibition, visitors can view Petri dishes containing the cultivated microbial colonies. A life-size reproduction of Rembrandt's masterpiece also shows where the samples were taken, and which microorganisms were found there.
A study in progress

At the opening of the exhibition on November 11, the installation included the findings of two of van Bloois' sampling sessions. Four more will be added over the upcoming months, allowing the museum's visitors to follow the results of the study as it unfolds.
That means the exhibition's visitors "will be figuring out what I've found as I'm figuring it out myself," explains the microbiologist. "We really take them through that journey with us."

blocks.caption: Microbiologist Eline van Bloois will be taking samples from the original painting once a month, over a period of six monthsImage: Niels de Vries/ARTIS

blocks.text: People often fear microbes or associate them with disease, even though the vast majority of these microscopic organisms are actually harmless or vital to human survival.

Some of the organisms found on the painting "are very commonly found on human skin, for instance, and they're a healthy part of the microbiome; most humans actually have these bacteria with them," says van Bloois, adding that the presence of these microbes on the painting made sense, since humans are often near the work.

But another bacterium stood out in the samples: Microbacterium saccharophilum, a species first identified at a sugar refinery in Japan in 2013. How this microorganism ended up on the Dutch "Night Watch," or when, is a guessing game.

"It's part of the fun and part of the frustration in microbiology. You cannot ask the microbes where they originate from," says van Bloois. "It would make our lives a bit easier, but it's also fun to have a little bit of a mystery."
The samples also revealed bacteria from soil, often found in plant roots. Could these organisms somehow harm the painting? Could plants start growing on the work?

Van Bloois explains why this is highly unlikely: On the painting, the bacteria can form inactive spores, but for the study, the researcher "provided them with all the nutrients and the right temperature and the right humidity that allowed them to grow again."

Still, studying these organisms may eventually contribute to understanding how paintings age, how environmental conditions affect cultural heritage, and how museums can better preserve priceless works of art.
As to whether the microorganisms could date back to Rembrandt's time, the microbiologist says that's also "highly unlikely" — but here again, microbes cannot reveal their origin story.
When art and science meet

As part of the larger "Operation Night Watch" team, van Bloois is definitely inspired by this "group effort where everyone is just really enthusiastic about telling these stories and adding to the knowledge surrounding 'The Night Watch'."
The microbiological samples revealed by the laboratory process resemble abstract art in miniature: colorful clusters, delicate textures and intricate patterns created by living organisms.
And as the study is unfolding publicly, it also feels like an artistic performance of its own.

The project also perfectly embodies the full name of the museum where the exhibition is held: Natura Artis Magistra, a Latin phrase that translates to "nature is the teacher of art and science," as the microbiologist points out: "It's really cool to see science and art all come together in this project."
The exhibition "The Night Watch Lives" runs at ARTIS-Micropia in Amsterdam until the end of May 2027.

articles.title: [Rappler’s Best] ‘Be very, very afraid’
articles.summary: This year's Social Good Summit brought together global, regional, and local perspectives on how AI has been both a boon and a bane to humanity — and what governance can do to stem a seeming point of…

blocks.text: We humans spent the last few days dissecting what’s been keeping us listless these days — artificial intelligence and the future of news.

Renowned historian and philosopher Yuval Harari warned us to be “very, very afraid” at this period in history. “AI is not a tool, it is an agent. It is something that can make decisions by itself. So it is taking power away from us,” he said.

But nothing is inevitable, Harari told Nobel Peace Prize laureate and Rappler CEO Maria Ressa in a pre-recorded fireside chat that aired on Saturday, November 21, at Rappler’s annual Social Good Summit (SGS) at Shangri-La The Fort in Taguig. “There are still choices to be made.”

With the theme, “We, The Humans: Reclaim our Future,” this year’s SGS brought together global, regional, and local perspectives on how AI has been both a boon and a bane to humanity — and what governance can do to stem a seeming point of no return.

items: We’re in a “new imperial age,” Harari said, warning the Philippines that it risks losing control of critical infrastructure because of its dependence on foreign technology. Read more.

Staunch human rights advocate Agnès Callamard, secretary-general of Amnesty International, pushed for collective resistance to Big Tech’s unfettered and opaque inroads into our personal and professional lives. To do that and to fight back, humans must first understand AI, Ressa said.

Singaporean economist and AI executive Leslie Teo outlined ways to develop AI as a positive force for society. Read more. (We will be publishing more stories and videos from the summit in the coming days. Watch out for them.)

blocks.text: AI was also raised as a “growing concern” by the parliamentary body of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), which held its 49th Summit in Manila last week. But whether the region intends to address it collectively is unclear.

In fact, the ASEAN Summit itself still failed to resolve critical regional issues that have been pending at the leaders’ desks: the civil war in Myanmar and the protracted negotiations for a South China Sea Code of Conduct. Read more.

In Turkey, the Antalya AI Pledge was launched on the sidelines of the COP 31 climate talks. It calls on governments and companies to take voluntary measures to power AI with cleaner energy. But China’s Alibaba is the only big tech company that has so far signed off on it.
Worse, the climate talks collapsed on Sunday, November 22, after leaders from the European Union and other countries rejected the final draft of a declaration that some deemed unambitious.

items: The draft acknowledged — for the first time — that global warming was on course to exceed the 1.5°C that countries had vowed to preserve. Read more.
The draft deal published on Thursday, November 19, removed any reference to ending the use of fossil fuels, prompting negotiators to extend their meetings to Sunday.
The first draft of the deal had already signaled tough negotiations ahead.

blocks.text: In Manila where realpolitik reigns, defense lawyers of Vice President Sara Duterte in her impeachment trial continued to mock the public with witnesses who are neither experts in their field, forthright in their answers, nor transparent in their practices. One was grilled over his “useless testimony.”

They got backups from ghosts — as the defense panel showed archived videos of the late senator Miriam Defensor Santiago and the late chief justice Renato Corona, who was convicted by the Senate impeachment court in 2013.

articles.title: Spying on survivors: Why RCMP watched Wab Kinew's father in the 1960s
articles.summary: Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew wants to know who spied on his father for the RCMP, and why. Documents obtained by CBC News reveal the late Anishinaabe leader Tobasonakwut Kinew was under surveillance in…

image.caption: Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew holds an RCMP Security Service report about his late father from the 1960s contained in an intelligence dossier compiled on the Manitoba Indian Brotherhood, forerunner of the Assembly of Manitoba Chiefs. (Randall McKenzie/CBC News)

blocks.text: Inside the Manitoba premier's office, Wab Kinew unravels a state secret.

With a mix of wry amusement and serious concern, he flips through censored copies of the RCMP's historic surveillance dossiers, each one marked in pen as "racial intelligence," compiled on Indigenous organizations from the 1960s to the 1980s.

What he learns he calls damning and alarming: the Canadian government spied on his father, the late Anishinaabe leader Tobasonakwut Kinew, in a countrywide infiltration initiative later dubbed the "Native extremism program."

"Finding out that there was surveillance by law enforcement, by national security, for what today we would consider very routine political organizing and activism, it shows you, I would say, the racism of the time," the premier told CBC News in October.

At home in Orillia, Ont., Wab Kinew's uncle Fred Kelly untangles the same tale of espionage and deceit. He too was spied on for lawful democratic activism in the '60s, though it's hardly a surprise. He strongly suspected it.

"I had no actual proof that I was being spied upon, but I knew it," said Kelly, also known as Kiizhebowse Makwa, a distinguished Anishinaabe elder, spiritual leader and former grand chief of Grand Council Treaty #3 in northwestern Ontario.
Anishinaabe elder gets proof of long-suspected RCMP spying

CBC News provided these documents to the family for the first time during a years-long investigation into Canada's Cold War-era program to spy on Indigenous leaders and activists, which the RCMP created and which CSIS revived in the late 1980s.

The story of this one famous family reveals how many RCMP surveillance targets were residential school survivors who went on to lead legitimate political movements to reclaim their identity. To them, it's no shock the government that openly suppressed First Nations culture in residential schools also tried to suppress their newfound political voice.
As former national chief Georges Erasmus put it in an interview earlier this year, "It is just the next chapter of oppression."
From residential school to resistance
Tobasonakwut Kinew was about seven years old when he was taken to St. Mary’s Indian Residential School in Kenora in northwestern Ontario in the 1940s, where he experienced almost a decade of horrors.

Catholic priests and nuns tried to strip him of his culture by cutting his hair short, changing his name from Tobasonakwut to Peter Kelly and giving him a number, 54. He suffered psychological, physical and sexual abuse.
Eight-year-old Tobasonakwut standing with his grandfather, Kaagagewannakweb, who came to visit him at St Mary's Residential School in Kenora, Ont., circa 1944-45. (Submitted by Diane Kelly)
Both as a CBC reporter and in his 2015 memoir, Wab Kinew candidly explored his father's residential school experience and how the resulting trauma nearly severed the ties that bind a family together.

"Look at my dad, he had the Indian agent deciding everything about his life in his early years, until he went to residential school when it was a boys' keeper and a priest … Then he left and it was back to the Indian Agent. And then this surveillance," Wab Kinew told CBC News.

"There's a longer history of government and corporate entities monitoring Indigenous families, assigning numbers, assigning qualitative evaluations of them, but seemingly not engaging with them as people."
Fred Kelly's experience was similar. He said he suffered physical and sexual abuse as well, and he too got the Irish surname Kelly at St. Mary’s, where he was taken at five years old.
"My impression of the residential school system was very much a system of incarceration to teach me and to force me to believe that my system, my original system of spirituality, was wrong," he said.
Fred Kelly (left) and Tobasonakwut Kinew (Peter Kelly) in their 20s in an undated photo taken in their community, Ojibways of Onigaming First Nation. (Submitted by Diane Kelly)

The 6,000 pages of formerly secret intelligence files gathered on First Nations leaders by the RCMP Security Service and obtained by CBC News under access to information law reveal another chapter in this story.

As the brothers joined a generation of Indigenous leaders getting organized politically, it was no longer priests and nuns giving them numbers but Mounties — giving them file numbers as perceived subversives.
Fred Kelly entered the national political spotlight in November 1965, when he organized a pivotal protest in Kenora against racial injustice, now hailed as the country's first civil rights march.
Newspapers called Kenora Canada's Alabama and compared the racial tensions to "Bloody Sunday" in Selma, where Alabama state troopers attacked peaceful Black civil rights marchers earlier in 1965.
"Our people did not do these kinds of things. Our people are rather stoic: If that's the way it is, that's what we've got to live with," Kelly recalled.
Indigenous people demand a better deal in Kenora, Ont. in 1965

Town council mocked him, saying he'd be lucky if four people showed up. Instead between 400 and 500 Anishinaabeg filled Kenora's streets, marching in a silent and peaceful but proud show of dignity that still inspires First Nations leaders 60 years later.
"We were not looking for love," Kelly said.
"We were looking for justice and equality."
'Known agitators'
The premier's father and uncle, or the "Kelly brothers," soon gained celebrity and notoriety.

The Globe and Mail ran the headline "Indian brothers predict Kenora race riots" after a group of white men attacked them in 1967, and CBC flew them to Toronto to discuss the incident on national television.

The RCMP Security Service, a domestic intelligence agency that became CSIS in 1984, took notice, too. Amid the paranoia of the Cold War, Mounties feared radicals and communists could infiltrate and exploit the First Nations rights movement.
By 1969, Mounties had Winnipeg-based human sources informing on the brothers. One informer meticulously tracked Fred Kelly's movements and politics, depicting him as a potentially violent subversive.
"The source considers him to be a radical and somewhat dangerous person," an intelligence investigator reported.

In a separate report, a Mountie in Winnipeg reported both brothers "have been connected with the 'Red Power' movement." The RCMP labelled them as "known agitators" and tracked their movements across Canada.

Fred Kelly is unsurprised, but he still denounces these reports as "the wrong interpretation of what I was seeking." He draws parallels between how residential school officials carried out their mission and how Mounties did theirs.
"That was probably an order. How they carried that out is something that they have to live with," he said.
"But they did it in much the same way as those Catholic priests believed in what they were doing."
Diane Kelly, Wab Kinew's sister, was stunned and disappointed to see these references to her father and uncle.
"These are the things that we've always suspected, not just as a family, but as Indigenous people," said Diane Kelly, a former grand chief of Grand Council Treaty #3.
Diane Kelly says it's shocking and disappointing but not really surprising to see the contents of the declassified surveillance files. (Brett Forester/CBC)
In the 1970s, her father was helping bring back that grand council, laying the foundation for the resurgence of the very political body she later led, she said.
"How was that terrorism? How was that being an agitator? It's about having pride in who you are and knowing who you are," she said.

By 1971, the Security Service explicitly targeted the legitimate Indigenous movement, writing in a secret, urgent-marked report that "the activities of the National Indian Brotherhood," now the Assembly of First Nations, were "of special interest to us."

"As stressed in previous correspondence forwarded to all divisions, the organized activity of our Canadian Indians are of interest," the report said, calling it "most desirable" if the brotherhood's annual spring conference was infiltrated with "human source coverage."
Singled out as top targets were Fred Kelly and Tobasonakwut Kinew, or Peter Kelly. Their movement, in other words, was compromised.
Jeffrey Copenace, chief of Ojibways of Onigaming First Nation, where the brothers and premier are from, is outraged.

Chief of the Ojibways of Onigaming Jeff Copenace speaks to reporters following the First Nations Summit at the Canadian Museum of History in Gatineau, Que., in July 2025. (Spencer Colby/The Canadian Press)
"These two men should be celebrated along with all of the other Treaty 3 and First Nation leaders that have been trying to attain human rights in Canada," he said.

"To think that these two men had their privacy infiltrated, that there's all kinds of documentation about them that they're not aware of that's just coming to light now, it's a bit sad. It's just a little bit heartbreaking."

In response to the rise of the American Indian Movement and arrival of Red Power activism, the RCMP Security Service intensified the surveillance and expanded the dragnet by formally establishing a full-time "Red Power desk" in Ottawa in 1973.

items: Why Mounties paid 5 informers to spy on Dene leaders: Inside a secret surveillance operation
How RCMP spies infiltrated the 1970s Indigenous rights movement

blocks.text: Here, intelligence officers tapped phones and paid informers to infiltrate groups like the National Indian Brotherhood and Dene Nation. The RCMP files name 150 Mounties involved, dozens of organizations monitored, and hundreds of individuals targeted.
"When you hear these actions, it's hard to believe that reconciliation is really a tangible thing in Canada," said Copenace.
What now?
At the Manitoba legislature, Wab Kinew has questions. First, naturally, is "who were these informants?" But that evolves into a call for all-around clarity.
"Was the RCMP paying people? Were people giving this information under duress?" he said.
"Does the way that this information enters the permanent record speak to whether it is credible or not? Were people being induced? Bribed?"

Using informers to infiltrate legitimate movements is far from harmless, said John Carlson, who is Anishinaabe from Red Rock Indian Band in northwestern Ontario and an associate professor of criminology at the University of Ottawa. He argues this countersubversion program had a chilling effect on political activism and free expression.
Associate professor John Carlson teaches his students at the University of Ottawa about the significance of the silent march in Kenora led by Fred Kelly in 1965. (Brett Forester/CBC News)
"That's the legacy. It's purging the movement of what the RCMP, I'm sure, would call subversive ideology and organizational practices," Carlson said.
"But I would call [those practices] relevant to fighting for a society where Indigenous dignity, self-determination and relations, responsibilities and values could also shape this society."
Ultimately Tobasonakwut Kinew and Fred Kelly became political and community leaders, leaving an indelible mark on Canadian history.

Fred Kelly was part of the team that negotiated the Indian Residential Schools Settlement Agreement that led to the Truth and Reconciliation Commission. Tobasonakwut Kinew personally reconciled with Pope Benedict in 2009, presenting him with an eagle feather and ceremonial pipe. Both brothers were on Parliament Hill in 2008 to witness prime minister Stephen Harper's historic apology for the residential school system.

Tobasonakwut Kinew (Peter Kelly) holds the Assembly of First Nations ceremonial staff on his way to a news conference after Pope Benedict's general audience in St. Peter's Square at the Vatican, April 29, 2009. (Pier Paolo Cito/The Associated Press)

As for the spying, RCMP Commissioner Mike Duheme issued a statement of regret after CBC News revealed the program's existence in May 2026, but the Assembly of First Nations continues to seek a full apology, access to uncensored files and answers.
Public Safety Minister Gary's Anandasangaree office said in September that he is working with relevant federal departments to support the release of those documents.

For Wab Kinew, the files confirm Canada's intelligence service of the 1960s "was racist," but he believes those organizations today have a more progressive and egalitarian view. On that front, Manitoba's first Anishinaabe premier finds a silver lining in his relationship with the RCMP today.
Mounties still follow him around the country, as they did his father. It's just no longer the secret spy branch. It's the executive protection unit.

articles.title: DA plans P18B budget for agri mechanization in 2027 to boost production
articles.summary: The Department of Agriculture (DA) said on Monday that it is eyeing up to P18 billion in the 2027 budget for agricultural machinery.

blocks.text: Published November 23, 2026 5:57pm
The Department of Agriculture (DA) said on Monday that it is eyeing up to P18 billion in the 2027 budget for agricultural machinery.

Most of the government’s budget for mechanization is under the Rice Competitiveness Enhancement Fund (RCEF), including the P9 billion allotted for rice machinery. But the DA is seeking a bigger allocation for farm machinery for other crops.

“But of course, the Department of Agriculture through its other programs also have machineries. I would safely assume we can easily almost double that,” said DA Secretary Francisco Tiu Laurel Jr. in a press briefing during the Asia Pacific Conference on Sustainable Agricultural Mechanization.
“So we might have about P15 to 18 billion for 2027 available for farm machinery and motor vehicles,” he added.
The Philippine Center for Postharvest Development and Mechanization (PhilMech) said that an additional P50 billion is needed to fully mechanize the rice sector alone.
“In the span of six years, we only mechanized around 60 % to 70% of our rice. So we're still needing 30% more,” said PhilMech director Dionisio Alvindia in the press briefing.
“That could value around P50 billion more to mechanize the whole system,” he added.

The Philippine government is pushing for accessible and sustainable mechanization of the agriculture sector to boost production, without leaving small farmers behind despite the modernization efforts.

“Modernization must be practical, accessible, and responsive to the realities of our farmers. It requires appropriate technologies, affordable financing, supportive policies, reliable after-sales services, and just as importantly, the skills to operate and maintain these machineries,” said Tiu Laurel Jr.
Meanwhile, the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) noted that farmers will only invest in technologies that will boost their income.

“Farmers are some of the most innovative, risk-taking individuals that you will ever meet. But when we think about the evolution of technology and adoption of it, a farmer will not invest in a new technology unless she knows that it saves her money or helps her make a profit,” said FAO Deputy Director General Beth Bechdol in the press briefing.
However, the DA assured that mechanization of the agriculture sector won’t mean replacing farmers or any other human force in the sector.
“Machines should make farmers more productive, not make farmers irrelevant,” said Tiu Laurel Jr. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Sandiganbayan rejects bail plea of Marcoleta, co-accused in P75-M plunder case
articles.summary: The Sandiganbayan Third Division has denied the bail petitions of Sen. Rodante Marcoleta and his three co-accused, ruling that the evidence of guilt against them in their P75-million plunder case is…

blocks.text: November 23, 2026 | 5:57pm
Senator Rodante Marcoleta boards a Philippine National Police coaster at the Sandiganbayan on July 6, 2026, upon his arrest over a plunder case.
The STAR / Michael Varcas

MANILA, Philippines — The Sandiganbayan Third Division has denied the bail petitions of Sen. Rodante Marcoleta and his three co-accused, ruling that the evidence of guilt against them in their P75-million plunder case is strong.

In a resolution promulgated on Monday, November 23, 2026, the anti-graft court rejected Marcoleta’s motion for bail, along with the separate petitions filed by his co-accused, former lawmaker Mike Defensor, Aristotle Viray, and Joseph Espiritu.

“In this case, the evidence of guilt against Sen. Marcoleta, Defensor, Espiritu, and Viray is strong. Sen. Marcoleta was then a representative of the SAGIP party- list in the House of Representatives at the time material to this case,” the Sandiganbayan Third Division said.
Because the charges involve plunder under Republic Act No. 7080, which carries the penalty of life imprisonment, the offense is non-bailable unless the court finds that the evidence of guilt is weak.
As a result, Marcoleta and his co-accused will remain detained at the Quezon City Male Dormitory as they face trial.

According to the anti-graft court, it is undisputed that Marcoleta, who was serving as a SAGIP party-list representative at the time, received three separate donations in January 2025 totaling P75 million: P30 million from Defensor, P25 million from Espiritu and P20 million from Viray.

The Sandiganbayan noted that Marcoleta failed to declare the funds in both his Statement of Contributions and Expenditures (SOCE) for the 2025 elections and his Statement of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth (SALN) as of June 30, 2025.
In its resolution, the court pointed out inconsistencies in how the senator treated the money.
While Marcoleta linked the donations to his 2025 senatorial campaign, he argued before the Commission on Elections that they were personal funds and even paid donor’s taxes on the amounts.

The anti-graft court emphasized that legitimate electoral contributions are exempt from donor's tax, meaning the payments undermined his claim and indicated the funds were gifts received by reason of his public office.

The court also cited Marcoleta’s own admission on the television program “Sa Ganang Mamamayan” that he received donations from friends while serving as a congressman, which was corroborated by the counter-affidavits of Espiritu and Viray before the Office of the Ombudsman.
Plunder and conspiracy

The anti-graft court explained that under Section 1(d)(2) of the Plunder Law, each of the three donations constituted a distinct act consummated upon receipt, exceeding the P50-million threshold required for plunder.

The resolution stated that Marcoleta took advantage of his close relationship with the donors, and even personally solicited the contribution from Viray, placing private interest above his legal duty to disclose by agreeing to keep their identities secret.
To establish conspiracy among the four accused, the Sandiganbayan outlined seven key circumstances:

items: The donations were made within a four-day span in January 2025.
The deeds of donation were all executed in Quezon City and were identical in form and substance, differing only in donor names, execution dates, and amounts.

All three deeds were notarized on the same day, Nov. 14, 2025, before the same notary public, ten months after execution and just a week after Marcoleta publicly admitted receiving the donations despite declaring zero contributions in his SOCE.
An employee of Marcoleta, rather than the donors themselves, paid the donor’s taxes.
The contact number of Marcoleta’s employee appeared on the official donor’s tax receipts.
The donor’s taxes were paid shortly after the Comelec Political Finance and Affairs Department (PFAD) issued a show-cause order directing Marcoleta to explain the omissions in his SOCE.
Marcoleta used the deeds and tax receipts as proof of good faith in his verified position paper before the Comelec PFAD.

blocks.text: Marcoleta and his co-accused previously pleaded not guilty to the charges against them.

articles.title: Dela Rosa seeks dismissal of absenteeism complaint
articles.summary: Anti-corruption group Wag Kang Ku-corrupt had asked the Senate ethics panel to investigate the senator’s prolonged absence, determine if he violated Senate rules and ethical standards, and impose…

blocks.text: BATO. Senator Ronald 'Bato' dela Rosa speaks to members of the media, at the Senate on May 13, 2026.
Rappler

Anti-corruption group Wag Kang Ku-corrupt had asked the Senate ethics panel to investigate the senator’s prolonged absence, determine if he violated Senate rules and ethical standards, and impose appropriate sanctions if warranted

items: Senator Ronald 'Bato' dela Rosa has requested the Senate ethics committee to dismiss a complaint regarding his prolonged absence from the Senate, arguing that it lacks sufficient grounds.
The complaint was filed by the anti-corruption group Wag Kang Ku-corrupt, which sought an investigation into Dela Rosa's absence and potential violations of Senate rules.
Dela Rosa is also involved in a legal battle concerning an arrest warrant issued by the International Criminal Court related to his role in the anti-drug campaign during the Duterte administration.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
MANILA, Philippines – Senator Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa has asked the Senate ethics committee to dismiss a complaint against him over his prolonged absence from the Senate.

In a response submitted to the Senate committee on ethics and privileges, Dela Rosa, through his legal counsel Israelito Torreon, sought the dismissal of a complaint filed by anti-corruption group Wag Kang Ku-corrupt in February.
The group had asked the Senate panel to investigate the senator’s prolonged absence, determine whether he violated Senate rules and ethical standards, and impose appropriate sanctions if warranted.

In a notice, the Senate ethics panel informed dela Rosa that they had found the complaint to be compliant with requirements “both in form and in substance” following an executive session on October 22. The panel directed Dela Rosa to submit a written response within 15 days of receiving the notice.
Dela Rosa’s office confirmed receiving the notice on November 19.
In his response, Torreon argued that the complaint should be dismissed for “insufficiency in form and substance, and for failure to state any offense cognizable by the Committee.”

Dela Rosa also asked the committee to hold the proceedings in abeyance pending the resolution of his camp’s motion for reconsideration of the Supreme Court ruling that denied his plea for a temporary restraining order (TRO) against the enforcement of the International Criminal Court warrant.
He also asked the committee to deny the motion included in the complaint, seeking the suspension of his Senate office’s operations, including the release of salaries and operational expenses.

“In the event the Committee proceeds further, furnish respondent with copies of all records on which it intends to rely, and afford him a hearing, through counsel, with the opportunity to examine the complainants and their witnesses and to present evidence,” he added.
Senate ethics committee chairperson Vicente “Tito” Sotto III confirmed receiving Dela Rosa’s response.

“I received the answer via email on Saturday, November 21, 2026, 8:51 pm. It was submitted through his counsel and not signed by him personally. This answer will be considered in the next Ethics hearing that will be scheduled at the soonest time,” Sotto told reporters in a Viber message.
In October, Dela Rosa again asked the SC to reverse its earlier ruling denying his plea for a TRO against the enforcement of the ICC arrest warrant.
Dela Rosa is among the former officials of the Rodrigo Duterte administration implicated in the bloody anti-drug campaign, which human rights organizations say resulted in nearly 30,000 deaths.

The ICC Pre-Trial Chamber I issued an arrest warrant against the senator in November 2025 over his alleged role in the drug war. The court identified him as a co-perpetrator in the case, saying those involved “controlled a structure of power” that enabled them to “direct and control the actions” of those who carried out the killings.
The warrant remained under seal until May 11 of this year, when it was made public.

Dela Rosa had been absent from the Senate for months before appearing on May 11 to support Senator Alan Peter Cayetano’s bid for the Senate presidency. He then remained inside the Senate building for three days as he sought refuge from possible arrest.

A shooting incident erupted on the night of May 13, allegedly triggered by Senate Sergeant-at-Arms Mao Aplasca, Dela Rosa’s Philippine Military Academy classmate. Hours later, at around 2:30 am, Dela Rosa left the Senate building, accompanied by his political ally, Senator Robin Padilla.
Dela Rosa has since stayed out of public view.
In seeking a reconsideration of the SC ruling, Dela Rosa’s lawyer argued that the enforcement posture against the senator had “escalated” while the motion remained unresolved.

The motion also cited developments since the original petition, including the Department of the Interior and Local Government’s declaration of Dela Rosa as “armed and dangerous” and the P50-million bounty offered for his arrest. – Rappler.com

articles.summary: President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and First Lady Liza Araneta-Marcos took Sunday and Monday off to rest and recharge following weeks of hectic activities.

blocks.text: Published November 23, 2026 5:41pm
President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and First Lady Liza Araneta-Marcos took Sunday and Monday off to rest and recharge following weeks of hectic activities.
In a Facebook post on Monday, Nov. 23, the First Lady shared a photo of herself with the President, saying they had decided to take a break after a “whirlwind of activities these past few weeks.”
“After a whirlwind of activities these past few weeks, we finally decided to take Sunday and Monday off to slow down, rest and recharge,” Liza said in the post.
The First Lady said they had no major plans and were simply enjoying some "peace and quiet" and much-needed downtime together.
“No big plans, no fuss ... just a little peace and quiet and some much-needed downtime together,” she said.
“And so far, we're loving it!” she added.
The Philippines hosted the 49th ASEAN Summit and Related Summits in Manila from Nov. 16 to 18, with Marcos presiding over the meetings as the country's chair of the regional bloc.
The President then traveled to Shenzhen, China, to attend the 33rd APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting on Nov. 19 and 20.—LDF, GMA News
