articles.title: PNP considering to visit Sara Duterte over alleged threats
articles.summary: The Philippine National Police (PNP) on Monday said it is willing to visit Vice President Sara Duterte to gather details about the threats she reportedly have received.

blocks.text: Published November 23, 2026 4:56pm
The Philippine National Police (PNP) on Monday said it is willing to visit Vice President Sara Duterte to gather details about the threats she reportedly have received.
At a press briefing, PNP spokesperson Police Brigadier General Allen Rae Co said the police are open to personally meeting with Duterte to establish the facts surrounding her allegations.

“If she wants that we will go, we will be the ones to go to her para po kunin ang kanyang statement or 'yung facts po or the threats that she is saying, ay very much willing to do so po ang Philippine National Police,” Co said during a press briefing.
(If she wants that we will go, the PNP is very much willing that we will be the ones to go to her to get her statement or the facts or the threats that she is saying.)
While the PNP can conduct a motu proprio investigation, Co said that authorities need to know the specific incident or alleged crime being reported.
He said the PNP had invited Duterte to submit evidence or documents supporting her claims.
“If you told us that a crime was committed against you, hindi po sinasabi kung what crime, hindi po namin masisimulan,” he said.
(If you told us that a crime was committed against you, they wouldn't tell us what crime, we couldn't start.)
Asked whether the PNP had monitored any threats against the Vice President, Co said authorities had not detected any direct threats against her.

Over the weekend, Duterte said she has five "documented threats" against her. Yet, she cannot present the threats amid her impeachment trial "because the prosecution maliciously withdrew the charge of grave threats."
Duterte also reiterated that she is concerned for her personal safety.

"When I say that I do not feel safe in this country, I speak not only for myself but also for the many Filipinos who have experienced, or fear experiencing, the failure of law enforcement to make this country a place where people can live with the assurance that their fundamental rights will be respected," she said.
In September, the PNP said Duterte has yet to report to the PNP any threat against her and her family. — RSJ, GMA News

articles.title: PH extends 14-day visa-free entry for Chinese nationals until January 2028 -- DFA
articles.summary: The 14-day visa-free entry privilege for Chinese nationals has been extended until January 15, 2028, the Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) announced Sunday.

blocks.text: Published November 23, 2026 4:53pm
The 14-day visa-free entry privilege for Chinese nationals has been extended until January 15, 2028, the Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) announced Sunday.

In a press release, the DFA said the extension aligns with President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.’s directive to “boost international tourist arrivals and investment in the Philippines, while maintaining existing immigration and national security safeguards.”
The visa-free privilege applies only to Chinese nationals visiting strictly for tourism or business and staying up to 14 days.
To qualify, travelers must hold a passport valid for at least six months beyond their intended stay, along with confirmed hotel accommodations and a return or onward ticket.
The privilege remains non-extendable and non-convertible to any other Philippine visa category.

“The extension remains subject to existing immigration and security safeguards, including the allowed entry of Chinese nationals availing of the visa-free entry privilege through the Ninoy Aquino International Airport (NAIA) in Metro Manila and Mactan-Cebu International Airport (MCIA) in Cebu only. Travelers must comply with applicable eTravel registration requirements and have no derogatory records with the Bureau of Immigration (BI),” the DFA said.

“Further, admission into the Philippines remains subject to inspection, screening procedures, and determination by the BI, including applicable identity verification, watchlist checks, and risk-based assessment,” it added.
The agency emphasized that throughout the implementation of the 14-day visa-free policy, it will maintain close coordination with the BI.
DFA reminded Chinese travelers transiting through the Philippines en route to a third destination that they must secure the appropriate Philippine transit visa before entry.—LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Kenya and DR Congo agree to restore ties after tensions over conflict
articles.summary: The two leaders committed to upholding sovereignty and "non-interference in the internal affairs of states".

blocks.text: Kenya's President William Ruto and his Congolese counterpart Felix Tshisekedi have agreed to restore full diplomatic ties between the two countries following tensions over the conflict in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo.
Relations between the two countries have soured since 2023 when DR Congo accused Kenya of hosting leaders launching a rebel alliance, including the M23.
This led DR Congo to recall its envoy to Nairobi. Relations deteriorated further when Kinshasa refusing to accredit Kenya's nominated ambassador.
On Sunday, the two leaders affirmed their commitment to "sovereignty, territorial integrity, non-interference in the internal affairs of states".

The agreement was announced in a joint statement issued after the summit held in the town of Oyo in Congo-Brazzaville, facilitated by the nation's President Denis Sassou Nguesso, with Togolese leader Faure Essozimna Gnassingbé as mediator.
Tshisekedi and Ruto also agreed to "good neighbourliness and peaceful settlement of disputes" as well as "strengthen cooperation within regional mechanisms".
DR Congo and Kenya are both members of the East African Community (EAC).

DR Congo, which joined in 2022, is the latest entrant to the bloc, but its membership has been complicated by its accusation that Rwanda, a fellow member, backs the M23 rebels. Rwanda denies the claims despite overwhelming evidence.
DR Congo has also accused Kenya of hosting Congolese political and rebel leaders whom it says are working to destabilise the country.
When the Congo River Alliance (AFC), a political-military alliance including the M23, was launched in Nairobi in 2023, DR Congo responded by recalling its ambassador to Kenya.

The tensions were stoked further in March last year after Kenya named a consul-general to Goma, the capital of DR Congo's North Kivu region, after it fell to M23 forces, who control many eastern parts of the country.
DR Congo said naming the envoy amounted to disrespect for the country's territorial integrity and seemed to legitimise the group's occupation.
Relations deteriorated further after Kenya hosted a meeting of Congolese opposition figures, including former President Joseph Kabila, in October 2025.
Kabila was in 2025 sentenced to death in absentia on charges including war crimes and treason. He denied the accusations, but did not appear in court to defend himself.
He has since been named the leader of the Front for the Refoundation of the Nation (FRN), the new rebel coalition that took over from the AFC.
Sunday's meeting between Ruto and Tshisekedi also included other issues including deepening trade cooperation, economic development, and regional integration.
The two also sought to collaborate to control the spread of the Ebola virus.

On Sunday, the head of the World Health Organization (WHO), Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, said the frequency of attacks across the country's east had increased since the end of October, seriously affecting the Ebola response.
Tedros said heavy fighting in an area close to where the Ebola outbreak first emerged had disrupted work and the wider Ebola response.
More than 5,700 people have died and 11,000 infected with Ebola in DR Congo since the outbreak was declared in May.
The latest outbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo species of the virus, has spread beyond DR Congo borders, with cases reported in Kenya, Uganda and Nigeria.

articles.summary: The Commission on Appointments (CA) on Monday confirmed the nomination of Commission on Audit (COA) Commissioner Douglas Michael Mallillin as the agency"s chairperson.

blocks.text: Published November 23, 2026 4:28pm
The Commission on Appointments (CA) on Monday confirmed the nomination of Commission on Audit (COA) Commissioner Douglas Michael Mallillin as the agency’s chairperson.
At a hearing, the Committee on Constitutional Commissions and Offices endorsed Mallillin’s nomination, which was confirmed by the CA in a plenary session.

Mallillin, who was appointed COA commissioner in February 2025 and confirmed in June of the same year, would serve the unexpired term of ex-COA chairperson Gamaliel Cordoba, which ends February 2, 2029.

In his opening statement, Mallillin said the chairmanship carries greater responsibility and authority to introduce reforms and innovations with technological advances, as well as to improve the government’s financial oversight.

Senator Imee Marcos initially objected to the “immediate” endorsement of Mallillin’s nomination and sought its deferment, citing concerns over the COA’s independence and the need for a clearer explanation of the nominee’s plans for the agency.
Marcos said she wanted assurances that the COA would not be used to pursue political opponents.
Mallillin committed to upholding the COA’s independence as mandated by the Constitution and said confirmation would help ensure the commission’s continued operations.
For his part, Mallillin committed to upholding the COA’s independence as mandated by the Constitution and said confirmation would help ensure the commission’s continued operations.

“We would appreciate that the nomination be confirmed so that the Commission on Audit will continue to function outside the en banc and the other functions necessary for the commission proper,” he said.
Marcos later withdrew her request for deferment after Mallillin gave assurances that the concerns raised would be addressed. –NB, GMA News

articles.title: Douglas Michael Mallillin confirmed as new COA chair
articles.summary: Prior to his nomination, Mallillin was ad interim commissioner at the same agency, following a stint as deputy commissioner at the National Telecommunications Commission.

blocks.text: November 23, 2026 | 4:25pm
The Commission on Appointments holds a committee meeting on Monday, November 23, to consider the nomination of the Douglas Michael Mallillin as Commission on Audit chairperson.
YouTube / Commission on Appointments livestream
MANILA, Philippines — The Committee on Appointments approved on Monday, November 23, the nomination of Douglas Michael Mallillin for Commission on Audit chairperson.
Mallillin, an outgoing ad interim commissioner at COA, will replace Gamaliel Cordoba, who was appointed associate justice on November 16.
He will complete the remaining three years of Cordoba’s seven-year term and serve as chairperson until Feb. 2, 2029.
Sen. Imee Marcos initially moved to defer Mallillin’s nomination, citing concerns about the alleged impartiality of the commission.

“The nominee, Mr. Mallillin, has served as a commissioner of COA since February 2025, and while I recognize that the commission acts as a collegial body and that not every action of the institution can automatically be attributed to an individual commissioner, his tenure nevertheless has raised legitimate questions about what steps he took to safeguard the institution against political interference and selective enforcement,” Marcos said.
Responding to Marcos’ statement, Mallillin stressed the urgency of confirming the nomination to ensure the commission’s ability to function.
The commission, Mallillin said, has had vacancy issues due to Cordoba’s appointment to the Supreme Court and Commissioner Mario Lipana’s health condition.
Marcos later withdrew her objection and allowed Mallillin’s nomination to be approved.
Prior to his time at COA, Mallillin was deputy commissioner at the National Telecommunications Commission and an assistant prosecutor for the Department of Justice.

articles.title: DOJ to form panel to vet Truth Commission findings on drug war killings
articles.summary: The Department of Justice (DOJ) will form a fact-finding panel to review the Truth Commission's report on drug war killings under the Duterte administration, following the presentation of the…

blocks.text: Published November 23, 2026 4:24pm

The Department of Justice (DOJ) will form a fact-finding panel to review the Truth Commission's report on drug war killings under the Duterte administration, following the presentation of the commission's preliminary findings.

Speaking at the Truth Commission's national conference on Monday, Justice Secretary Fredderick Vida said the DOJ would need to thoroughly examine the evidence gathered by the commission to ensure that any charges eventually filed in court would be strong enough to withstand legal scrutiny.

"Yes, definitely we will have a panel to review everything because we will check on the verifiable facts. What are the pieces of evidence? Are they purely testimonial? Are they purely physical evidence?” Vida said.
“The whole gamut, the whole spectrum, right? Because we don't want to file weak cases if ever they will be filed,” he added.
During the conference, former International Criminal Court (ICC) judge and current Truth Commission chairperson Raul Pangalangan presented the group's initial findings.

While emphasizing that the report was still preliminary, the commission said the evidence gathered was already sufficient to conclude that the drug war killings under former President Rodrigo Duterte were “state-organized.”
It also said the government's “official account cannot be accepted at face value” and that, in cases brought forward by victims' families, “no one has been held to account.”
The Truth Commission also presented the following key findings:

items: 8,320 documented killings, a figure expected to increase
Victims were overwhelmingly men of working and parenting age
Killings were concentrated in urban communities
Operations began almost everywhere at once and followed the police
Many killings bore the marks of execution
The official “manlaban” account did not hold up
Official records were incomplete and at times unreliable
Families had effectively carried out the State's investigative work
The drug war did not end in 2022
The commission proposed 27 reforms, five of which it said could not wait

blocks.text: Challenges in case build-up
The DOJ acknowledged that building cases from the available evidence would be challenging, particularly in establishing the credibility and admissibility of accounts provided by victims' families.
“Yes, very challenging, kasi yung sinabi nila kanina eh di ba kapag victim, totoo naman to eh, ‘Sabi kasi nung ano nakaluhod na yung anak ko nung binaril.’ Sabi nga nila. Di ba hearsay?” Vida said.
(Yes, very challenging, because, as mentioned earlier, a family member might say, ‘Someone told me my child was already kneeling when he was shot.’ Isn't that hearsay?)
"Who was actually there when it happened? These are the challenges in conducting the investigation and building up a case," he added.
Duterte is currently detained at the ICC detention facility in The Hague, with his trial proper for crimes against humanity scheduled to begin on November 30.
Vida said he was not in favor of holding local proceedings simultaneously with the ICC trial, stressing that the DOJ must first determine the appropriate legal strategy.

“I don't like simultaneous proceedings. That's different, right? Because you're running into the possibility of a conflict. It could be complementary, or it could involve sequencing. It depends on the proper and appropriate legal strategy,” he said.
The Justice secretary said the department remained committed to fulfilling its mandate “for the people and by the people.”— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Up to 1.1m people eligible to join class action against Jetstar over alleged failure to refund Covid flights
articles.summary:
Jetstar accused of issuing customers credits instead of cash refunds for flights cancelled between 2020 and late 2022

  • Get our

blocks.text: More than 1 million Jetstar customers could be eligible to join a class action alleging the airline failed to refund them for flights it cancelled during the pandemic, the firm leading the lawsuit has said.

The federal court on Monday confirmed it had ordered notices be sent to customers informing them of their eligibility to participate in, or opt out of, the lawsuit, with a potential trial set for March 2027.

Echo Law, the firm leading the class action, said it wanted to alert the public to the notices – which were due to be distributed by 4 December – to ensure they understood it was not a scam. About 1.1 million people will receive them.

The class action alleges Jetstar issued customers flight credits instead of the cash refunds they were entitled to for flights cancelled between 2020 and late 2022, after cancelling thousands of scheduled domestic and international flights.
Echo Law ran a separate class action against Qantas over its handling of Covid-19 travel credits, which the airline in March agreed to settle for $105m with no admission of liability.
In its case against Jetstar, the firm alleges the airline breached its legal obligations to customers by failing to provide refunds for cancelled flights, instead offering customers credit vouchers.
It alleges Jetstar misled customers and engaged in unconscionable conduct in breach of Australian consumer law.
It also alleges that, by holding customers’ funds that ought to have been refunded, Jetstar unlawfully benefited from this conduct.
Jetstar has denied the allegations and is defending the class action
after newsletter promotion

“During the Covid-19 pandemic, Jetstar took a range of steps to respond to rapidly changing travel restrictions, while continuing to support customers affected by disruptions,” a spokesperson for the airline said.
“We provided customers with a range of options during this period depending on the circumstances, including travel credits, fee-free flight changes and refunds.
They said customers with a Jetstar Covid-19 voucher could use it whenever they were ready to, as the airline had removed the expiry date in 2023.
However, Andrew Paull, a partner at Echo Law, alleged Jetstar’s policy of “pushing” customers to accept vouchers was designed to preserve the airline’s cash position.
“It held onto ordinary Australian’s [sic] money and expected customers to just be happy with credits, or in some cases nothing, when we allege they were entitled to cash refunds,” he alleged.

Paull alleged many customers had ended up paying Jetstar more than their original booking to use their credits on new fares, as they were led to believe they had little choice but to do so in order to avoid losing the value of their flights.
The firm’s lawsuit against Jetstar is scheduled for mediation in December and is expected to go to trial if the parties fail to reach an agreement.
Echo Law said the litigation funder Court House Capital was backing its class action against Jetstar.
Court House Capital’s chief investment officer, Heather Collins, accused Jetstar of seeking to “delay resolution while continuing to hold onto money that belongs to Australian families”.

articles.title: Constitutional law expert brands defence bill allowing secret security rules ‘lazy and irresponsible’
articles.summary:
Anne Twomey says lack of proper debate around bill is ‘flabbergasting’ amid concerns over extension of ministerial powers

Labor’s new defence bill is “lazy and irresponsible” lawmaking, one…

blocks.text: Labor’s new defence bill is “lazy and irresponsible” lawmaking, one of Australia’s leading constitutional scholars has warned, claiming provisions for the government to secretly class any facility as a special security zone could raise serious legal issues.

Prime minister Anthony Albanese claimed on Monday that critics of the ‘accelerating capability and protecting bases’ bill were “jump[ing] at shadows”, accusing them of “absurd” claims. But parliamentary crossbenchers opposed to the bill, which was rushed through parliament with little public scrutiny, were joined on Monday by Prof Anne Twomey, who expressed alarm about what she called an increasing trend of ministers exercising discretionary powers without parliamentary oversight.

“Yes it’s important we have defence legislation that’s flexible to deal with uncertain times, but let’s remember we’re trying to defend our democratic system of government, and we don’t want to throw it out at the same time,” Twomey told Guardian Australia.

In a video on her Youtube channel, Twomey – professor emerita at the University of Sydney – claimed it was “flabbergasting that it was not the subject of proper debate or scrutiny before this law was enacted”.
“This notion of permitting secret alterations to commonwealth, state and territory laws is a really serious development.”

The wide-ranging bill criminalises entering or photographing a defence security zone or a person or thing within, entering or leaving it, with a maximum penalty of up to seven years’ jail time, a $152,880 fine, or both. Security zones can include regular defence bases but can also extend to emergency, temporary or mobile sites as decided by a minister, with wide-ranging powers to “effectively do anything”.

The minister can make a “capability declaration”, which allows for certain activity to be carried out “without contravening certain other laws, or changes the way that other laws apply” – including state and territory laws. Such a declaration can also be held back from being declared as a legislative instrument.

After passing the Senate last week, the final bill passed the lower house on Monday evening. Labor and the Coalition supported the bill, with only a handful of crossbenchers – including Kate Chaney, Monique Ryan and Andrew Wilkie – resisting.

The Greens, David Pocock, Digital Rights Watch and other civil society groups also strongly opposed the bill. But Albanese, in his first public comments on the legislation, said “people shouldn’t jump at shadows”, claiming the powers were necessary and “just practical”.
“It will be accountable obviously for things that are designated, but we live in unsafe times,” he said on Monday.

“I find it remarkable in 2026, there’s a question over whether we need to designate areas as being protected. And we live in times where we know there are more conflicts in the world today than at any time since World War II.”
Greens leader David Shoebridge called the changes “extreme wartime powers”, and “an assault on civil liberties”, claiming people may be charged for breaking laws they weren’t even aware of.
Pocock said Albanese’s response was “disingenuous”.

“We need to protect sensitive defence facilities from threats posed by drones and other technologies. But that doesn’t mean handing the defence minister extraordinary powers without proper safeguards,” he told Guardian Australia.
“At a bare minimum, far stronger safeguards are needed around the use of ministerial powers, the need to protect civil liberties and greater transparency.”

Twomey, in her video, branded the legislation “quite disturbing”, noting declarations could be made secretly – which she said raised “serious rule of law issues” – and called out what she said was a concerning movement of giving ministers more discretionary power.

“Instead of working out what laws need to change to accommodate defence needs and then balancing them against the needs and rights of the community, the parliament has effectively just given up and instead given the power to the minister or indeed senior public servants or defence officers to make decisions that exclude the application of existing laws to defence activities.
“This is a lazy and irresponsible abandonment by parliament of both its scrutiny and its lawmaking roles, raising the risk that these powers will be misused in the future.”

WASHINGTON, USA – Alice Huang, the Chinese woman at the heart of Nvidia’s recent scandal, kept in contact with an official from China’s top spy agency for more than a year during her affair with former CEO Jensen Huang, the New York Times reported on Sunday, November 22.

Alice Huang was in touch with an officer from China’s Ministry of State Security from the spring of 2025 until the fall of this year, the report said, citing people with knowledge of intelligence reports that describe the encounters.

A spokesperson for Jensen Huang declined to comment. Spokespeople for Nvidia and the Chinese embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Reuters has not been able to reach Alice Huang for comment.
Alice Huang previously led Singapore-based Megaspeed International, an important Nvidia customer that once accounted for billions in Nvidia chip sales.
US authorities have been investigating Megaspeed since 2024 over concerns it smuggled Nvidia’s advanced AI chips to China.
Sunday’s report comes as US officials have cast doubt on initial suggestions that Alice Huang was a spy, as the newspaper reported last month.
That October 29 article touched off a scandal that led to Jensen Huang’s resignation two weeks later and a steep drop in Nvidia’s stock price.
Trump administration officials have repeatedly said they have not concluded that Alice Huang spied for China.
US Attorney General Todd Blanche said this month the Justice Department had not yet reached a conclusion on whether she was a Chinese spy.
US Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton repeated that on Sunday.

“Attorney General Blanche has been very clear that this is a matter under investigation, both Ms Huang and her company, for various matters,” Clayton told CNN’s “State of the Union” program. “And I’m going to let that investigation play out.”

The scandal has also prompted a deeper look at Washington’s approach to export controls on China, with lawmakers from both parties questioning whether the Trump administration has been too lax on enforcement and regulation of the prized semiconductors.
The affair between the two itself is of less interest, Senator John Kennedy, a Louisiana Republican, told NBC’s “Meet the Press.”
“I hope he had a good time,” Kennedy said on Sunday. “It was the most expensive sex since Helen of Troy.” – Rappler.com

articles.title: PNP on alert ahead of VP Sara impeachment verdict, says DILG chief
articles.summary: The Philippine National Police was instructed to prepare for the worst-case scenario ahead of the eventual impeachment verdict on Vice President Sara Duterte.

blocks.text: November 23, 2026 | 3:31pm

Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla and Philippine National Police (PNP) chief Gen. Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr. holds a press conference at the PNP headquarters in Camp Crame, Quezon City on May 10, 2026.
The STAR / Miguel de Guzman
MANILA, Philippines — The Philippine National Police was instructed to prepare for the worst-case scenario ahead of the eventual impeachment verdict on Vice President Sara Duterte.

In an ambush interview with reporters on Monday, November 23, Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla said he had told the police to brace for the outcome, as the verdict could stir intense emotions among both Duterte's supporters and critics.
“Dapat ikalma nila (PNP) 'yung mga tao kasi in political trials like that, emotions get very high on both sides so dapat gawin ng pulis gigitna para hindi magkagulo,” Remulla added.
(They need to calm people down because in political trials like that, emotions run very high on both sides, so the police must stand in the middle to prevent chaos).
"We always expect the worst. Wala naman expect na best dito sa PNP eh. We always anticipate, we always prepare,” he added.
(There is no expecting the best here in the PNP. We always anticipate, we always prepare.)

While Remulla said the PNP is preparing for every eventuality, he expressed confidence that the public would ultimately respect the Senate impeachment court's decision, noting that many Filipinos have likely already formed their own conclusions throughout the proceedings

“Alam na nila kung ano ang totoo at hindi. I think sa sarili nilang puso at sa isip humusga na sila so tingin ko handa na rin naman lahat tanggapin kung ano ang magiging hatol ng ating Senado,” Remulla said.
(In their own hearts and minds, they have already judged, so I think everyone is ready to accept whatever the verdict of our Senate will be.)

The Senate impeachment court, which is set to resume hearings on December 1, is currently hearing Article II of the Articles of Impeachment, which tackles the vice president's alleged ill-gotten wealth and irregularities in her Statement of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth.

articles.title: Some flood control items in 2027 budget funded twice, says Lacson
articles.summary: Sen. Ping Lacson said his staff has found flood control items with "double appropriations" in the P7.2-trillion spending bill, which will be up for plenary debate at the Senate this week.

blocks.text: November 23, 2026 | 2:51pm

MANILA, Philippines — Flood control projects are back in the national budget, and with them an old problem in public works spending: duplicate and overlapping appropriations, a senator flagged on Monday, November 23.
Sen. Ping Lacson said his staff has found flood control items with "double appropriations" in the P7.2-trillion spending bill, which will be up for plenary debate at the Senate this week.
Lacson said he would move to delete the extra entries during the Senate's period of amendments and, if needed, at the bicameral conference committee.

"Meron pa rin kaming nasilip. Double appropriations. Flood control na nga, doble pa yung appropriations," Lacson said in an interview with DZMM. (We found something else: double appropriations. It's flood control, of all things, and the funding is doubled.)
His claim adds to a growing list of warnings about the 2027 budget since the start of the legislative budget season.

Civil society coalitions, business groups and senators, including Lacson, have raised concerns over lump-sum allocations, duplicate and nearly identical entries, and thousands of projects allegedly added by the House without publicly available supporting documents.

The same irregular items have previously been flagged in the 2023 to 2025 budgets, some of which were later found to be funding ghost and substandard flood control works. A joint statement by business groups in late October warned the public has "already paid dearly for this practice" and that the 2027 "must not repeat that history."

In August, the Department of Public Works and Highways, then led by Secretary Vince Dizon, said it had cut its 2027 project list to 11,395 from the usual 20,000 or more, as part of reforms to prevent "duplicate and overlapping projects."
However, Lacson said such items are still carried in the proposed 2027 budget.
The DPWH for 2027 is seeking at least P107.4 billion for flood control works, the lowest allocation for the program since 2019.

In 2025, the DPWH slashed P252 billion from its proposed 2026 budget after investigations revealed the department had long funded substandard flood mitigation structures, duplicated existing allocations, and masked non-existent "ghost" projects.
Lacson's latest claim comes after a separate allegation he made over the weekend: that there are 30 non-existing multi-purpose buildings parked in the proposed 2027 budget.

"We have taken drone shots of at least one ‘ghost multi-purpose building’ that received numerous fund allocations in 2024, 2025, 2026 and is being included again for funding under the 2027 budget measure," Lacson said in a statement Sunday, November 22.

Citing initial findings, Lacson said MPBs also carry "commissions" of up to 10%. That is lower than the 15 to 30% in kickbacks he said earlier this year went to proponents of anomalous flood control projects.

There are at least 3,950 multi-purpose buildings in the Senate version of the bill, on top of another 1,584 covered by the Local Government Support Fund's financial assistance subprogram for local governments, Lacson said.

Earlier, the People's Budget Coalition, an alliance of more than 40 civil society groups, said the House more than doubled funding of the multi-purpose buildings to P83.7 billion from P41 billion in the executive proposal.

House members defended the increase, including Rep. Terry Ridon (Bicol Saro), co-chair of the House infrastructure committee, who argued the amount reflected public need and covers facilities such as senior citizens' centers.

articles.title: Five takeaways from the failed climate talks COP31
articles.summary: The COP31 summit in Antalya was the longest-running climate talks in UN history.

blocks.text: The COP31 summit in Turkey came as evidence of climate change could not have been clearer - 2026 bought glacier collapses, record European heat, and wildfires across Asia - but also when geopolitical divisions could not have been deeper.
The result was the longest-running climate talks in UN history failed to deliver on its central political agreement – the Antalya Pacts - to further climate action.
Despite two countries, Australia and Turkey, leading the charge in their joint hosting of the negotiations, they could not bring the nations together.

After a dramatic and fractious final day where countries walked out over the absence of mention of fossil fuels in the text and money issues, questions are being asked more loudly than ever before about whether the COP process can still deliver.
Here are five, key takeaways from the talks which the hosts hoped would become known as the "implementation COP".
Much of the coverage of COP31 has focused on the failure to get the central political agreement passed.
But much of the work at these summits is putting into action agreements made at previous meetings.

On money that is going towards adaptation for example, countries need to agree how is it being distributed, is it making an impact and how can this be tracked, and which areas are particularly vulnerable.
In fact, there were 164 other items on this year's agenda that were being thrashed out in the negotiating rooms.
And some of those were agreed at the talks.
The funds raised from a global system of carbon credits – money given in exchange for releasing greenhouse gases – will go towards helping developing countries adapt to the impacts of climate change.
They agreed to advance a just transition framework designed to protect workers and communities as global economies shift toward clean energy.
But there were many more that could not be agreed and some will now be picked up at COP32, including crucially the work programme responsible for driving forward action on cutting emissions.
The economics have been changing too.
Solar panels, batteries and electric vehicles have become increasingly competitive.
As clean energy develops its own commercial momentum, formal negotiations may become less important in determining its direction and pace.
Against the headwinds of inflation new investment announcements emerged at COP as part of the "Action Agenda".

This is the part of the COP process that tries to mobilise action outside of formal talks from businesses, investors and cities – this year the focus was on electrification. Turning more of our energy from fossil fuels to electricity.

"We are not entering the age of electricity, we have arrived at the age of electricity," Fatih Birol, head of the IEA, told the BBC. He says energy security and climate policies are now "closely aligned".
That doesn't make COP irrelevant.

Governments still have a crucial role in facilitating the transition, according to Dr Jennie Dodson, a senior director at the World Business Council for Sustainable Development which includes among its members the likes of Amazon and Apple.
"A key message from business is we can go so far, a lot of it is cost competitive, but there are policy barriers both around infrastructure and permitting".
COP31 has shown how the role of these annual UN climate conferences is changing.
For the first 30 COPs, the emphasis was on building the international framework for tackling global warming.
The great diplomatic breakthrough came in Paris in 2015, when almost every country agreed to keep global warming well below 2°C and to pursue efforts to limit it to 1.5°C.

Paris also established machinery designed to turn promises into progress. Every five years, governments assess collective progress in a global stocktake and submit new national climate plans, known as NDCs.

Then came further agreements: a fund for climate damage at COP27, a commitment to transition away from fossil fuels and triple renewable energy capacity at COP28, a new climate finance target at COP29 and increased support for adaptation at COP30.
The international architecture for tackling climate change has, in other words, largely been built.
Now comes the harder business of making it work. That's why this year's conference in Antalya, Turkey, had been billed as an "implementation COP".

The emphasis now is shifting towards delivering commitments already made. Camilla Born, who helped develop the UK's strategy for COP26 and now heads the campaign group Electrify Britain, told the BBC this is making COP more procedural - less about fundamental negotiations than ensuring the machinery actually works.
This could mean doing away with a cover text – the central political agreement that countries sign up to with new pledges.
It is not a requirement to have one, and for many years countries managed without. Australia chose to push one for this COP, and it is where they fell down.
On many of the procedural issues Camilla Bonn spoke of, they did agree things. That may be important. It isn't necessarily exciting.
And there is a fundamental limit to what this machinery can achieve. Under the Paris Agreement countries have no mechanism to force them to meet their emissions targets.

So, when critics berate the COP process for failing to tackle the problem fast enough, it isn't really the system that is at fault, says Alden Meyer, a veteran climate negotiator now at the climate think tank E3G.
The COP process, he suggests, is "like a mirror that we hold up to ourselves every year". If the reflection is disappointing, the problem is the governments, not the mirror.

articles.title: Rule-breaking is contagious — and good examples barely help
articles.summary: Seeing someone break a rule makes people more likely to break it too, a new study finds, especially when the rule-breaker is on their side politically. Watching others behave well barely made a…

image.caption: Image: Guo Lei/Xinhua/picture alliance

blocks.text: Most people stop at a red light, even when the road is empty. But what happens when the person next to them walks straight across?

A new study suggests they become more likely to follow. In an online experiment led by researchers at the University of Amsterdam, people who saw someone from their own political camp break a rule outright were nearly twice as likely to do the same. Seeing someone follow the rule barely made a difference.

A small number did more than copy. They broke the rule by more than the person they had watched. According to Lucas Molleman, an assistant professor of developmental psychology at the University of Amsterdam who led the research, a few bad actors like these can "basically take off the guardrails of the group."
How was the study done, and what are its limits?

The researchers wanted to know how seeing other people's choices affects whether someone sticks to a rule. They recruited 750 adults in the United States, roughly half Democrats and half Republicans, a week before the 2024 presidential election.

Participants watched an animated shooting star cross a row of 100 squares and were told to click the square where it shone brightest, which was always near the middle. Squares further to the right paid more money, so there was a reason to cheat.

Each person chose first on their own. They were then shown what a previous participant had done, whether that person had followed the rule, bent it or broken it outright, and which party they supported. Then they could change their answer. The task was repeated six times.

The experiment had no real-world stakes, and nobody was punished for cheating. Other researchers say that matters. "That's not how the world works," Eugen Dimant, a behavioral economist at the University of Pennsylvania who was not involved in the study, told Science News. Punishment and social pressure, he argues, also shape whether rule-breaking spreads.
Internet addiction: When life is only online
Is rule-breaking contagious?

Rule-breaking spread in the experiment. When people chose on their own, they picked the square furthest to the right, the most lucrative and most blatant violation, about 23% of the time. After seeing someone from their own party make that choice, they did so almost 40% of the time.
Small violations had only a small effect. Blatant ones had a much larger one.
Most people matched what they had seen or stayed below it. But just over 4% went further, breaking the rule by more than the person they had watched.
Do good role models make people follow rules?
Good examples had little effect. Seeing a previous participant stick to the rule rarely changed what others did, even when that person was from their own party.
People also differed. Some followed the rule every time and others broke it every time, whatever they saw. The rest shifted depending on what others had done.
Are people more likely to break rules when their own side does?
People were more likely to copy rule-breaking when it came from their own side. The effects were stronger when the person being watched shared the participant's political leanings.

Not everyone reads that as contagion. Stephen Reicher, a social psychologist at the University of St Andrews in Scotland who was not involved in the study, told The Guardian that if influence depends on who the other person is, it does not spread the way a disease does. He pointed out that people who see a riot often turn up afterwards to help clean up.
Can a few bad apples spoil the whole group?
To see how individual choices might add up, the researchers ran computer simulations. They created a digital version of each participant and placed them in groups of 100.

In some scenarios, the handful of people prone to escalating pushed the whole group towards heavy rule-breaking. But when the simulated groups contained the same share of committed rule followers as the real experiment, rule-breaking leveled off at a moderate level.
What does this mean in real life?
Molleman calls the work fundamental science and says the real world is far more complex. He sees possible links to situations such as drivers speeding together, or protests that turn violent.

He also says it challenges how people see themselves. In individualist cultures such as the Netherlands and the UK, he said that people tend to believe they make their own decisions. But "in many, many cases we are very much influenced by what others are doing."
This article is an excerpt from our podcast Science Unscripted.

articles.title: Maguindanao massacre victims' kin urge CA to resolve pending appeals
articles.summary: Families of the Maguindanao massacre victims on Monday renewed their appeal to the Court of Appeals (CA) to resolve pending appeals in the 2009 case, including those involving civil damages and the…

blocks.text: Published November 23, 2026 2:09pm

Families of the Maguindanao massacre victims on Monday renewed their appeal to the Court of Appeals (CA) to resolve pending appeals in the 2009 case, including those involving civil damages and the legal recognition of photojournalist Reynaldo “Bebot” Momay as the 58th victim.
Lawyer Gilbert Andres, executive director of the Center for International Law (CenterLaw) Philippines, filed an 11-page second motion for resolution before the CA on behalf of 19 families.

“Seventeen years na po silang naghihintay, ‘yung iba po ay namatay na po, ‘yung iba po ay naghihintay na sa kanilang mga beds, ‘yung iba po ay may mga sakit na po kaya hindi po sila namin kasama,” Andres told reporters.
(They have been waiting for 17 years. Some have already passed away, others are bedridden, and some are ill, which is why they could not join us today.)
“Kaya sila po ay nagsusumamo at talagang nanghihingi sa ating kagalang-galang na Court office na talagang agaran na po desisyunan lahat po ng pending appeals sa Court of Appeals,” he added.
(That is why they are appealing and earnestly asking the honorable court to immediately decide on all pending appeals before the Court of Appeals.)
The motion was filed on the 17th anniversary of the Nov. 23, 2009 massacre, the deadliest election-related violence in Philippine history.
The attack also remains the deadliest single incident targeting journalists worldwide, with 32 journalists and media workers among the 58 people killed.
The victims’ families also renewed their appeal for Momay to be officially recognized as the 58th victim of the massacre.
The Quezon City Regional Trial Court had acquitted the accused of Momay’s murder and dismissed his family's claim for civil damages.
Momay’s body was never recovered. The only physical evidence linked to him found at the crime scene was a set of dentures.
Earlier on Monday, Chief Justice Rodil Zalameda urged the CA to resolve the pending appeals in the case, saying justice should not be delayed further after 17 years.

“I therefore urge the Court of Appeals to resolve the pending appeals with dispatch, consistent with due process and rights of all parties. Let us ensure that justice is not delayed any further,” Zalameda said.
Andres welcomed the chief justice’s call, saying it reinforced the families’ appeal for the CA to act on the long-pending cases.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Chief justice to CA: Resolve pending appeals in Ampatuan massacre now
articles.summary: During the Supreme Court’s Flag Ceremony on Monday, November 23, Zalameda called on the appellate court to “resolve the pending appeals with dispatch.”

blocks.text: November 23, 2026 | 1:44pm
Police investigators look for evidence next to a backhoe after a vehicle and human remains were dug up from a shallow grave in the town of Ampatuan, Maguindanao in a Nov. 25, 2009 file photo.
AFP, File
MANILA, Philippines — Chief Justice Rodil Zalameda has urged the Court of Appeals to resolve the ongoing appeals related to the Ampatuan massacre.
Speaking at the Supreme Court’s flag ceremony on Monday, November 23 — the 17th anniversary of the killings — Zalameda urged the appellate court to “resolve the pending appeals with dispatch.”
“As we speak of protecting those who stand for justice, we must also remember the victims of the Ampatuan Massacre, whose 17th anniversary we commemorate today,” Zalameda said.

“The victims and their families have waited long enough. I therefore urge the Court of Appeals to resolve the pending appeals with dispatch, consistent with due process and rights of all parties. Let us ensure that justice is not delayed any further,” he added.
Meanwhile, the Center for International Law has filed an urgent motion before the Court of Appeals seeking the immediate resolution of pending appeals in the Ampatuan massacre cases.
The motion also reiterates the call for judicial recognition of Reynaldo “Bebot” Momay as the 58th victim of the massacre.

Background on the case. The tragedy, also named the Maguindanao massacre, took place on Nov. 23, 2009, leaving 58 people dead — including 32 journalists — as they traveled to file the certificate of candidacy of Esmael Mangudadatu.
On Dec. 19, 2019, Quezon City Regional Trial Court Branch 221 convicted the Ampatuan brothers of 57 counts of murder and sentenced them to reclusion perpetua without parole.

Twenty-eight co-accused, including police officers, were convicted of 57 counts of murder and sentenced to 40 years in prison, while 15 others were sentenced to six to 10 years as accessories. Fifty-five individuals, including Datu Sajid Islam Ampatuan, were acquitted.

articles.title: Israel’s destruction of Gaza has created a ‘toxic wasteland’, experts find
articles.summary:
Scientific and satellite findings warn of widespread contamination in Gaza, posing grave threats to public health ‘for generations to come’

Israel’s destruction of Gaza has left a…

blocks.text: Israel’s destruction of Gaza has left a devastating environmental legacy with poisoned water, contaminated soil and toxic air threatening the life-support systems that the population depends on for survival, according to a report.

Israel’s military assault has created widespread contamination across the entire strip, the report by Oxfam and the Conflict and Environment Observatory (Ceobs) finds, with heavy metals, explosive residues, asbestos from destroyed buildings, and sewage making the air, soil and water dangerous for Palestinians for decades to come.

Oxfam International’s executive director, Amitabh Behar, said: “Israel’s ongoing genocide in Gaza includes military assaults on its environment, which are environmental war crimes threatening life now and for generations to come.”

He said the “destruction and contamination of Gaza” have “fundamentally degraded the environmental conditions necessary for human safety and survival” and breach Israel’s legal obligations under international humanitarian and human rights law.

“Palestinians living in Gaza are being exposed to toxins … through air, food, water and via direct contact with contaminated soils and debris. These risks will persist for generations to come, unless clean-up, remediation and recovery actions are prioritised.”

blocks.caption: Land bulldozed by Israeli forces near the Nuseirat refugee camp in central Gaza last week. Photograph: Omar Ashtawy/HL/Getty

blocks.text: In 2025 and earlier this year, the UN independent international commission of inquiry found that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza and that Israeli officials, including the prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, incited these acts. The Israeli mission in Geneva said Israel rejected the commission’s “libellous sham”. Netanyahu is separately wanted by the international criminal court (ICC) for war crimes.

Oxfam’s report gives the most comprehensive picture to date of what it calls the “toxic wasteland” created by the Israeli assault which has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians and wounded at least 175,000, while thousands still remain unaccounted for under the rubble.

Using satellite imagery, remote sensing, scientific analysis and other open-source data, it concludes contamination in Gaza is “widespread, severe and consequential, with serious implications for public health and civilian survival”.

Behar said: “It is horrifying to begin to understand the extent of toxic contamination being faced by the population, who can neither escape nor protect themselves properly from the dangers. In an area as small, oppressed and densely populated as Gaza, continuous exposure is inevitable, with people surrounded by waste and sewage, spreading pests and the risk of disease growing.
“Raw sewage is pouring into the sea and leaking into the ground, while the destruction of Gaza’s sanitation systems leaves people with little protection from the contamination around them.”

blocks.caption: Displaced Palestinians living near a rubbish-filled sewage waste flow in Gaza City. The destruction of sanitation systems leaves people with little protection from contamination. Photograph: Ahmad Hasaballah/Getty

blocks.text: He added the “associated health consequences will be severe, with children and pregnant women among those facing the highest risks”.

The UN Environment Programme (UNEP) estimates that Israel’s military operations have generated more than 61m tonnes of debris across the territory, turning Gaza’s destroyed homes, neighbourhoods and infrastructure into a vast reservoir of potentially hazardous materials.

The report’s author, Lama Abdul Samad, a global water and sanitation specialist at Oxfam, said tackling the environmental damage in Gaza will be “highly challenging because contamination is dispersed across the urban rubble, farmland, water systems and soils, while unexploded ordnance continues to restrict safe access to most areas”.

blocks.caption: Children walk past an unexploded missile at a Gaza City rubbish dump. Photograph: Majdi Fathi/NurPhoto/Shutterstock

blocks.text: “The analysis highlights the urgent need for Israel to grant access for a detailed environmental assessment on the ground to clarify the risks to public health and identify options for urgent harm-reduction measures. Restoration is likely to require extensive clearance, monitoring and specialised remediation of affected areas from contaminants such as explosive residues, organic pollutants and heavy metals.”
Behar said that as international attention increasingly turned to Gaza’s reconstruction, environmental recovery must not be treated as an afterthought, but as a vital undertaking in parallel.
“Rebuilding Gaza without simultaneously understanding and addressing the extent of environmental contamination risks creating long-term public health consequences for generations to come,” he said.
The Israeli government has been contacted for comment.

articles.title: San Francisco is enjoying an AI boom, but worries about a crash are growing
articles.summary: AI employees in the industry's epicentre - San Francisco - worry that the sector is overheated.

blocks.text: Leading AI firms OpenAI and Anthropic – which have been hiring top engineering talent, often on eye-popping salaries – are based here. Anthropic, the company behind the Claude chatbot, last week listed on New York's Nasdaq stock exchange.
Thousands of other AI start-ups have also sprung up, external in San Francisco.
Signs of the boom are evident in soaring rents and house prices, falling office vacancies, and buses and billboards plastered with cryptic AI adverts.

But what if there is a significant downward correction in AI share prices and a resulting big fall in investment in the industry? The International Monetary Fund last month became the latest organization to warn, external that this was a possibility.

Concerns have since continued due to the scandal surrounding Jensen Huang, the former boss of AI firm Nvidia, based south of San Francisco, causing some wider AI stock falls. However, Nvidia remains highly profitable, and Wednesday of this week it reported that its latest quarterly profits had doubled from a year earlier to $65bn (£49bn).
What are the thoughts of AI workers in the city, and should San Francisco – no stranger to tech's boom-and-bust cycles – be preparing for a possible crash?

One AI worker, employed by one of the largest companies in the city, is convinced that a crash is coming. "I am certain that the house of cards will come down… and I'm sure it will affect me," says the man who asked that we didn't use his name.
He questions whether leading US AI companies can generate enough revenues to justify their enormous spending commitments as cheaper, increasingly capable AI models emerge, especially from China.
But he isn't losing sleep over it. "Why worry about things I can't control?"
Another San Francisco-based AI worker, who also asked to remain anonymous, says that a significant market correction is "totally possible".

Yet he adds that most people don't think of it as the core risk. Instead, he says that the bigger concern in his circles, and the one he shares, is the existential risk that AI could pose to humanity.
"In some weird way, a market correction being the worst-case outcome feels great."
If there is an AI crash, San Francisco could be hit far more than Silicon Valley which lies 40 miles to its south.
That's because the AI boom is very much centred on the city itself rather than the wider San Francisco Bay Area, which includes Silicon Valley.

One study, external found that 60% of all venture capital invested in US AI firms from 2023 to 2025 went to the companies located in San Francisco, dwarfing the significantly smaller percentage given to companies in Silicon Valley.
But some factors suggest that the impact of a crash in San Francisco may be softer than some fear.
For all the investment they have attracted, AI companies are employing relatively few workers in the city compared to previous tech booms. So there may not be that many jobs to lose in a downturn.

"Hiring isn't necessarily on the scale as we would have thought with the amount of venture capital and new company formation," says Jeff Bellisario, executive director of the Bay Area Council Economic Institute, a business-affiliated think tank.

Ted Egan, the chief economist for the City and County of San Francisco, adds that "because of AI, it is a good time for tech again in the city, but we are not seeing tonnes of overall tech job growth".
Despite the expansion of the AI sector, the city remains about 35,000 jobs shy of its pre-pandemic peak, estimates Enrico Moretti, an economics professor at the University of California, Berkeley.

Instead, much of the spending by AI firms in the US is going towards data centres and computing power, relatively little of which are located in the Bay Area. San Francisco might be the brains of the AI boom, but it isn't the brawn.

Nonetheless, a significant correction could still be "very painful" for San Francisco, warns Moretti. Less AI hiring and potential layoffs would ripple through the local service sector, likely to affect jobs in everything from restaurants, to retail, to personal services like dog walking.
"It is the spillover on service jobs that would actually be the main effect," he says.
Office vacancies could also rise, reducing downtown foot traffic, while rents and house prices could weaken.

But AI isn't the only force driving San Francisco's recovery. Healthcare and tourism – which the city has been working to encourage, including by improving downtown safety and cleanliness – are also growing,, external which may help cushion against a possible AI downturn.
"Tourism is not fully back, but the growth has been healthy," says Egan, adding that it is a sign of confidence in San Francisco.
All told, Egan doesn't expect an AI crash to fundamentally alter San Francisco's economic trajectory.

"The city's economy has not been screaming during this AI boom, so I wouldn't expect it to grind to a halt if there was a slowdown in AI spending," he says. "I think of it primarily as a hiccup that we should expect, rather than a major course correction for the city's economy."

As to whether and how San Francisco's city government should prepare, there are limits to what it can do, note Bellisario and Moretti. But encouraging growth in sectors beyond technology and maintaining financial reserves could help.

For Goldboss, the dog-walking company owner, her philosophy is to "build while it is here". If the next tech bust comes – "always a reality in San Francisco" – she will try to adapt to what the market needs. "It is just the risk you kind of have to take," she says.

articles.title: Lacson challenges Marcos' Iran reason for economic slowdown
articles.summary: The Iran war hit the whole ASEAN. But Lacson asks, why did Philippine growth fall further?

blocks.text: November 23, 2026 | 7:30am
Composite image shows Sen. Ping Lacson at a Senate hearing on Oct. 23, 2026 and President Bongbong Marcos at an ASEAN event on Nov. 17, 2026.
Lacson office; ASEAN PH; Philstar.com composite

MANILA, Philippines — Sen. Ping Lacson rejected President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.'s attempt to trace the Philippines' economic difficulties entirely to the Iran conflict, pointing to faster growth in other Southeast Asian countries.

"With all due respect Mr. President, blaming the US-Iran conflict will not suffice. Our ASEAN neighbors face the same oil-price pressures, yet Vietnam's GDP rises to 9.95%, Indonesia is steady at 5.47%, Singapore and Malaysia with 5.4% and 5.3% respectively," Lacson said Sunday, November 22.
The Philippine economy, in comparison, grew by 2.1% in the third quarter, slowing from 2.4% in the previous three months, according to the Philippine Statistics Authority.
Lacson was responding to Marcos' defense of his economic managers after the senator urged the administration to reassess their performance.
"All the difficulties we're going through can be clearly directly traced to the war in Iran," Marcos said November 20 at a press conference in Shenzhen, China.

The senator said, however, he wasn't seeking a change in the Cabinet's composition. His call, he said, was for the administration to reconsider the policies behind an economy that is slowing more sharply than those of several regional peers.
"Our growth is lowest at 2.1% and still decelerating. I did not posit a cabinet reshuffle, but a long hard look at our economic team to revisit some of our economic policies," he added.

The country's economic weaknesses extended beyond what is directly attributed to oil prices. Agriculture, forestry and fishing contracted by 4.8%, while industry was virtually flat. Gross capital formation, a measure of investment, declined by 0.2%.
Household consumption, traditionally the economy's main engine, grew by only 2.4%.
More than an external shock. The Iran conflict has nevertheless inflicted visible economic damage by raising energy and transport costs.

Headline inflation accelerated to a three-year high of 7.8% in October from 7.2% in September. Transport prices rose 20.1% from a year earlier, while housing, water, electricity, gas and other fuels increased by 9.3%.
But the administration's own economic planners have identified a broader set of pressures.
In July, the Development Budget Coordination Committee cited governance-related concerns and weaker business and consumer confidence alongside geopolitical tensions.
It also warned that high inflation could restrain consumption and investment, while slower remittances, weaker visitor arrivals and El Niño could further depress growth.
The DBCC cut its 2026 growth projection to between 3.5% and 4.5%, reflecting both domestic and external risks.

articles.title: Turkey: Thousands protest closure of critical media outlets
articles.summary: Protesters gathered in Istanbul to show their support for press freedom in Turkey. The protest was called just days after the police raided Sozcu TV and arrested several senior staff members.

image.caption: Protesters' placards read in Turkish: "No to trustee takeovers!" and "Where did all those truckloads of money go?"Image: Emrah Gurel/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Several thousand people in Istanbul took to the streets on Sunday to protest the closure of several opposition-linked media outlets in Turkey.
Protesters chanted, cheered, and whistled as they marched several kilometers through the city, calling for press freedom and freedom of expression.

They carried a huge banner that read: "We want freedom of thought, freedom of the press, and freedom for journalists." The protesters were also carrying placards that read, "The press cannot be silenced."

blocks.caption: Protesters held up copies of the opposition newspaper SozcuImage: Emrah Gurel/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: What sparked the protests?
Turkey's main opposition party, Yeni Parti, called for a protest just days after police raided Sozcu TV, one of the last opposition-aligned television channels.
Senior staff members were arrested during the raid. A government-appointed trustee was installed, and the TV company was placed under compulsory administration.
It was the third takeover in a year following similar actions against Tele1, Halk TV, Turkey's most-watched news channel, and the leading digital news website, T24.
Timur Soykan, a journalist who was briefly detained for criticizing the government, said that the government was doing everything in its power to silence journalists but was failing to do so.
Soykan asked the public to support Halk TV journalists, who plan to continue broadcasting on a new YouTube channel.
Increasing crackdown on critical media in Turkey
Over the past decade, press freedom has faced sustained pressure in the form of prosecutions, digital censorship, and government accusations that journalists are spreading "fake news."

In the last two months alone, Turkey has arrested several journalists for their reporting on a multibillion-dollar investment fund scandal. At least two of the journalists remain in pretrial detention.
According to the media rights group MLSA, twenty-five journalists are currently imprisoned in Turkey.
This year, Reporters Without Borders ranked Turkey 163rd out of 180 countries in its Press Freedom Index.

articles.title: Democrats win largest House majority since 1992 after flipping North Carolina seat
articles.summary: Democrats have now won at least 258 seats in the midterms compared to Republicans, who hold at least 173 seats.

blocks.text: The Democratic Party has won the largest majority in the US House of Representatives since 1992, after Democrat Chuck Hubbard unseated Republican Representative Virginia Foxx in North Carolina.
The race was called on Sunday, with Hubbard beating Foxx by 330 votes with 99% counted. It was one of the closest contests of the recent midterm elections, in which Democrats also secured the Senate.
The party has now won at least 258 House seats in the midterms compared to Republicans, who hold at least 173 seats, with four races still yet to be called.
Neither party had won as many House races since 1992, when Bill Clinton won the presidency and Democrats won a total of 258 seats.

items: View the 2026 midterm election results

blocks.text: Sunday's result came after Foxx, who has represented North Carolina's 5th Congressional District since 2005, requested a recount. This is allowed under state law when the margin of victory is under 1%.

She conceded on Sunday, saying in a statement: "After running a campaign focused on my track record of commonsense solutions and conservative values, I'm humbled and grateful that so many North Carolina voters responded by supporting my candidacy, even if we came up just a few votes short."
Hubbard, meanwhile, wrote on X that he had spoken to Foxx, "who graciously conceded following the results of the recount process".

He added: "I deeply appreciate her commitment to a smooth transition of the office and constituent casework. We may not always agree, but we both love North Carolina and the people of the Fifth District."

Hubbard's win, which comes after he lost to Foxx in the 2024 midterms by nine percentage points, followed a number of Democratic victories in deeply Republican districts including South Carolina, Texas, Alaska and Iowa.
Hubbard, like many Democrats running in the midterms, focused on the rising cost of living in the US during the war with Iran - a top issue for voters.
President Donald Trump himself has suggested inflation caused by the war in Iran was probably to blame for the Republican losses, as well as Vice President JD Vance.
Hubbard has also said he will also prioritise working families and small businesses, supporting public education and expanding access to affordable healthcare, according to his website.

The remaining House races yet to be called are in Tennessee and Minnesota, while two elections in Louisiana will go to a runoff in December. In Tennessee's fourth district, Democrat Victoria Broderick leads by fewer than 300 votes, and in Minnesota's first district, Democrat Jake Johnson is winning by fewer than 500 votes.

Democrats may use their upcoming majority in the House and control of the Senate to investigate conflicts of interest and other actions by the president and those close to him, while the Senate also has the power to confirm or block the president's cabinet and judicial nominations. They will also be able to pass legislation through Congress easily, though Trump still has to give final sign off for it to become law.
However, even with control of both chambers of Congress, they will still have limits on their power as Trump can veto legislation.

image.caption: The house was reduced to rubble by a drone strikeImage: Marwan Ali/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: The United Nations reported on Sunday a drone attack on a residential area in Khartoum, Sudan's capital.
A UN building located in a civilian neighborhood was damaged in the attack, according to the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA).
"It is unacceptable that we are put at such risk," said the UN's Resident and Humanitarian Coordinator in Sudan, Denise Brown.
What do we know about the attack?
The AFP news agency reported that explosions were heard around Khartoum Airport and in other parts of the city from approximately 2:00 a.m. to 4:30 a.m. local time.
According to a witness, a drone strike completely destroyed a house. There were no immediate reports of casualties.
Meanwhile, a Sudanese army source said the drones had been launched from Ethiopia.
Sudan has repeatedly accused Ethiopia of allowing attacks to be launched from its territory. However, Addis Ababa has denied these accusations.
Sudan's civil war — the limits of humanitarian aid
Drone strikes are intensifying in Sudan

Sudan has been engulfed in a civil war since April 2023. The army of de facto ruler Abdel-Fattah al-Burhan and the RSF militia led by Mohamed Hamdan Daglo have been fighting for control of the country.
The conflict has killed tens of thousands of people and displaced more than 14 million.
According to UN data, the use of drones has dramatically altered the course of the war this year, killing more than 1,100 people in the first six months.
The UN also said that of the hundreds of child casualties this year, two-thirds were killed or injured by drone strikes.
Just days ago, a Sudanese army drone strike killed 15 people, including four children, in a West Kordofan village. The army was advancing through the state and recapturing territory from the RSF.
